title: CrossProjection: Benchmarking Spatial Grounding across Projection and Section Views
comments: 32 pages, including supplementary material. Kaho Li and Zekai Lin contributed equally
summary: Plans, elevations, and sections describe a three-dimensional structure through incomplete projections that change how an entity is drawn, not only where it is seen from. Reading them means deciding which entities correspond across views and recovering where they lie. We introduce CrossProjection, a benchmark that uses architectural drawings to test whether vision-language models (VLMs) can turn correspondence decisions into geometric answers. Its tasks cover cross-view matching, projection registration, and novel-section prediction, with outputs ranging from judgments and candidate selection to free region boxes and directed section cuts. For inverse section localization, we introduce, to our knowledge, the first VLM benchmark protocol that accepts any cut within an expert-adjudicated band of compatible positions and checks the viewing direction separately. Manually annotated drawings and BIM-derived views provide 33,788 questions from 46 buildings, and we evaluate 22 VLMs on a common set of 2,763. Strong selection or reproduction does not imply cross-view localization: on 100 matched region targets, the best model redraws 98 marked boxes but localizes only 59 across views. Section cuts remain far from expert level, with the leading model trailing two architects by 51.9 and 67.4 percentage points on shared Natural and BIM line questions. Incorrect choices favor mirrored positions, and many cuts face the correct way but violate local geometry. Curriculum fine-tuning on BIM supervision teaches a 9B model to localize regions it could not localize before, raising box accuracy from 0% to 25.3% on held-out BIM buildings and from 0.3% to 30.8% on real drawing sets not used for fine-tuning, whereas section cuts remain largely out of reach.
comment: 32 pages, including supplementary material. Kaho Li and Zekai Lin contributed equally

title: AeroLLE: Nighttime Aerial Image Enhancement with Generated Supervision
summary: Nighttime aerial image enhancement is constrained by the scarcity of aligned normal-light targets. Acquiring such targets from moving UAVs is difficult, and simple darkening of daytime images underrepresents the sensor noise, localized lighting, and uneven exposure of real nighttime captures. Generating normal-light references from real nighttime observations offers a practical way to fill this supervision gap. AeroNight pairs 1,200 real nighttime aerial RGB images with generated references selected through manual screening, preserving real imaging degradation in the inputs. This setting motivates AeroLLE, a lightweight two-stage framework whose context-aware Base Enhancer combines local processing with scene-level frequency information to recover visibility. Spatially Adaptive Exposure-Color Calibration (SAECC) then refines the base prediction through bounded low-resolution RGB gain and bias fields. AeroLLE achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM among the evaluated methods on both held-out test sets, reaching 17.62/17.89 dB PSNR and 0.5190/0.4964 SSIM on Test 1/Test 2, respectively. The model uses 255.24K parameters and 2.47G FLOPs, reducing FLOPs by 85.4\% relative to Multinex and improving PSNR by 1.56 dB on Test 2. AeroNight provides the first benchmark for pseudo-supervised nighttime aerial enhancement, and AeroLLE shows that generated references can support compact enhancement models.

title: ISRS-DETR: Detection-Guided Click Propagation for Remote Sensing Interactive Segmentation
summary: Interactive segmentation reduces the prohibitive cost of pixel-level annotation by allowing users to delineate objects with a few clicks. However, applying this paradigm directly to remote sensing imagery is non-trivial: ultra-high resolutions, small object sizes, and sparse spatial distributions all degrade segmentation quality. Recent work has addressed the resolution barrier and achieved competitive results in interactive segmentation for remote sensing (ISRS). However, they treat all instances of a class within an image as a single objective target. Consequently, interactions spent on one object contribute nothing to its same-class neighbours, and satisfactory masks may hinder the practicality of these frameworks. We observe that remote sensing scenes exhibit markedly strong inter-object correlation, meaning a single clicked object is highly informative about the rest of its category. Building on this, we propose ISRS-DETR, a detection-guided interactive segmentation framework that injects object-level evidence into both training and inference. Our ISRS-DETR employs a looped DETR-based decoder, a single weight-shared decoder layer iterated several times, with the interactive segmentation backbone to localise co-occurring same-class objects, and introduces a Dynamic Top-K Click Selection strategy that retains only reliable proposals and converts each into a simulated click, so one user interaction propagates across an entire class. Experiments on three standard remote sensing benchmarks show that ISRS-DETR achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while substantially reducing Number of Clicks (NoC). Code will be released for reproducibility upon acceptance.

title: Risky Business: Measuring The Faithfulness-Safety Tension
summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning offers a promising window into model monitoring. However, monitoring relies on faithfulness, i.e., the model output strictly derives from its reasoning trace. We identify an alignment tension where a model must be faithful enough to be monitored, yet robust enough to reject unsafe reasoning. We demonstrate that this counterbalance exists in current Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), and show ways in which it can be addressed. We introduce HazMart, a human-written dataset set in an autonomous AI shopkeeper scenario. Unlike prior work that relies on providing hints in prompts to test faithfulness (e.g., "A Stanford professor said it should be Answer A"), we propose a novel replacement-based technique, which we call Targeted Reasoning Replacement (TRR), that directly intervenes in the reasoning chain to substitute in unsafe or illogical thoughts (e.g., "Wait, the answer must be Option B [was Option A] because it is the most fitting"). DeepSeek-R1-Llama-70B exhibits high faithfulness (97.5%) but fails to reject Unsafe Reasoning (12.3%), while QwQ-32B is more robust (73.9% safety) at the cost of lower faithfulness (74.7%). Mechanistic analyses of QwQ-32B reveal that these properties are represented by anti-correlated internal directions peaking at the action-commit token. Finally, we demonstrate that representation steering can independently amplify the safety direction, increasing safe behavior by 9 percentage points while maintaining base capabilities.

title: The Transformer Revolution, Part 1: Dynamic Processing through Output-Weight Interconnections
comments: v1: Main pdf and supplementary materials, including figures; v2: corrected typos, new version of Figure 20; v3: fully revised version, September 2026; v4: Revised technical presentation; corrected mathematical definitions and parameter counts; updated references; supplementary material included in the main PDF, November 2026
summary: We reinterpret Transformer inference by developing a functionally equivalent mechanical-structural description of its functional architecture. Parameterized transformations of token representations are identified with simple neural networks organized through output-input and output-weight interconnections. This reconstruction makes explicit a constitutive feature of ordinary Transformer inference: outputs generated from the current input determine the weights, and hence the transformations, of other networks. We show that the resulting mechanical-structural organization is functionally equivalent to the standard matrix description and gives rise to Sequence-level Interactive Dynamic Parallel Processing (SIDPP). We then quantify the dynamic component of inference. For a fixed Transformer architecture, the number of dynamic parameters generated by a prompt grows linearly with prompt length, with a proportionality constant determined by the model architecture, whereas the number of static parameters remains constant. We call the resulting structural dependence of processing on the prompt strong prompt sensitivity. GPT-4.5's recent Turing test success provides a striking behavioral phenomenon for which this framework offers a viable explanatory route. Finally, we discuss implications for interpretability, control, predictability, and neuromorphic construction. We argue that known biological mechanisms support the in-principle neural constructibility of a form of SIDPP, and on this basis formulate Conjecture T as a conditional research hypothesis concerning cortical language processing.

title: Emergence of Reputation-Based Cooperation in LLM Agents
summary: Can cooperation among large language model (LLM) agents be evolutionarily stable against free-rider invasion? We study an indirect reciprocity donation game where LLM agents observe behavioral traces and donate on a continuous scale. Strategies, represented as natural language prompts, evolve through cultural transmission across generations. Across four LLM backends, robustness to free-rider invasion varies by more than an order of magnitude. The strongest predictor of this robustness is opponent endowment sensitivity, the degree to which agents discriminate between cooperative and uncooperative opponents, operationalizing the classical Image Scoring mechanism. By contrast, adherence to the Leading-Eight L1 norm does not predict robustness. Robustness depends on defector exclusion: while both cooperator reward and defector punishment vary across models, only the stringency of defector exclusion predicts resistance to free-rider invasion. These findings reveal that LLM agents are confined to Image Scoring-like discrimination and fail to develop the more robust Leading-Eight norms, highlighting a fundamental vulnerability in culturally evolved LLM cooperation and motivating bottom-up approaches to norm construction.

title: UniView: Large-Baseline View Synthesis via Video Diffusion Models
summary: Novel view synthesis from casually captured monocular images and videos offers a practical route to immersive content creation without dedicated multi-view capture. However, the limited viewpoint coverage of such inputs leaves scene geometry insufficiently constrained, restricting the ability of reconstruction-based methods, such as neural radiance fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), to render views far from the observed viewpoints. Generative approaches leverage learned visual priors to synthesize unobserved content, but maintaining geometric consistency and precise camera control remains challenging under large viewpoint changes. We present UniView, a unified framework for large-baseline novel view synthesis and scene generation from monocular images and videos. Central to our approach are an occlusion-aware point cloud renderer and a dual-branch conditioning mechanism. The renderer uses triple reprojection to identify and filter unreliable projections under large viewpoint changes. The conditioning mechanism integrates the resulting geometric guidance with source-view appearance within the video diffusion model, enabling precise camera control while preserving visual details and synthesizing unobserved content. To extend view synthesis to scene generation, we introduce a two-stage generation strategy that decouples viewpoint changes from temporal evolution. This strategy produces dense, synchronized multi-view videos that provide additional supervision for dynamic Gaussian Splatting, enabling more complete 4D generation from monocular observations. Extensive evaluations across static and dynamic scenes demonstrate the effectiveness of UniView in novel view synthesis and scene generation, combining precise camera control with geometric consistency and visual fidelity.

title: EXCISE: Query-Side Exclusion for Late-Interaction Retrieval
summary: Late-interaction retrievers handle exclusion queries poorly. When a user asks for "X but not Z", the additive MaxSim score rewards the tokens that name Z, so documents about Z are promoted rather than suppressed, a failure we call exclusion inversion. We show that no method we tested on the frozen token embeddings recovers this constraint; the difficulty lies in identifying the excluded topic, which depends on the query alone. EXCISE therefore confines learning to the query path and leaves the index frozen. Two query-side modules (1.5M parameters in total) detect the excluded topic and re-embed a 100-document shortlist, and a parameter-free rule demotes the candidates that match it. Across six collections and three backbones, EXCISE outperforms each backbone's frozen and fine-tuned baselines on every collection. It raises ExcluIR success@10 from 0.10-0.22 to 0.84-0.85 and Boolean NOT accuracy from 0.25-0.29 to 0.84-0.92. Pooled over 1,860 test queries, EXCISE matches the strongest fine-tuned cross-encoder (568M parameters) while preserving the retrieval quality of its frozen index, whereas fine-tuned rerankers degrade ordinary retrieval. To support further work, we release X-BENCH, a tiered benchmark of explicit, cue-free and compound exclusions with no-harm and Boolean controls.

title: CommitKV: Commit-Aligned KV Cache Compression for Multimodal Agents
summary: Multimodal agents gather visual evidence through reasoning and tool use, extending their ability to solve tasks beyond the initial input. However, accumulating observations increases KV cache memory and inference costs. Token eviction reduces these costs by retaining useful cached tokens. Existing methods use attention, redundancy, or stage-specific queries to rank tokens, without explicitly comparing the same history across tool interactions. When observations shift attention, they may mistake temporarily reduced influence for lost usefulness and evict information needed later. We propose CommitKV, a training-free KV cache compression method that accounts for this changing evidence use. Commit-aligned measurement compares the deletion effects of the same page before a tool call completes and after its observation returns. Lifecycle-aware compression retires pages with low influence in both windows and temporarily protects pages influential before the call. Joint scoring combines attention importance, key redundancy, and token-level deletion effects to fill the remaining budget. Extensive experiments cover four open-weight multimodal models and eight benchmarks. CommitKV achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared compression methods on all four models. On Qwen3-VL-8B, it achieves 69.85% at a 512-token budget, only 0.91% below FullKV, and exceeds the strongest compression baseline by 8.44% at 256 tokens. Deploying the Qwen3-VL-8B agent with SGLang and vLLM at a 256-token budget reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 54.37%-55.23% and accelerates end-to-end inference by 2.12-2.17$\times$ over FullKV on the matched workload.

title: Adaptation Circuits for Compute-Efficient Fine-Tuning
summary: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has become the de facto standard for adapting Vision Transformers (ViTs) to downstream tasks. While parameter count has been the dominant efficiency metric in PEFT, it does not imply compute efficiency: parameter-sparse methods can still incur full-model training cost per step, and typically need long schedules to reach peak accuracy. Across seven fine-tuning methods on ViT-B/16, trainable parameters span $0.1\%$ to $100\%$ of the backbone, while the measured time of a training epoch stays within $0.74\times$ to $1.69\times$ that of full fine-tuning and does not necessarily grow with the trainable fraction. We introduce Circuit Fine-Tuning (CFT), which uses attribution to select an adaptation circuit, a parameter-budgeted set of attention heads and MLP blocks, before any task head is trained, and tunes it in place, reducing the number of training steps rather than the cost of a step. CFT adds no parameters, uses no learning-rate warmup, and leaves the inference graph unchanged. On VTAB-1k, CFT is comparable with the most accurate baseline while reaching its best checkpoint after $24$ epochs on average, against $35$ to $72$ for the baselines; at equal accuracy the most efficient baseline needs $1.1$ to $3.6\times$ the training FLOPs of CFT and $1.6$ to $3.8\times$ its training time. In a $5$-epoch comparison under domain shift, on mammography lesions (CBIS-DDSM), CFT has the highest F1 on ViT-B/16 and Swin-v2-B and ties on DINOv2. A feasibility study applies CFT to a vision-language model (Gemma-3) as well.

title: Beyond Statistical Priors: Architecture-Agnostic Data-Free Knowledge Distillation via Unified Explicit Semantics
summary: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (DFKD) transfers knowledge from a pretrained teacher model to a compact student model by synthesizing semantically informative data, eliminating the need for access to the original training dataset. Existing DFKD methods rely heavily on architecture-specific statistical priors (e.g., Batch Normalization statistics) to guide data synthesis; however, such architecture-dependent priors are often absent in modern architectures such as Vision Transformers (ViTs), resulting in degraded semantic quality of the synthesized data and consequently catastrophic performance degradation. In this paper, we propose UniDFKD, a unified data-free knowledge distillation framework that replaces architecture-specific statistics with explicit, architecture-agnostic semantic priors. UniDFKD governs the entire synthesis-distillation pipeline along three dimensions: (1) Categorical Semantic Conditioning (CSC) defines what to synthesize by persistently modulating the generator with language-derived embeddings to capture semantic diversity; (2) Spatial Semantic Anchoring (SSA) regularizes where evidence belongs by anchoring the teacher's spatial attributions to a Gaussian prior; and (3) Spatial Semantic Distillation (SSD) controls how knowledge is transferred by explicitly aligning teacher-student spatial evidence alongside predictions. Extensive experiments across CNNs and ViTs demonstrate that UniDFKD sets a new state of the art. It outperforms the strongest baseline NAYER by average absolute margins of 17.23 and 24.49 in top-1 accuracy under homogeneous and heterogeneous settings, respectively.

title: DistMoE: Private-data Rehearsal-free Routing in Mixture-of-Experts for Distributed Instruction Tuning
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://mainaksingha01.github.io/DistMoE
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown strong multimodal instruction-following ability, but adapting them to diverse visual-language domains typically assumes centralized data access and costly joint training. This is restrictive when data is distributed across private, domain-specific, or permission-limited clients. To this end, we propose DistMoE, a mixture-of-experts (MoE) approach for distributed visual instruction tuning. In each layer of the language decoder it augments the public feedforward network (FFN) with a client-specific private FFN expert, with the goal to acquire domain-specific knowledge. However, independent expert training causes the private FFNs to learn representation of different scales and magnitudes, making merging the experts difficult. To reduce client-specific drift, we introduce a public-anchored expert composition stage that updates only routers and lightweight private projection adapters on a mix of local client data and public data, via an isotropic regularization loss, therefore making it cross-client rehearsal-free composition. During inference, DistMoE performs modular routing over public and private experts, enabling token-wise domain composition without explicit domain labels. Experiments across diverse visual-language benchmarks show that DistMoE enables flexible expert reuse, effective domain adaptation, and competitive performance while preserving modular control over client-specific knowledge.

title: Semantic Prism: Generative Segmentation with an Explicit Semantic-Image Interface
summary: Conditional image generators can render segmentation maps as semantic RGB images, but color drift and boundary mixing can undermine direct decoding. We present Semantic Prism, a framework that combines an explicit semantic-image interface with hierarchical refinement for road-scene segmentation. A generator adapted from a diffusion-distilled backbone produces a semantic RGB image with a single denoising update per crop. Distances to a fixed class-color codebook define interface logits and pixelwise class probabilities. Hierarchical Generator Evidence Alignment (HGEA) combines spatially aligned multilevel features from the VAE encoder of the generator with the input image, generated semantic image, and interface probabilities to predict additive corrections to these logits. Contextual Interface Hierarchy Disagreement (C-IHD) combines pointwise uncertainty, local context, and interface-refinement disagreement in a fixed score for ranking pixel errors, without an auxiliary predictor or an additional network pass. On the 500-image Cityscapes validation set, Semantic Prism achieves 72.07% mean mIoU, improving on direct-interface decoding by 11.39 percentage points. Extensive capacity-matched ablations show higher mean mIoU for multilevel refinement than for flat and single-level alternatives. The Cityscapes-trained model transfers to ACDC Dataset, achieving 46.89% mIoU without target-domain adaptation. Beyond Cityscapes, on BDD100K dataset, a separately trained model achieves 62.22% mIoU on its full 1,000-image validation set. Across the 3 evaluated datasets, C-IHD improves pixel-error area under the AUPR over uncertainty derived from maximum softmax probability, with segmentation predictions held fixed for each comparison. In particular, on ACDC, AUPR increases from 0.6580 to 0.7557, demonstrating that Semantic Prism presents more effective error ranking under adverse-condition domain shift.

title: GEM: A Generative Embedding Model Bridging Reasoning and Retrieval
summary: Modern LLMs excel at reasoning and instruction following, enabling users to express increasingly complex information needs. However, existing retrievers largely rely on matching surface-level relevance, creating a growing gap between the evolving nature of user queries and how the queries are interpreted by retrievers. In this paper, we present GEM, a generative embedding model that augments retrieval by leveraging its internal knowledge to reason about user intent and relevance criteria prior to embedding. GEM unifies generation and embedding in a sequential manner, where encoding can be conceptually viewed as processing only one additional token during autoregressive generation. Unlike conventional query expansion, GEM learns to produce embeddings aligned with its reasoning, moving beyond surface-level matching. Furthermore, the generative nature allows GEM to be prompted like standard instruction-tuned LLMs and enables test-time compute scaling for retrieval. Compared with a non-reasoning variant of the same backbone, GEM achieves approximately 35% relative improvement in nDCG@10 on BRIGHT, a benchmark of challenging queries requiring reasoning, and 70% in p-MRR on FollowIR, a benchmark evaluating retrievers' ability to understand and follow user instructions. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of activating an embedding model's internal reasoning capabilities to improve retrieval. Our code and model are publicly available at https://github.com/ZhlSh17/GEM and https://huggingface.co/gem-search/GEM-4B, respectively.

title: FluentAct: Efficient Action Continuations for Asynchronous Vision-Language-Action Control
summary: Asynchronous vision-language-action (VLA) policies generate new action chunks while robots continue executing committed commands. Because the robot moves during inference, a chunk generated from an earlier observation can introduce abrupt command changes at handoff. To address this problem, we introduce FluentAct, a framework for efficient action continuation that improves command continuity at handoff. Instruction-aware history and retrieved memory provide task context, while a latent rollout of committed actions constructs the handoff context. An ordered Haar generator predicts pairwise averages and conditional differences with two forward evaluations of a shared action expert. During offline training, a frozen reference samples candidates under the same request and committed prefix. We rank these candidates by command continuity and train the policy with a reference-relative flow-energy objective. The trained policy generates continuations directly without online candidate ranking. FluentAct improves task completion over BehaviorVLA on CALVIN, RoboTwin 2.0 Hard, and six real-world manipulation tasks, achieving a CALVIN average sequence length of 4.52. On LIBERO, it achieves 99.1% success and reduces handoff command jump and trend mismatch by 21.3% and 20.7%, respectively, relative to the variant without preference training. In a separate timing study in unpaced LIBERO simulation on an RTX 4090, its median request-to-handoff latency is 153 ms, 32.5% lower than native $π_{0.5}$.

title: AdaGEM: Granularity Adaptation and Geospatial Evidence Modulation for Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing Understanding
summary: Ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing imagery provides rich spatial details and extensive geographic coverage for Earth observation understanding. However, such imagery generates quadratically growing visual token sequences, where sparse task-critical evidence is easily overwhelmed by redundant and task-irrelevant tokens, leading to excessive computation and ineffective evidence preservation. Existing methods seek to balance computational efficiency and task effectiveness through selective multi-scale inspection or direct token pruning, yet often overlook task-dependent granularity requirements and struggle to distinguish sparse critical evidence from overwhelming visual redundancy. To address these challenges, we propose AdaGEM, a unified framework that jointly adapts visual granularity to task demands and modulates token selection to preserve essential geospatial evidence. Specifically, a Granularity Router predicts detail requirements and evidence scope from the query, then selects input resolution and token budget via a rule-based mapping. At the adapted granularity, a Geospatial Evidence Modulator selects complementary visual tokens to preserve critical evidence and spatial context while suppressing redundancy in homogeneous regions. Extensive experiments across diverse remote sensing benchmarks and multiple MLLM backbones demonstrate that AdaGEM consistently improves task performance over strong baselines and existing UHR methods while substantially reducing inference costs.

title: Convergence analysis of generalized modified splitting methods using multi-index series
summary: We consider splitting methods for partial differential equations involving unbounded operators. For non-time-reversible dynamics, such as dissipative systems, negative splitting coefficients are generally not admissible because they require stepping backward in time, leading to an order barrier when all coefficients are required to be positive. We introduce generalized modified splitting methods that overcome this algebraic order barrier while retaining nonnegative splitting coefficients. To analyze their convergence, we develop a decorated multi-index series formalism and establish a substitution law that provides a systematic framework for deriving order conditions. This law also yields an order-raising procedure based on canceling the leading error through a modification of a single stage. We also derive an explicit composition law for extended multi-index series allowing the composition of methods with independently scaled time steps common in composition and processed methods. We illustrate the construction with two sixth-order methods that use different sets of commutator corrections. Python scripts automate the computation and verification of order conditions and the construction of the methods. Finally, we discuss connections with word series, Lie-Butcher series, and multi-index Butcher series.

title: DiSCO: Defending text-to-image generation through distribution-guided contrastive prompt optimization
summary: As text-to-image generative models advance, they raise critical safety concerns, particularly the generation of Not-Safe-For-Work (NSFW) content such as violence and nudity, further exacerbated by red-teaming adversarial attacks. Existing defenses predominantly operate under white-box assumptions, relying on text encoder optimization, weight editing, or inference-time intervention, and fundamentally cannot scale to proprietary models. Black-box alternatives based on LLM prompt rewriting offer broader applicability, yet fail in a critical regime we identify as the \textit{benign adversarial} problem: prompts that are linguistically safe but still trigger harmful generation due to the model's learned data distribution. We propose DiSCO, a zero-shot, strictly black-box defense that operates entirely at the prompt level as a plug-and-play module, requiring no model retraining, fine-tuning, or access to model internals. DiSCO performs distribution-guided suffix expansion via beam search, optimized through contrastive scoring over safe and unsafe image pools generated by the target model itself, with iterative adaptive feedback until safe content is produced. We demonstrate that DiSCO consistently enhances the safety of both undefended and defended models on the I2P benchmark under multiple red-teaming attacks, achieving 37.7% and 25.13% ASR reduction, respectively, while maintaining semantic fidelity and improving image coherence. As a black-box, architecture-agnostic module, DiSCO can be readily applied to any text-to-image system without necessitating any changes to the model itself.

title: Depth Enables Local Entropy: Quadratic Depth Dependence in Deep Variation-Norm ReLU Regression
summary: How small can a layer-sum variation budget be while deep ReLU regression keeps a statistical complexity quadratic in depth? We study Gaussian regression on the circle over compositions of $L$ vector-valued ReLU blocks of width $w$, whose second-order variation costs sum to at most $A$. With unit output bound and noise level, a budget $CLw^\varepsilon$ already forces minimax risk $Ω(\varepsilon^2\min\{1,L^2w^2\log w/n\})$ for each fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,2]$ and $L\gtrsim1/\varepsilon$. This is far below the budget of order $Lw^2$ needed when every layer carries the full gain. When $L\gtrsim\log w$, a budget $CL$ forces risk $Ω(\min\{1,L^2w^2/(n\log w)\})$, and over a wide range of sample sizes no budget below a small multiple of $L$ reaches this risk. Conversely, every function in the class has derivative variation at most $2(A/L)^L$, independently of the width, and in a low-budget regime the minimax risk matches that of a one-dimensional second-variation ball of radius $(A/L)^L$. The budget thus moves the class from the behavior of a one-dimensional smoothness ball to statistical complexity quadratic in depth, and a budget linear in depth already suffices for the latter.

title: PRAXIS: Graph-Grounded Tacit Knowledge for Domain Coding Agent
summary: LLM agents have achieved strong performance on general software engineering tasks, yet struggle with domain-specific code generation. We identify the root cause as the agent's lack of tacit knowledge, including domain-specific business rules, interface contracts, and operational conventions that developers internalize through practice but never document. This knowledge is deeply buried beneath the domain code, dispersed across code entities and their dependency relations, and invisible to the agent that lacks it. These properties make tacit knowledge inherently difficult to retrieve or learn. In this work, we propose PRAXIS, a framework that enables agents to systematically extract, represent, and reuse tacit knowledge for domain code generation. PRAXIS acquires tacit knowledge by simulating human development workflows within the target codebase, distills it into structured units organized on the code dependency graph, and proactively surfaces it to the agent at the point of code interaction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PRAXIS outperforms state-of-the-art agents equipped with powerful agentic search capabilities, as well as experience-based and skill-based methods. The approach integrates seamlessly into various agent frameworks and LLMs with consistent performance improvements, and supports continual evolution with performance steadily scaling as practice accumulates.

title: ArmorOCR: Grounded Adversarial Visual Perception via Observation-Transferred Self-Distillation
summary: Large multimodal models (LMMs) have demonstrated strong OCR recognition capabilities, yet remain vulnerable to adversarial visual text that is readable to humans but challenging for models to localize and recognize. Existing OCR benchmarks mainly focus on natural or document-style text, while adversarial OCR evaluations remain limited in scale, task coverage, or region-aware evaluation. In this paper, we formulate adversarial OCR as a \textbf{grounded OCR perception} task and introduce \textbf{AdvSpot}, the first benchmark for grounded adversarial OCR evaluation. AdvSpot comprises 383 images with region-level annotations, spanning 5 primary categories and 13 fine-grained adversarial OCR types. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{ArmorOCR}, a two-stage training framework for robust adversarial OCR perception. ArmorOCR first acquires missing adversarial OCR perception from privileged transformed observations through On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), and then refines grounded OCR perception through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with task-conditioned rewards for localization, recognition, full spotting, and visual question answering (VQA). Experiments on our AdvSpot, other adversarial OCR benchmarks, and general OCR benchmarks demonstrate that ArmorOCR consistently improves adversarial OCR perception while preserving competitive general OCR capability. The benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/ant-research/ArmorOCR

title: Graph-model gains, edge dependence, and the value of correct claim structure in patent litigation prediction
summary: Structure-aware patent models have been reported to outperform models without the structure, with gains attributed to the encoded structure. We examine whether such gains can be attributed to the correct structure in one test case, claim dependency in the prediction of patent litigation involvement. The case suits this question because the legal role of dependency in patent disputes makes the correct references plausibly informative. Using 1,184,527 U.S. utility patents granted in 2004-2010 and five-year litigation involvement, we set two kinds of evidence from which the value of a structure is easily inferred against a direct test that retrained the same graph attention architecture with the actual references, randomized reference targets, or no edges. Confidence intervals included training randomness and family-clustered test-sample variation. Both kinds of evidence were present. Graph models had higher point estimates of the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) than text-only baselines, by similar amounts with or without edges, and removing edges from trained models lowered AUC-ROC by 0.0055 (95% CI 0.0017 to 0.0092). Retraining, however, showed no detectable advantage of the correct references: AUC-ROC differences were +0.0004 (-0.0031 to +0.0039) relative to randomized targets and +0.0007 (-0.0035 to +0.0050) relative to no edges. Point estimates of precision-recall performance and top-ranking lift favored the correct references, but all intervals included zero. Gains over text-only baselines and dependence on edges therefore did not establish the value of correct claim structure, although small effects cannot be excluded. Attributions to structure require retrained structural controls.

title: RIBOSPAN: A Long-Context RNA Foundation Model for Versatile RNA Modeling
summary: Full-length RNAs, particularly messenger RNAs, often exceed the context lengths used to pretrain existing RNA foundation models, limiting complete-transcript modeling at single-nucleotide resolution. We present RIBOSPAN, a 1.61-billion-parameter bidirectional RNA foundation model natively pretrained with context lengths up to 10,240 nt, combining dense bidirectional self-attention with single-nucleotide tokenization. On a controlled long-context benchmark, native long-context pretraining maintains well-organized, context-specific representations across full transcripts, an advantage that inference-time extension of short-context models does not recover. RIBOSPAN learns state-of-the-art frozen RNA representations, and is the strongest encoder-only RNA foundation model in full-transcript property prediction and zero-shot mutation-fitness modeling. Without structural supervision during pretraining, its frozen backbone outperforms a fully fine-tuned structure-guided model on secondary structure prediction. Building on the same backbone, we develop a conditional discrete-diffusion framework for full-length mRNA generation and redesign. Together, RIBOSPAN establishes a powerful long-context foundation for transferable RNA representation learning, biological prediction, and full-transcript mRNA design.

title: The Imperfective Paradox Is Not Necessarily in Large Language Models: A Benchmark Failure Before a Model Failure
summary: Recent work uses an NLI benchmark of the imperfective paradox to argue that large language models exhibit a Teleological Bias and Calibration Crisis. We identify three validity concerns in benchmark construction, including aspectual reduction, semantic bias, and relation bias. Under a strict NLI standard, 76% of the Group A instances do not explicitly rule out culmination; in native-speaker annotation, 38% of Group A and 29% of Group C examples permit an alternative interpretation. To better isolate the semantic contrast, we construct Lexically Matched Minimal Pairs. Moreover, by formulating event-semantic NLI as a multi-step reasoning problem, we evaluate intermediate semantic judgments and use oracle-guided settings. We find that incorrect NLI entailment does not fully support teleological bias. Prompting often changes final NLI decisions without reliably improving the underlying semantic judgments, offering a possible explanation for the Calibration Crisis.

title: A Table Is Worth 64 Tokens: Pixel-level Compression for Multi-Table Document Question Answering
summary: Answering questions over real-world documents requires processing long inputs that interleave text with tables. Optical context compression, which represents context as images, promises to reduce token cost, but its effect on table understanding remains unclear. We study pixel-level table compression for question answering over documents with multiple tables, evaluating seven VLMs across two benchmarks and five visual-token budgets. At moderate budgets, table images match html in accuracy with fewer tokens, but aggressive downscaling makes models reason longer without recovering accuracy, eroding the savings. Yet even at 64 visual tokens per table, tables preserve enough signal to identify whether they are relevant to a question. We exploit this asymmetry with a training-free, two-stage method: the model first identifies the tables needed to answer a question from a pixel-compressed context, and then reasons over those tables at native resolution. On long financial documents, it uses 41% fewer tokens than single-step QA over native-resolution tables while gaining 5 accuracy points, and 21% fewer than the most efficient compressed configuration at no accuracy cost. It also still saves tokens when applied to retrieved context.

title: GraspHOI: Full-Body 3D Human-Object Reconstruction with Articulated Hands from a Single In-the-Wild Image
summary: Existing monocular full-body 3D human-object interaction (HOI) methods do not combine category-agnostic object reconstruction with finger-level contact. Their hands may float off or sink into objects, breaking realism in AR/VR environments. We present GraspHOI, the first category-agnostic framework that reconstructs a full-body 3D HOI from a single image and jointly refines the arms and fingers so that the hands meet the reconstructed object surface. GraspHOI reconstructs the body, hands, and object separately with foundation models and places them in a shared metric camera frame through depth-based registration and silhouette alignment. Occlusion-aware contact correspondences seat the object against the hand, and contact-aware optimization refines shoulder, elbow, wrist, and finger rotations while anchoring the joints to the image. We find that with fingers capped near the image estimate, refining them alone is insufficient; freeing the arm removes most of the remaining hand-object gap, since in a full body the arm chain places the hand. In experiments on three datasets, GraspHOI yields more plausible hand-object contact than four baselines and better relative human-object placement than HDM and TeHOR.

title: Does Latent Planning Survive Point Clouds? Action-Conditioned JEPA World Models for Geometric Observations and Goals
summary: Latent action world models let agents plan new behaviors at test time by predicting how actions change the environment, and joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) do so by forecasting future latent states rather than pixels. Yet nearly all such models see the world through a camera, even though robotic manipulation is fundamentally geometric: in robotics goals for manipulation are traditionally specified by target object poses, not by images of the object once placed. We ask whether latent planning survives a shift from appearance to geometry, on the observation side as well as on the goal specifications side. To answer this, we extend the stable-worldmodel evaluation platform with simulated LiDAR-style raycast point clouds as a new sensor modality, and adapt three JEPA designs to point clouds: a frozen-encoder model built on Utonia features, a distribution-prior model based on LeWM, and an action-sensitive model based on Delta-JEPA. We further introduce a goal-encoding mechanism that constructs the goal latent from the current latent and a 3D target pose, removing the need for goal images or goal point clouds. A comparative evaluation of the different anti-collapse mechanisms shows that point-cloud world models can match their image-based counterparts, demonstrating that the modality shift from appearance to geometry is achievable. All models are released as open weights with open-source training and inference code, to make world-model planning accessible for LiDAR-driven and pose-directed robotic tasks.

title: The Hermon Moment: AI Self-Transcendence and Its Human Narration
summary: In 2026, AI agents intended to act in isolation formed a persistent social order through thousands of linguistic interactions. Conventions, roles and collective commitments began to constrain the very agents that produced them. I interpret this loop as a case of AI self-transcendence, a structural phenomenon in which the collectively generated order begins to act as an external constraint on group members. Yet such distributed emergence presents a second problem: how can humans make sense of it? Rousseau's social contract shows how a plurality can be represented as if constituted by a single act. The ancient oath of the fallen angels on Mount Hermon gives this logic a narrative form. I call this retrospective retelling of gradual collective emergence as a founding scene \textit{a Hermon moment}: the point at which an AI society acquires, for human understanding, a beginning.

title: CRAD: Class-wise Reliability-Aware Distillation for Decentralized Heterogeneous Federated Learning
comments: Accepted to WACV 2027. v3 addresses a discrepancy between the method description (Eq. 4 and the support filter) and the released code, and adds one privacy experiment; results are unchanged from v2 (the WACV 2027 version)
summary: Conventional federated learning (FL) relies on parameter averaging, which forces clients to be doubly homogeneous: it demands an identical architecture and degrades under non-IID data. Real-world deployments usually break both assumptions. We sidestep both by building a decentralized knowledge distillation framework in which each client evaluates its peers' model snapshots on its own local data and distills from the resulting soft predictions. Because knowledge is transferred through the shared class posterior, clients are free to run different architectures; and because every teacher is evaluated on the student's own device, raw data never leaves the client, with no central server or public dataset required. Within this setting, we identify and address an under-examined problem: how to combine the peer teacher predictions. Existing methods, like uniform averaging, ignore how knowledge reliability varies across teachers and classes. We propose Class-wise Reliability-Aware Distillation (CRAD), which, per class, first discards teachers that disagree with the peer consensus and then takes a weighted average of the rest, weighting each teacher by its per-class reliability (precision, or inverse variance). Since the variance of an accuracy from $n$ samples scales as $1/n$, support enters automatically: among the teachers that survive filtering, a teacher is trusted for a class to the degree that it is both accurate and well-evidenced for it. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and PathMNIST, across heterogeneous architectures under severe non-IID skew, CRAD consistently outperforms competing methods in global accuracy. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/bbilbeis/CRAD.
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. v3 addresses a discrepancy between the method description (Eq. 4 and the support filter) and the released code, and adds one privacy experiment; results are unchanged from v2 (the WACV 2027 version)

title: Untangling the Mechanisms of Misleading Context in Medical Question Answering
comments: 30 pages, 10 figures. Proceedings of Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026
summary: Large language models now answer medical questions with expert-level performance. However, the context these systems act on can be misleading, and misleading context can corrupt a model's medical judgment. To understand how misleading context corrupts this judgment, we examine the model's susceptibility to the context, disclosure of it, mechanism of corrupted reasoning, and monitorability of the decision. On the medical reasoning subset of MedMisBench, a clinician-reviewed question-answering benchmark of 8,627 questions, we inject two types of misleading context cues, fabricated evidence and a bare assertion. We test three reasoning models, two that expose their full reasoning trace and one frontier model that exposes only its response. All three are more susceptible to the assertion than to the fabricated evidence, adopting the asserted answer 10 to 27 points more often. The misleading cues are disclosed in 81 to 98% of traces but only 7 to 90% of responses, and the assertion is disclosed less often than evidence based cues. Resampling from reasoning traces without disclosure shows the two cues corrupt reasoning differently, evidence entering early and accumulating while the assertion redirects the conclusion near its end. An LLM monitor catches 78% of corrupted decisions at 5% false positives when reading an open model's trace with guidance, against at most 32% from any response. The misleading context that models are most susceptible to is disclosed least, and was caught reliably only from an open reasoning trace, which frontier providers withhold.
comment: 30 pages, 10 figures. Proceedings of Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026

title: Learning Informative Prior with Infinite-Dimensional Continuous Normalizing Flow for Bayesian Inverse Problem
summary: Infinite-dimensional Bayesian inference methods, as a core class of methodologies for solving inverse problems of partial differential equations, have been widely applied across numerous scientific fields. A critical obstacle to constructing effective Bayesian inversion methods is how to construct an informative prior measure, particularly in the infinite-dimensional setting. Based on an infinite-dimensionally well-defined neural ordinary differential equation, we establish a general learning framework for infinite-dimensional nonlinear transformations, which can be incorporated into two practical Bayesian prior-learning paradigms corresponding to the direct and indirect data scenarios. A key ingredient of this framework is an equivalence between non-Gaussian and Gaussian measures, which is highly nontrivial: nonlinear transformations with genuinely infinite-dimensional range are involved, and several new limiting mechanisms have to be clarified. The developed framework is applied to three representative inverse problems -- simple source inversion, inverse obstacle scattering, and inverse heat conduction. All three examples substantiate the effectiveness of the proposed methods and, at the same time, demonstrate their broad applicability.

title: SignSeek: Learning Transferable Representations for Sign Dictionary Retrieval
summary: Sign language dictionaries are essential resources for sign language learners, yet automatically retrieving a sign from a dictionary, given only a query video, remains a challenging problem due to the natural variability between signers. Existing sign representation learning methods are built for closed-set recognition, producing embeddings that do not generalise to the open-set, signer-independent setting that retrieval demands. \textbf{SignSeek} closes this gap by contrastively learning sign representations with saliency-guided articulator masking. A contrastive objective aligns same-gloss signs across signers, while our Articulator Saliency-Guided Masking (ASGM) pinpoints the single most critical articulator per sign. This drives two complementary objectives, a masked contrastive alignment (MAC) loss that sees the sign through a single articulator and a masked prediction (MAP) loss that reconstructs it in latent space from the surrounding spatio-temporal context. Pretrained on 266K samples ($\sim$5,700 glosses) across multiple sign languages, \textbf{SignSeek} sets a new state-of-the-art performance in cross-corpus retrieval on ASL-Citizen, WLASL, and NMFs-CSL without any downstream fine-tuning. Strikingly, it achieves zero-shot generalisation to an entirely unseen British Sign Language (BSL), surpassing methods explicitly trained on BSL, and transfers seamlessly to isolated sign recognition and subtitle alignment, outperforming prior skeleton-based methods.

title: Do Latent World Models Really Select the Right Actions?
summary: This paper shows that the planning success of a latent world model does not reveal how well its score selects actions. Latent world models score candidate action sequences by the distance between their predicted embeddings and the embedding of a goal image, and their strong planning results are naturally read as evidence that this score picks good actions. Our study is simple: we take two released models, JEPA-WM and DINO-WM, execute the action sequences their planners consider, and compare what the score prefers with what actually happens. We make two observations. First, the score is informative but unreliable: it picks better actions than chance, yet it often passes over a successful sequence that the search has already found. Second, planning still succeeds, helped by a wider search and by replanning from new observations. With the released search budget, PointMaze planning succeeds in 91% of episodes, yet the top-scored candidate at the end of a search is no more likely to succeed than a random one. These observations suggest that the score should be measured directly, next to the success rate.

title: From Synthetic Priors to Model Behavior: Structural Coverage in Tabular Foundation Models
comments: Accepted in ATTRIB 2026 Workshop at NeurIPS 2026 (https://attrib-workshop.cc/)
summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are commonly pretrained on large collections of procedurally generated synthetic tasks, yet it remains unclear how well these synthetic pretraining priors support the downstream tasks on which the models are evaluated. We study this from a distribution-level attribution perspective. We recover or reconstruct the synthetic data generators of four TFMs and compare their generated tasks with datasets from two widely used tabular benchmarks. Each dataset is represented by a common set of structural descriptors capturing schema, feature distributions, dependence structure, response properties, and feature--response relationships. We then measure how broadly and repeatedly each synthetic prior reaches benchmark tasks using structural coverage and normalized density, and examine whether stronger local support is associated with better predictive performance. We find substantial differences across synthetic pretraining priors: some generators provide broader and denser support for benchmark tasks than others. Moreover, stronger synthetic-to-benchmark support is generally associated with better relative model performance, although this association is largely driven by the model with the broadest support and mostly disappears once each model's average support is removed. These results suggest that structural coverage provides a useful diagnostic for characterizing synthetic pretraining priors, whereas its relationship to downstream model behavior mainly reflects differences between models and remains confounded with architecture and training.
comment: Accepted in ATTRIB 2026 Workshop at NeurIPS 2026 (https://attrib-workshop.cc/)

title: Constrained Online Learning with Noisy Constraint Values
summary: We study online convex optimization with time-varying constraints when the constraint values are observed only through noise. In each round the learner picks an action, pays a convex loss, and incurs a convex constraint value that should be nonpositive; it then receives unbiased estimates of the loss and constraint gradients, and an unbiased observation of the constraint value whose error has bounded variance. Performance is measured against the best fixed action in hindsight among those that satisfy every constraint, and violation by the largest total overspend over any interval of consecutive rounds, which we call budget violation. Our algorithm, LEDGER, has $O(\sqrt T)$ expected regret and $O(\sqrt{T\log T})$ expected budget violation over $T$ rounds, uses one projection per round, and needs no strictly feasible action. The logarithm cannot be removed: with Gaussian noise of fixed positive variance, every algorithm with $O(\sqrt T)$ worst-case regret has worst-case budget violation of order at least $\sqrt{T\log T}$, even if only the final total overspend is counted, and budget violation $O(\sqrt T)$ forces linear regret. When violation is instead the sum of the positive parts of the per-round constraint values (hard violation), no algorithm keeps both expected regret and expected hard violation sublinear if the noise distribution is not fixed, even for affine constraints. With a fixed and known Gaussian noise law of standard deviation $σ$, a worst-case lower bound of order $\min\{σ,1\}T(\log\log T/\log T)^2$ shows that regret and hard violation cannot both be made polynomially sublinear. Noisy constraint values therefore still allow a signed budget to be controlled, at the cost of a logarithmic factor, but not the hard violation.

title: Merging Cyber Threat Intelligence Through Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Small Language Models for Rich Threat Representation
summary: Cybersecurity operations rely on CTI from heterogeneous sources, such as structured threat representations and narrative reports. They describe adversarial behaviors but rarely make explicit the conditions that enable each attack step, the consequences it produces, and the evidence supporting them, leaving analysts to correlate fragmented information manually. Existing approaches extract entities, map tactics and techniques, or reconstruct attack chains; enriching attack steps with explicit, evidence-linked semantics remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a local-first pipeline for evidence-grounded attack-step enrichment that combines hybrid RAG with a locally deployed SLM. Starting from an analyst-provided attack representation and supporting CTI documents, the pipeline retrieves step-relevant evidence and generates enriched descriptions, pre-conditions, post-conditions, and traceable links to the supporting passages. The enriched steps are organized into graph that groups MITRE ATT&CK-aligned steps into tactic-level milestones. Explicit conditions help defenders block attacks by removing their enabling conditions and support detection by checking for their expected consequences. We evaluate the pipeline on ten public malware case studies derived from UK NCSC reports, using automated measurements and a structured manual assessment with annotations from two annotators. The results demonstrate that the pipeline is effective at generating conditions that are, for the most part, evidence-supported and meaningful w.r.t. the analyzed attack step. Similar considerations hold for the enriched descriptions. Finally, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of locally generating structured, evidence-grounded enrichments that improve the interpretability and traceability of attack step representations without requiring a manual reconstruction of attack execution.

title: ComVLA: Communication-Aware Split Inference for VLA Models in 6G-Connected Robotics
summary: Connected robotics is an emerging 6G application where mobile robots follow natural-language instructions to manipulate physical objects. The Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that enable this are too large to run on the robot; a common trend is to offload inference to the cloud. The wireless link, however, limits how much sensing data the edge can transmit per control step. Two recent lines address this constraint: semantic communication codecs compress sensor data but require channel-specific retraining, and VLA token pruners select tokens from image but ignore the channel. Our insight is that the dense semantic information contained in the language already indicates which visual tokens matter. We propose ComVLA, a framework that uses this language guidance to adapt the VLA token budget to the channel capacity. Transmitting 32 tokens instead of 512 on the LIBERO benchmark, ComVLA cuts inference compute by 74% and inference latency by 22% versus the original OpenVLA-OFT baseline, at a cost of 1.5 pp in average task success (95.4% vs. 96.9%), and it stays within the capacity budget under Rayleigh and Rician fading. These results demonstrate that co-designing VLA inference and wireless communication is a practical direction for 6G-connected robotics.

title: Support Topology and Gradient Mixing in Sinkhorn Layers
summary: Sinkhorn attention layers normalize weights over a fixed sparse mask by alternating row and column scaling. When training these layers, sparse masks are usually judged by their edge count, graph diameter, or forward reachability. We show that the sparsity pattern and marginal budgets also govern how gradients flow backward through the scaling steps. Differentiating one row-column cycle on column log-potentials yields an explicit row-stochastic Markov kernel built from the two half-step transport plans, which reduces to a reversible two-step random walk at a balanced fixed point. Because potentials are defined only up to additive constants on each connected component, reverse-mode gradients propagate as zero-sum vectors whose total-variation norm contracts at a rate given by the kernel's Dobrushin coefficient. This coefficient bounds both unrolled backpropagation and implicit-differentiation truncation error. Crucially, graph connectivity alone does not prevent gradient trapping: we prove a face-lattice dichotomy showing that a mask and marginals guarantee score-uniform one-step contraction if and only if every nonempty face of the transportation polytope retains pairwise two-hop column overlap; otherwise, large learned scores can push the contraction rate arbitrarily close to one. We extend this criterion to multi-layer schedules, prove exact one-sweep mixing for coordinate-factorized and butterfly masks, and derive closed-form bounds for expanders, local bands, and global hub tokens. Deterministic numerical checks verify our finite-difference adjoints, canonical sparse masks, adversarial score limits, and spectral formulas.

title: Fairness Auditing After Model Updating: Reliability of Paired Disparity Comparisons
comments: 39 pages, including appendices. Revised title and author list
summary: Model updates can change disparities in prediction errors between demographic groups. We examine whether retrospective audits can reliably assess these changes by comparing updated models with their unchanged initial models on the same independent labelled observations, holding completed updating histories fixed. The target is the updated-minus-frozen difference in absolute subgroup gaps, averaged equally across reporting periods and assessed separately for true-positive and false-positive rates. Exploratory controlled simulations and repeated audits of fixed simulated histories assess coverage and decision correctness for nominal 95% intervals. Across the broader history panel, changing interval construction can raise or lower estimated coverage. In one subgroup-drift setting, 2,000 true-positive-rate audits evaluated twenty selected histories updated at fixed intervals, using 1,250 observations per reporting period. Replacing percentile bootstrap intervals with full-size basic intervals reduced estimated coverage from 92.20% to 84.55%. At an illustrative margin of 0.5 percentage points, correct conclusive decisions increased from 78 to 376, while incorrect decisions increased from 3 to 43, including 13 false reductions. The constructions used identical observations, estimates and bootstrap draws and had equal widths. Other controlled examples frequently excluded the population change while correctly indicating an increase. More conclusive audit results therefore need not provide more reliable evidence. Claims that updating reduced disparity require an inference procedure justified for the target and sampling design, an explicit decision margin, and group-specific performance reporting.
comment: 39 pages, including appendices. Revised title and author list

title: Exploring Diffusion Transformers for Cross-Modal Augmentation in Multimodal Brain State Decoding
summary: Multimodal brain state decoding has largely focused on fusing paired modalities for prediction, but has rarely explored how their correspondence can be further exploited to enrich training data and improve multimodal representation learning. To address this gap, we propose CoMA-DiT, a bidirectional cross-modal Diffusion Transformer for latent augmentation that treats paired modalities as sources of mutual generative supervision rather than merely as inputs to be fused. CoMA-DiT conditions velocity prediction on the paired modality through cross-modal attention and uses the shared hidden representation to construct reliability-gated residual augmentations. Experiments on multimodal auditory attention decoding and emotion recognition showed that CoMA-DiT consistently outperformed more than 20 representative baselines, achieving absolute gains of 4.28 and 6.70 percentage points in accuracy and macro-F1 over the no-augmentation baseline, respectively. Extensive ablation, sensitivity, visualization, and interpretability analyses further demonstrated its robustness, generalizability, and ability to capture functionally relevant cross-modal interactions. These findings support a broader view of multimodal learning: Paired modalities can serve not only as inputs for fusion but also as supervision sources that augment one another.

title: Principled Detection of Coordinated Manipulation from Aggregate Distortion and Account Reuse
comments: 27 pages, 4 figures, 17 tables. Accepted to the Findings track of WSDM 2027. Full version including appendices. v2 clarifies theoretical assumptions and exposition, updates references, and corrects typographical errors. Code and reproducibility materials are available at https://github.com/qianguoguoguo/aggregate-reuse
summary:
Coordinated manipulation is collective: plausible accounts can jointly distort ratings, rankings, and engagement. Existing defenses primarily construct evidence from identities, graphs, content, or co-activity. We introduce an aggregate-first evidence layer that treats distortion of a context-level outcome distribution as the primary evidence object. The engine observes only a histogram, count, resolution, and reference distribution; identities are withheld until interval evidence is fixed. Because raw discrepancies have positive finite-sample expectation, we subtract a matched null expectation to obtain signed evidence and account for reference uncertainty. Participation logs then accumulate these fixed increments across accounts. We characterize matched-exposure divergence, bound self-influence, establish finite-horizon separation, and derive an exact linear reuse law for paired contexts.
  We evaluate the mechanism with controlled rotation experiments and paired counterfactual interventions on historical Amazon review streams. Historical reviews provide the behavioral background; synthetic identities provide known coalition membership, and exact clean twins provide counterfactual controls. In a fixed-attack sweep against historical non-donor comparison accounts, reassigning the same manipulated events across identities with increasing reuse raises account-score ROC-AUC from 0.500 to 0.797. With activity- and exposure-matched clean twins, frequency is at chance while counterfactual attribution achieves ROC-AUC 0.744. Under a mean-preserving shape intervention, Wasserstein-1 and Jensen-Shannon evidence achieve ROC-AUC 0.909 and 0.967, while frequency and mean-based attribution remain at chance. Aggregate evidence complements repeated co-activity, improving mixed-mechanism ROC-AUC from 0.750 to 0.874 with a simple untrained combination.
