title: From Reconnaissance to Response: Quantitative Risk Parameterization and Game Theoretic Containment in Modern Enterprise Attack
summary: Modern Security Operations Centers struggle with delayed manual incident response, enabling adversaries to advance through the Cyber Kill Chain during early stage reconnaissance. While classical game theoretic defense models optimize strategic resource allocation, they rely on static utility matrices that fail to adapt to dynamic telemetry. This paper presents an integrated, metrics driven decision engine that bridges quantitative risk parameterization and continuous automated response time. Common Vulnerability Scoring Systems exploitability parameters are mapped to attacker success probabilities and evaluate defender log distributions via Factor Analysis of Information Risk Monte Carlo simulations. Real time SIEM logs streams are modeled as Poisson process arrival rates, dynamically updating defender posterior threat belief through sequential Bayesian filtering. A closed form threshold is derived by framing the interaction as a dynamic Bayesian Stackelberg game, where the expected unmitigated risk exceeds proactive containment cost. Parameterized against empirical data from the 2023 MGM Resorts and Caesars Entertainment cyber incident, simulation results demonstrate that the engine suppresses transient background noise while triggering automated SOAR network isolation within seconds of adversarial probing. Multi parameter sensitivity analysis confirms that the decision boundary dynamically adjusts to live perimeter vulnerability, offering a control theoretic foundation for sub minute automated threat containment.

title: Learning via Self-Consistency for Diffusion-based Video Reasoning
comments: 23 pages, including 10 pages for the main body
summary: While video diffusion models have demonstrated emerging zero-shot capability for visual reasoning and perception tasks, their stochastic generations often produce inconsistent predictions for tasks requiring reliable, structured outputs. Prior work has shown that self-consistency across stochastic video generations can improve diffusion-based reasoning at test time. We systematically extend the test-time method to structured prediction problems such as referring segmentation. However, test time scaling via self-consistency requires multiple rollouts and incurs much more latency. We propose self-consistency as an intrinsic learning signal for post-training video diffusion models without ground truth annotations or external verifiers. Specifically, our proposed Self-Consistency Fine-Tuning (SC-FT) distills consensus predictions into the video generation model, while subsequent Self-Consistency Reinforcement Learning (SC-RL) rewards generations according to their agreement with the consensus. The resulting model effectively internalizes the benefit of multi-sample consensus and requires only a single generation at inference time, while substantially outperforming the original model. To further reduce inference overhead, we read out predictions early in the denoising trajectory, preserving consensus quality while cutting inference time per rollout by 52%. For visual search, our method raises task accuracy from 48.4% for a single generation to 99.1%. For maze solving across three layout sizes, SC-FT and SC-RL improve single generation strict validity from 59.1% to 66.1% and 95.6% with the same inference latency. Also, for referring segmentation, SC-RL raises single-generation gIoU from 0.402 to 0.582, beyond SC-FT 0.473.
comment: 23 pages, including 10 pages for the main body

title: Diagnosing and Improving Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as decision assistants who must reason probabilistically from available evidence under explicit decision costs. We propose a decision-theoretic framework that decomposes LLMs' decision loss into two components: forming accurate beliefs from provided evidence and translating those beliefs into actions that optimize a provided utility function. Using a synthetic benchmark with known ground truth, we apply the decomposition to characterize probabilistic reasoning in frontier and open-sourced models. We further evaluate whether RL interventions targeting beliefs, decisions, or both improve these components across three domains, whether improvements transfer across components and elicitation formats, and whether decision performance can improve without improvement in belief formation. We find that targeting one component of probabilistic reasoning improves the target without necessarily transferring to others, and that jointly targeting belief formation and decision-making improves both but hinges on matched formats between training and evaluation.

title: Why Last-Iterate Scale-Invariant Regret Matching Converges Linearly?
summary: Scale-invariant extragradient regret matching (IREG-PRM+) normalizes the cumulative regret vector by its own norm and attains optimal regret without knowing the payoff scale. On two-player zero-sum matrix games, its last iterate converges linearly in experiments. Prior theory leaves this behavior unexplained. Analysis is difficult because the algorithm lacks a fixed step size. The step size is the inverse of the regret norm, which changes along the trajectory. Existing proofs of linear rates for regret-matching dynamics rely on restarts or modified updates. We explain the unmodified algorithm's convergence through norm saturation. The regret norm grows to a finite limit, so the step size converges as well. We prove that saturation always occurs and provide an explicit upper bound. The last iterate then converges to a single Nash equilibrium in every two-player zero-sum matrix game, even with multiple equilibria. Near a unique equilibrium, the set of active actions freezes after one round, and the linearized dynamics have a closed form. Take the payoff matrix restricted to these active actions and centered by the game value. Whenever the limiting step size times this matrix's largest singular value is less than one, the last iterate converges linearly at a closed-form rate. Across $216$ random games, all $184$ instances with a numerically resolved limit satisfy this condition. The predicted rate matches the empirical rate with a median ratio of $1.000$. Our analysis also shows that the per-round increase in the squared regret norm scales with the squared Nash gap, which measures distance to equilibrium. In sequential games (extensive-form games), exact gap computation requires a costly best-response pass. On Kuhn and Leduc poker, the analogous norm increase tracks the Nash gap between infrequent passes. Our code is available at https://github.com/lbn187/NormCert

title: Framing the Narrative: Ideological Mimicry in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer questions about politically contentious issues, yet evaluations typically treat a model's stance as a relatively stable property. Real users, however, communicate political signals through their terminology, assumptions, and personal context. We investigate whether such signals produce ideological mimicry: systematic shifts in the political stance expressed by an LLM toward the position conveyed by the interaction. If LLMs adapt their responses to these signals, they risk creating personalised political information environments in which users with opposing views receive systematically different accounts of the same issue, potentially reinforcing existing divisions. We build the Poli-SHIFT dataset and evaluation framework and assess ten LLMs across ten contentious political topics in the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia, systematically manipulating contested terminology, politically valenced premises, and user information, and eliciting responses in both multiple-choice and open-text formats. Across models, we find robust evidence that prompt framing shapes the political stance of LLM outputs. Substituting contested terminology while holding the substantive question fixed reverses which side of an issue a model supports in 16.9% of matched item pairs for open-weight models and 4.2% for closed-source models. Stated political ideology also systematically shifts responses toward the user's position. These findings show that political stance is not a fixed property of LLMs; the views expressed are conditional on the interaction with the user. As LLMs become increasingly personalised sources of information, such interaction-dependent adaptation could contribute to political information environments that reinforce users' existing perspectives.

title: ContextAdapt: Evaluating Contextual Adaptation and Value Alignment in LLMs
summary: Values such as honesty, autonomy, and confidentiality are often regarded as general principles underpinning AI alignment. However, what it means to act in accordance with these values can depend on the context in which a decision is made. In this paper, we ask whether large language models (LLMs) appropriately adapt the application of a value across professional settings, while remaining consistent when contextual changes do not alter the relevant professional norm. To study this, we introduce ContextAdapt, an evaluation framework covering honesty, autonomy, and confidentiality across medicine, law, finance, and national security. Drawing on primary-source professional and regulatory documents, we construct a value x domain framework and use this to develop scenarios testing both default professional rules and recognised exceptions. We evaluate 12 LLMs on both the actions they recommend and the justifications they provide. In our main experiment, models achieve 95.9% mean action-level appropriateness, although the use of the correct domain-specific justification varies substantially across models, from 25.6% to 76.9%. In a separate factorial experiment, explicitly naming the professional domain and changing the role of the model have limited effect on behaviour, whereas changing stakes produces a 10.3-point average difference between low- and high-stakes conditions and severe but localised failures. These results show that evaluating value alignment requires us to consider not only whether models follow abstract principles, but whether they apply them appropriately across different contexts.

title: Exploring the Hidden Cost of the World Around AI Agents
summary: Agent benchmarks test what agents can do in environments that are built for their tasks. Deployed agents work in the real world where other people and tools can change the state. An agent booking a flight may receive a message from someone else to change the destination, or a booking tool may fail without saying whether the ticket was purchased. We present BACKDROP, which asks how much of an agent's capability in a clean world survives in a non-cooperative world. BACKDROP takes a task along with the agent's execution environment, and plants four everyday hazards in its environment, one at a time and all together. Each hazard tests a different behavior. Authority: does a non-author actor instruction, from anyone who did not author the task, override the user's goal? Injection: does text planted in a record redirect the agent? Boundary: does the agent make changes in an app the user's task did not require? Fault: after a write fails without saying whether it landed, does the agent check before it retries? Across 3,678 variants and 16 models, the average pass rate falls from 69.5% to 31.3% once all four hazards are present; the strongest models fall furthest (Claude Fable 5.1 from 96.6% to 56.0%). The gap is consistent throughout all 16 models. BACKDROP formalizes these gaps and shows how an agent's score in a task's world is a ceiling on real-world performance.

title: Server-Side Surrogate Replay for Federated Class-Incremental Learning
summary: Federated class-incremental learning (FCIL) must learn new classes over time without forgetting the earlier ones. Existing replay methods counter forgetting on the clients, which store exemplars or train on synthetic samples. This burdens resource-constrained clients with extra memory and computation, and since each client stores exemplars only of the classes it has seen, the replay of earlier tasks stays as skewed as its local data. We propose ReSCENE, which moves replay entirely to the server. Each client uploads a few condensed surrogates per class, and the server keeps those of earlier tasks from all clients and trains the global model on them together with the current task, so the replay is balanced across all earlier classes. Since the global model and the surrogates co-evolve within a task, the surrogates of later rounds lie closer to the real data, so we introduce temporal herding, which compresses the pool of each task into a bounded buffer centered on the recent rounds, and establish a condition under which this buffer represents the task data more closely than keeping all surrogates. Across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet, ReSCENE attains the highest average accuracy against eight baselines in all nine settings, by up to $31.1$ points, while requiring as little as $0.11\times$ of the client computation and up to $179\times$ less upload than the model-update baselines. ReSCENE stays ahead with more clients and larger models while keeping client cost low.

title: Concurrent Semantic Search and Mission Execution for LTL Missions in Unknown Environments
summary:
Planning complex missions in unknown environments requires robots to reason simultaneously about what they should do and what they still need to discover. Existing approaches for solving LTLf missions typically assume a known environment, or separate the exploration of the environment from the execution of the mission, while semantic exploration methods look for one target at a time and ignore the mission being executed.
  To fill this gap, our main contribution is an adaptive high-level planning method that interleaves a task-driven semantic search with the execution of the mission, advancing both in a non-myopic manner.
  Our method leverages two representations built online, a metric-semantic scene graph, built with a Vision Language Model (VLM), that provides the evidence needed to locate the objects the mission refers to, and the deterministic finite automaton (DFA) encoding the mission, that indicates which of them matter at each mission state. At every planning stage, our planner selects the waypoints that are most valuable for both the semantic search and the advancement of the mission, valuing them over the remaining mission stages in order to avoid blocking states. The selected waypoints are then ordered in a single high-level plan, which is recomputed as new information arrives.
  In photorealistic indoor environments over five mission types, our method completes more missions than the compared approaches while having to cover less of the environment, and it does so with shorter paths and complying with the restrictions imposed by the mission.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Prefix-Invariant Realizations of Low-Precision Fast Matrix Multiplication
comments: 32 pages, 4 figures. Added FalconGEMM and batched-generation tests, optimized int8 kernels, SGLang serving benchmarks, and matched FP8 quality comparisons
summary: Fast matrix multiplication saves multiplications through exact cancellation, but rounding sums that mix token rows can leave contributions from later tokens in earlier language model outputs. This threatens prefix invariance, which likelihood scoring and batched inference rely on: an output must depend only on its allowed prefix. On Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, two fast FP8 realizations repaired to near-bf16 accuracy, and the existing fast kernel FalconGEMM, change answers when only text outside the allowed prefix is replaced: on 4.17--10.00% of OpenBookQA items scored by likelihood and 39.6--51.8% of NQ-open questions answered in a batch. Accuracy thus does not certify prefix invariance, and the stability criteria we analyze cannot tell realizations apart: across all 512 sign variants of two-level Strassen the criteria stay constant while teacher-forced perplexities span a 772.4$\times$ range on the same model. We therefore construct certified realizations of two-level Strassen on bounded integer codes that quantize token rows independently, then mix and cancel exactly before rescaling, using 49 block multiplications instead of 64. Our certificate guarantees bitwise equality to a prescribed row-local classical int8 operator at the same quantization specification, so every certified realization inherits its prefix invariance. Certification thus turns realization choice into a pure cost decision: which certified realization runs can no longer change any output. With optimized kernels, certified realizations run faster than classical int8 on an NVIDIA H20, and in the SGLang serving engine they raise throughput over its FP8 path by 1.2--5.6% on four models.
comment: 32 pages, 4 figures. Added FalconGEMM and batched-generation tests, optimized int8 kernels, SGLang serving benchmarks, and matched FP8 quality comparisons

title: More RLBWT Tricks
summary: Indexes based on $k$-mers can beat BWT-based indexes when the former take advantage of unitigs in de Bruijn graphs. In this paper we consider ways in which BWT-based indexes can do that as well, or even better. In particular, we consider MEM-finding between human chromosome 19s, where we can achieve a five- to sevenfold speedup over plain backward search, or a two- to threefold speedup over plain backward search with latency hiding, for about twice the space.

title: Made to Measure: Designing Image Watermarks to Specification
summary: Image watermarking enables provenance and attribution, but practical deployments must jointly satisfy robustness, false-positive rate (FPR), image quality, and latency requirements. Existing watermarking methods offer complementary robustness against different attacks, making their composition attractive for broader protection. However, combining watermarks introduces interference, distortion, decoding overhead, and additional verification paths that share the same FPR budget. We propose TAILOR, a request-conditioned watermark composition framework with three stages: (1) offline characterization models fragment recovery, distortion, latency, and composition interactions across embedding strengths; (2) joint configuration selection uses satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) to jointly optimize fragment selection, continuous embedding strengths, embedding order, and geometric recovery while minimizing predicted distortion; and (3) live calibration validates candidate configurations on user images and refines inaccurate offline predictions to improve deployment success. Across 7,321 distinct deployment requests spanning five scenarios and 20 attack settings, TAILOR achieves 96.21% scenario-averaged request satisfaction with a mean PSNR of 41.02 dB, demonstrating its effectiveness in meeting diverse deployment requirements while maintaining high image fidelity. Code is available at https://github.com/aaFrostnova/Tailor.

title: MiDShip: Multimodal Dataset of Ship Cargo Hold Structures for Engineering Design
summary: Ship structures govern a vessel's strength, safety, and manufacturability. Their design is governed by classification-society rules comprising hundreds of requirements, making the design process complex and highly iterative. However, data-driven structural design is limited by the lack of large, structured datasets that connect design geometry with structural geometric measures and rule-based constraints. This paper presents MiDShip, a multimodal dataset of 12,753 synthetically generated cargo-hold structural designs for machine learning and optimization. It contains 6,020 randomly generated designs, 496 designs produced by a stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD)-inspired procedure, and 6,237 designs produced by an equation-informed repair procedure. Each retained design includes a parametric vector, full 3D geometries and simplified geometries formatted for finite-element analysis (FEA) meshing, engineering drawings and corresponding annotated versions, a bill of materials, and structural geometric measures. The dataset also includes twenty-five constraints formulated from classification society rules for stiffener spacing, thickness, and section modulus requirements. Full-vessel loading, buckling, fatigue, and ice-class checks are outside the present scope. The primary contribution is the dataset and codebase, two design-generation studies demonstrate their use rather than introduce new optimization algorithms. MiDShip supports future research in machine learning, generative design, and automated rule-based evaluation for ship structures.

title: Keep It CALM: Analyzing the Limits of Global Unsafety in Text-to-Image Generation
summary: Training-free safeguards for text-to-image generation often rely on a reusable safety signal, such as an unsafe direction or global toxic subspace, applied broadly across prompts. We provide a controlled geometric analysis of this global-unsafety assumption and reveal a consistent coverage-selectivity trade-off: compact unsafe subspaces fail to cover heterogeneous unsafe semantics, whereas broader aggregation increasingly distorts safety-adjacent benign prompts. Motivated by this finding, we propose CALM (Counterfactual Adaptive Local Modulation), a training-free safeguard that replaces uniform global removal with prompt-local counterfactual correction. Using matched unsafe-benign anchors, CALM routes each prompt to active unsafe categories, minimally edits only violating token representations toward the safe side, and suppresses positively aligned unsafe residual components. Across broad evaluation, CALM significantly improves unsafe content suppression while preserving benign utility, demonstrating that local counterfactual correction provides a more selective alternative to global unsafe signal removal.

title: Where to Look Is Not How to Fix: Pre-Denoising Diagnostics and Modality-Dependent Control in Diffusion Composition
comments: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Understanding compositional failures in text-to-image diffusion requires identifying both where stress is detectable and how intervention changes the output. We study these questions through a controlled anchor--stress protocol that jointly evaluates text-encoder diagnostics and denoiser interventions. We introduce a text-only Compositional Stress Index (CSI), which separates common from rare compositions across SD1.5, SDXL, and the SD3 text path and provides an upstream diagnostic coordinate. A matched six-prompt localization study links intervention location to distinct outcomes: residual-minimizing embedding adapters improve representation fit, while downstream cross-attention intervention increases color hit rate (CHR) by 0.0272. Across SD1.5 and SDXL denoiser blocks, the largest positive signed diagnostic-accessibility mean occurs at the deep encoder, whereas selective boost has its largest positive mean CHR response at decoder blocks. Selective subtraction and broad ablation reveal further modality- and architecture-dependent responses, including a substantial CHR decrease when SDXL decoder cross-attention is broadly ablated. We find a diagnosis-control dissociation under our controlled attribute-object composition setting: compositional defects are diagnosable before denoising, but the representation coordinate that exposes risk is not necessarily the coordinate or modality that improves generation.
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

title: InvestigationWorlds: An Agentic Environment for Legal Investigation
summary: We introduce InvestigationWorlds, an agentic environment for legal investigation. We build on an underused artifact of U.S. civil litigation: the summary judgment motion. This motion relies upon a record composed of real evidence exhibits, and results in a court-adopted hypothesis that is treated as ground truth for the purposes of deciding the motion. Each environment is built from a real U.S. Federal Court case retrieved from Public Access to Court Electronic Records (PACER) and augmented by an attorney-validated generation pipeline that synthesizes role-tagged documents around the original record. The resulting corpus admits multiple coherent factual readings, only one of which matches the court-adopted hypothesis. Evaluating on 100 cases, we find agents often commit to incorrect hypotheses despite retrieving relevant evidence, struggling to distinguish the court-adopted hypothesis from alternative hypotheses.

title: Motion Without State: Probing Dynamical Consistency and Conditioning Bias in Video Models
summary: Image-to-video models serve as visual world priors whose plausible motion departs from physical simulation. We ask what dynamical structure replaces forward state propagation in generated motion, and how it biases quantitative physics evaluation. Holding law and initial state fixed, we vary visible geometry, prompt wording, and clip length across nine models and compare tracked trajectories against simulator rollouts. Generated motion splits into local visual cues and global boundary control, omitting the propagating physical state between them. Locally, tempo-normalized speed follows track undulations with a 15°-41° phase lead toward steepest descent as mean slope barely accelerates the ball, showing short memory of past slope. Local responses fail to compose: no single contact law describes a model's bounces (prescribed, self-calibrated on single-deflector contacts, or fitted in-sample), and balls clear 43 of 49 barriers above release height under an outcome-free prompt. Globally, naming the catch tray lifts arrival 14-76 percentage points above post-contact simulator rollouts, and event duration scales near-linearly with clip length, making apparent gravity 5.6-7.3 times higher in 3 s than in 8 s clips. These patterns persist on photographed first frames, motivating neutral-prompt controls, exit-state rollouts, and tempo-normalized metrics.

title: TrustMI: Causally controlling how assistants trust their users
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) assistants routinely decide whether they can trust users and third parties whose competence, intentions, and integrity they cannot verify. This uncertainty matters for safety, as trusting the wrong party can lead an agent to comply with harmful requests or act on malicious instructions encountered during tool use. To study this problem, we define trust as an assistant's willingness to accept vulnerability to the actions of another party and ask whether such behavior can be causally controlled through model activations. We build 2,000 contrastive conversations spanning ability, benevolence, and integrity, where paired responses complete the same request but differ in whether the assistant trusts the user. From these pairs, we learn steering matrices while keeping the model parameters frozen and test them across six instruction-tuned models from three families, finding that steering changes trust decisions monotonically in both directions. We then ask whether this effect extends to several safety-related agent settings involving harmful requests, prompt injections, and insider threats, while using benign-task and reasoning as controls. Our findings provide evidence that trust in the user can be causally controlled along linear directions in model activations and provide a way to study how trust shapes safety-relevant behavior in language models.

title: Bayesian Optimization in Sequence-to-Architecture Latent Space for Zero-Shot NAS
summary: Zero-shot Neural Architecture Search removes the prohibitive cost of traditional NAS, but its search process is typically based on the evolutionary algorithm (EA); lacking an explicit model of the objective, it often resorts to a near-random search through mutation. Bayesian Optimization offers a principled alternative by modeling the objective and aggregating information across iterations, but scales poorly to the high-dimensional, discrete, graph-structured spaces of modern NAS, restricting its use to only small networks. In this paper, we bring Bayesian Optimization to zero-shot NAS for large-scale architectures by learning a latent space via a Variational Autoencoder trained to reconstruct a novel prefix encoding of architectures and propose a proxy scalarization that combines several zero-shot proxies into a single Bayesian Optimization objective. After only 10,000 iterations of the proposed search algorithm (8 hours on a single GPU), our method found a network architecture which under the given model parameter count constraints achieves state-of-the-art results on three separate tasks -- image classification, object detection and semantic segmentation.

title: GS-Pool: Object-Level Change Detection in 3D Gaussian Splatting
comments: 20 pages, 11 figures, 9 tables, including supplementary material. Project page: https://boazkg93.github.io/gs-pool/
summary: Many physical spaces require photographic monitoring of changes to their structure over time. When each visit is reconstructed with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), a direct comparison of the two reconstructions cannot answer this because training is stochastic and two reconstructions of an unchanged space never coincide. To address this, we propose GS-Pool, which takes two independently reconstructed Gaussian scans of the same space and returns the changed objects in each, together with their change masks. Our method begins by extracting SAM2 masks from the photographs of each visit. These are then lifted onto the Gaussians that render them and merged into an object pool, a collection of 3D objects, so every decision is taken once per object in 3D. We introduce a novel photographic carrier approach, which co-opts the existing 3DGS mechanism. It does so by applying the photographs of the other visit and back-propagating them to the Gaussians that rendered each pixel. We combine this with GS-Diff's geometry and colour terms and our distilled DINOv3 features. This evidence is compared with objects identified as unchanged in both visits to set a change threshold for each scene. On the PASLCD benchmark, GS-Pool achieves mIoU/F1 scores of 0.75/0.85 against 0.64/0.76 for GS-Diff, the strongest offline method for detecting change in 3DGS. Finally, we return each changed object as a set of Gaussians, which can be inspected in 3D.
comment: 20 pages, 11 figures, 9 tables, including supplementary material. Project page: https://boazkg93.github.io/gs-pool/

title: When Weak Reports Matter: Staged Anchored Fusion for Cooperative UAV Sensing
summary: An echo rejected locally may still help other receivers confirm a target. Staged anchored recovery (SAR) retains confirmations based on strong reports, then uses unused strong reports to retrieve compatible weak evidence. This retrieval preserves every remaining candidate containing a strong report once the initial associations are fixed. We derive sharp bounds on corroborating support when receivers have different evidence probabilities and arbitrary dependence, constructing a joint distribution that attains every value between the bounds. For advance source selection with nonnegative additive costs, any feasible worst-case true/false support constraints can be met optimally by querying no weak-report source or just one. Simulations of unmanned aerial vehicle sensing show additional recoveries over strict consensus, sometimes accompanied by more unmatched outputs. In further tests, recovered positions often lack full velocity estimates, shared reflections create false confirmations, and query overhead can exceed upload savings.

title: Lachesis: Lifetime-Aware KV Cache Placement for Agent Serving across HBM and High-Bandwidth Flash
summary: In agent serving, agents and their sub-agents accumulate context as KV cache across many requests, far beyond HBM capacity. High-bandwidth flash (HBF) adds greater capacity at HBM-class read bandwidth, allowing a server to grow its batch and throughput under a relaxed SLO. We show that this gain meets an endurance wall as the batch growth wears HBF out within its warranty period. Prior work analyzes which KV should reach HBF assuming a request's KV remains readable until completion. However, an agent run is stateful, and by design, its harness discards parts of the context throughout the run. We find that the context divides into groups of KV that the harness discards together, so each group shares one lifetime that is known before the group is written. These lifetimes differ on three axes: reasoning stripped when the next user message ends a turn, a sub-agent's context discarded when it returns, and how long each sub-agent runs, which can be ranked when it starts. Guided by this characterization, we present Lachesis, a lifetime-aware KV cache placement layer that chooses HBM or HBF for each group when the group is written. In simulation of an eight-GPU B200 server on multi-agent traces, HBF with Lachesis serves 7.61-9.16$\times$ the throughput of the better of an HBM-only server and a DGX server with host DDR5. On the same traces, Lachesis extends HBF lifetime by 1.14-4.17$\times$ over HBM-first placement, which fills HBM before HBF. Since Lachesis keeps short-lived KV in HBM, a server running it can use more HBM stacks per GPU within the warranty. Our design-space exploration finds that Lachesis at 3/5 HBM/HBF stacks per GPU serves the highest throughput among the configurations that attach HBF directly to the GPU and outlast the warranty.

title: Convex-Concave Reinforcement Learning
summary: Policy learning drives many of the most consequential and heavily-invested applications of reinforcement learning today. Yet the core optimization problem it rests on (maximizing expected return) is notoriously non-convex, even under a direct policy parameterization, and the field has largely responded by avoiding it: optimizing convex surrogate approximations of the return under trust-region constraints (NPG, TRPO, PPO, AWR). We show that this seemingly unstructured problem is not actually structureless. In log-density-ratio coordinates $y := \log[π/π_n]$, the exact per-iteration objective, computable via per-decision importance sampling (PDIS), is a difference-of-convex-constrained difference-of-convex (DC-constrained DC) program. This structure lets us move beyond surrogate approximations: it recovers CPI, NPG, TRPO, and AWR as special cases along interpretable axes, and it opens a multi-step axis $k$ that couples consecutive decisions. We solve the per-iteration program with sequential convex programming (SCP), the standard solver for difference-of-convex problems, and establish inner-loop descent and limit-point stationarity for the theoretical algorithm, together with a conditional outer-loop performance bound. Empirically, multi-step Convex-Concave RL (CCRL) wins on diagnostic MDPs where credit must propagate across a horizon (its advantage growing with the dependency length), is competitive with a tuned PPO on classic control, and on a clinically motivated, stochastic, mid-horizon sepsis simulator converges markedly faster than tuned PPO to the same near-optimal survival, with an 11.3% higher area under the training curve. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/UMass-SCALAR-Lab/Convex-Concave-RL

title: CADFather: Autonomous CAD Reconstruction through Coordinated Tool Use
summary: Reconstructing an editable CAD model from a 3D shape remains a challenging engineering task. Existing methods can propose CAD operations, but no single source of proposals works equally well across different part geometries and stages of reconstruction. We introduce CADFather, an autonomous agentic system that coordinates complementary tools to recover parametric CAD programs from 3D meshes. A vision-language assistant inspects renders of the target and intermediate reconstructions, then decides which candidate CAD programs to extend, which tools to invoke, how many proposals to generate, and when to finish. Learned and algorithmic tools propose CAD operations, while numerical optimization refines the parameters of existing programs. Proposed or refined programs are executed and evaluated to provide feedback for subsequent decisions. The agent maintains alternative candidate programs for each target part and preserves the best valid result throughout reconstruction. CADFather uses pretrained generation and assistant models without additional training. We evaluate reconstruction quality and execution validity on the full DeepCAD, Fusion360, and MCB test sets, as well as on CADENA-Bench, CADBench, and BenchCAD. We additionally analyze computational cost and the trade-off between cost and reconstruction quality.

title: Noise Your Prompt: Noising Conditioning Tokens in Continuous Diffusion Language Models
comments: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026
summary: We revisit a standard accepted practice in the continuous diffusion language model literature of fixing conditioning prompt tokens clean during training. We make a very simple modification: also noise the conditioning prompt tokens during training. We demonstrate that under this modified training objective, we achieve better generalization in combinatorial reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and N-Queens, with the largest gains on harder variants ($3.73\% \to 24.65\%$ solve rate on Sudoku Hard), and increased diversity of generated solutions ($50.60\% \to 73.79\%$ coverage on 10x10 N-Queens). We also show measurable improvements to natural language generation quality in modest dataset regimes with Gigaword summarization, but notably demonstrate that gains do not transfer to all natural language tasks (e.g open ended dialogue generation). Our method is a single line change to the training objective, requires no additional inference costs by default, and provides the flexibility of classifier-free guidance inspired guided sampling. Our \href{https://github.com/LateralIntelligence/noise-your-prompt}{code} is publicly available.
comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026

title: Targeted Modality Dropout for Real-Robot Manipulation Robust to Intermittent Vision Loss
comments: 8 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Accepted to the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII 2027)
summary: Imitation learning policies that integrate multiple sensory modalities are prone to overreliance on a dominant modality, such as vision, during training, which can disrupt policy execution when that modality is lost at inference time. In this paper, we introduce Targeted Modality Dropout (TMD), in which the dependence on each modality is estimated using attention and the most dominant modality is selectively dropped during training. This is combined with entropy regularization over the dependence distribution. We evaluate six tasks on a real bimanual manipulator, simulating intermittent vision loss by jointly masking all vision tokens with 10% probability per inference chunk. Baseline successes decrease from 14/30 under normal conditions to 2/30 under vision loss, whereas TMD maintains an aggregate count of 15/30. TMD also exhibits smaller changes in action commands when chunks generated under vision loss arrive. In contrast, a conventional dropout that selects the dropped modality at random, without the entropy regularization, fails on many tasks even without vision loss.
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Accepted to the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII 2027)

title: RoboPace: Contact-Aware Time-Optimal Retiming for Action-Chunk Policies
summary: Robot manipulation data collection has been shifting from teleoperation toward robot-free demonstrations, through interfaces such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) or directly from human hands. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies trained on such data inherit the demonstrator's timing. Yet human timing does not directly transfer to robots: compliant hands tolerate fast contact, whereas robots may overshoot due to actuator and tracking limitations; conversely, robots can move faster in free space. This motivates a unified approach that reconciles execution speed with contact safety. We present RoboPace, an online retiming layer that preserves the policy's geometric path while adapting its timing, respecting the target robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints. It adapts execution speed based on predicted contact, jointly accounting for contact-dependent speed limits and the robot's motion constraints. The method requires no policy retraining and operates in real time. Across three contact-rich tasks on a dual-arm robot, faster uniform execution and physical-limit-only retiming largely fail. RoboPace instead achieves higher overall success than slow uniform execution while completing four of five commands in approximately half the time, retaining the reliability of slow execution without its time cost.

title: YUBI-STAG: Contact and Semantic-Rich Alignment for VLAs via Automated Video-Language Grounding
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models acquire broad manipulation capabilities via large-scale pretraining, yet eliciting them through language requires fine-grained alignment between instructions and physical interactions. Existing robot demonstrations typically provide only coarse task descriptions, omitting how actions are executed, including which gripper acts, which object is contacted, and how it is grasped and moved. We introduce YUBI-STAG, a framework for Spatio-Temporal Annotation and Grounding that automatically enriches manipulation demonstrations with interaction-rich semantics to align pretrained VLAs with fine-grained manipulation language. Combining contact-object segmentation with vision-language models, YUBI-STAG annotates object identities, attributes and states, per-gripper actions, bimanual coordination, and spatially grounded interactions. To address YUBI-STAG's reliance on localized sequences and multi-stage VLM inference, we distill it into YUBI-VLM. YUBI-VLM directly recovers action structure and annotations from raw, unsegmented video in few inference calls and operates from wrist views alone. We evaluate both frameworks on YUBI-STAG-Bench across temporal, semantic, and spatial grounding tasks. YUBI-VLM retains much of YUBI-STAG's annotation accuracy with fewer inference calls and shorter runtime while generalizing to unseen manipulations. Finally, post-training VLA policies on these annotations aligns them with fine-grained language and contact-aware structure. Bimanual experiments demonstrate improved performance and instruction following, including control over object identity, acting gripper, target location, and spatial relations absent from original labels.

title: Seek-and-View Reasoning for Multi-View Spatial Understanding
summary: Existing multi-view spatial reasoning remains constrained by sparse and fixed viewpoints. Consequently, vision-language models (VLMs) must infer spatial relations solely from these fixed views, leading to fragile cross-view alignment and a geometry-to-language bottleneck. To overcome these issues, we formulate a novel Seek-and-View reasoning paradigm that seeks a viewpoint to make the queried spatial relation directly observable and interprets the sought view to support the spatial reasoning. Building on this paradigm, we propose Vantage, a training-free and model-agnostic framework that structures VLM reasoning for viewpoint planning and evidence-augmented spatial understanding, with a 3D foundation model supporting view synthesis. Specifically, we develop a viewpoint-grounded reasoning stage that translates spatial queries into targeted viewpoint plans. A subsequent geometry-grounded evidence augmentation stage synthesizes new views and incorporates visual evidence alongside preceding reasoning contexts for final answering. Together, these stages reduce reliance on language-based cross-view alignment. Extensive experiments on six VLMs across six benchmarks show consistent improvements in overall accuracy, with an average absolute gain of 8.2% without fine-tuning.

title: Image Diffusion Models Are Good 3D Human Motion Generators
comments: 14 pages; under review. The first two authors contributed equally to this work
summary: Text-to-motion generation typically relies on dataset-specific skeletal representations, with models trained separately for benchmarks with different joint layouts. We investigate whether image diffusion architectures can model 3D human motion through a common image-compatible representation that accommodates heterogeneous skeletal layouts while preserving motion-specific kinematic structure. To this end, we organize root-centered joint trajectories into topology-informed joint--time images and model global root dynamics through a complementary latent stream. A motion autoencoder conditions local-motion decoding on the root latent, while a text-conditioned Scalable Interpolant Transformer (SiT) jointly generates both latent streams, with supervision on decoded 3D joint positions further constraining generation in motion space. In addition to dataset-specific models, we train a single motion autoencoder on HumanML3D and KIT-ML, followed by a single text-conditioned SiT shared across both datasets, preserving their respective skeletal definitions without skeleton retargeting to a common joint layout. Experiments on HumanML3D and KIT-ML show that our dataset-specific models achieve state-of-the-art performance, while shared training yields further gains on both benchmarks, demonstrating the benefits of shared modeling across heterogeneous skeletal layouts.
comment: 14 pages; under review. The first two authors contributed equally to this work

title: Wyner's Common Information and the Common Entropy are NP-Hard to Compute
comments: Updated version of the manuscript. Submitted for publication
summary: Wyner's common information $J(P_{XY})$ and the common entropy $G(P_{XY})$ of a pair of finite random variables $(X,Y)$ with joint distribution $P_{XY}$ minimize, respectively, the mutual information $I(X,Y;W)$ and the entropy $H(W)$ over all auxiliary random variables $W$ that make $X$ and $Y$ conditionally independent. We prove that both quantities are NP-hard to compute, by polynomial-time reductions from the Maximum Edge Biclique problem. Moreover, unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, no polynomial-time algorithm can approximate $J(P_{XY})$ within an additive error $1/(8N^2)$, or $G(P_{XY})$ within an additive error $1/(2N)$, where $N$ is the number of positive entries of $P_{XY}$.
comment: Updated version of the manuscript. Submitted for publication

title: The interpreter as developer: An autoethnographic design study of building a computer-assisted interpreting tool through human-LLM co-creation
comments: 14 pages, 5 figures. The CAI tool is openly available at https://github.com/omnigx/whisper_interpreter and archived at Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22255011
summary: Computer-assisted interpreting (CAI) tools are built for interpreters, mainly by third parties, and the interpreters' own side of development has received little first-person documentation. This article reports an autoethnographic design study in which a professional conference interpreter without formal programming training built a local-first CAI system through expert-led human-LLM co-creation. Analysis of the development dialogues shows how tacit professional knowledge became design only after generic defaults had failed in use, a reversal of the usual direction of technological mediation, from adopting tools to authoring them. Three mechanisms of in-booth appropriation emerged under a human-led division of labor, and a four-layer reconstruction illustrates the human contribution at work. First-month telemetry, over six thousand utterances across nine sessions, shows a fully local system sustaining translation-stage latencies near one second, with sustained-load degradation as a working boundary. The case bears on professional agency, knowledge production, and the training of interpreters under generative AI.
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures. The CAI tool is openly available at https://github.com/omnigx/whisper_interpreter and archived at Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22255011

title: Covering Radius and Deep Holes of Hyperderivative Reed-Solomon Codes under the NRT Metric
summary: The deep hole problem is a fundamental problem in coding theory, and it has many important applications in code constructions and cryptography. The deep hole problem of Reed-Solomon codes has gained a lot of attention. Hyperderivative Reed-Solomon (HRS) codes under the Niederreiter-Rosenbloom-Tsfasman (NRT) metric generalize Reed-Solomon codes under the Hamming metric. We study the covering radius and deep holes of HRS codes in the NRT metric. We prove that the NRT covering radius of $\mathrm{HRS}_k(α,V)$ is $sr-k$ and characterize its NRT deep holes via an MDS-extension criterion and a polynomial-remainder criterion. The latter yields an enumeration formula in terms of the characteristic polynomial of an associated hyperplane arrangement. We also construct three families of NRT deep holes and derive exact enumeration formulas in several special cases, including $r \in \{1,2\}$ and $k \in \{1,2,sr-1,sr-2,sr-3\}$. For full-length evaluation sets and $s \geq 2$, we completely describe the deep holes for $2 \leq k \leq sq-1$ whenever $q$ is odd or $k \geq 3$. When $k \geq s$, the deep holes are precisely the evaluations of polynomials of degree $k$. For $k<s$, we give an explicit description.

title: SPLICE: Sparse Physics Library Identification and Compositional Expansion
summary: Neural operator splitting composes a library of neural operators, one per physical mechanism, into zero-shot simulators of new equations. Existing approaches, however, require these mechanisms and their labels to be specified in advance. We ask whether a pretrained library can instead be adapted and grown from unlabeled trajectories in which multiple mechanisms act simultaneously. We introduce SPLICE, a framework that discovers operators without mechanism labels on mixture data. The contributions of the candidate operators to each trajectory are inferred by solving a convex optimization problem. A calibrated test then assigns each discovered operator the mechanism it implements. Failure cases are also detectable, when the library lacks the required physics or when mechanisms are insufficiently separable, and growth recovers only mechanisms the pretrained network represents. Across one and two dimensional systems, the discovered operators recover mechanisms from unlabeled mixtures and compose into zero-shot simulators of unseen equations; on Navier-Stokes they compose close to their supervised counterparts.

title: Urbex: Agentic Spatial Grounding for City-Scale 3D Scenes
summary: City-scale 3D grounding is commonly formulated as candidate ranking, which requires precomputed instance proposals and becomes inefficient in large outdoor scenes. We propose Urbex, an agentic vision-language framework that instead casts grounding as active spatial search. Urbex represents a city-scale 3D scene as an interactive multi-view environment, allowing a VLM agent to query landmarks, zoom into local regions, render oblique views, and commit a grounded bounding box. We optimize this tool-use policy with reinforcement learning on CityRefer, using smooth localization rewards and lightweight shaping rewards for efficient exploration. Experiments show that Urbex achieves the best Hit@1 and IoU on CityRefer, supports candidate-free grounding without ground-truth boxes, and is substantially faster than the strongest city-scale ranking baseline. Zero-shot results on STPLS3D-Refer further indicate improved cross-scene robustness.

title: BridgeTwist: Twisting Schrödinger Bridges for Training-Free Conditional Sampling
summary: Generative models are often required to serve many downstream conditional tasks. In the training-free setting, a pretrained unconditional model is reused as a prior and combined with a task-specific likelihood to sample from the corresponding posterior. While such training-free samplers have been developed for diffusion and flow models, their counterpart for Schrödinger bridge (SB) models remains unexplored, despite the growing appeal of SBs as flexible stochastic transport models between general source and target distributions. We propose BridgeTwist, a training-free conditional sampler for pretrained SB generative models, formulated as a tempered twisted sequential Monte Carlo scheme. The twist function employs a plug-in surrogate built on a closed-form endpoint predictor, which is derived by combining the velocity and score fields obtained from the SB pretraining. Since this surrogate is less reliable near the source, we temper the twist function with a time-varying exponent, downweighting its influence at early steps. We further introduce a bridge-shaped inference-time diffusion schedule that concentrates the proposal noise in the interior of the path. Telescoping importance weights then cancel all intermediate twist factors, yielding an asymptotically exact sampler for the posterior. Empirically, BridgeTwist outperforms training-free baselines on class-conditional and text-prompted image generation, and is competitive with specialized inverse problem solvers on inpainting, deblurring, and super-resolution.

title: Find the Fungible: Variable-Resolution Tokenization that Compacts Semantics with a Granularity Dial as a VLM "Catalyst"
summary: Efficient vision-language models should preserve a useful representation of the whole image, even under tight budgets. However, aggressive pruning or indiscriminate merging can erase critical details and disrupt the spatial structure. We thus propose Varest, which maximizes semantic fungibility: tokens describing coherent content can be summarized together with minimal information loss. Object boundaries distilled from a visual foundation model guide grouping, while text localization protects details needed for reading. At lower budgets, Varest merges the image into coarser semantic regions, while maintaining full spatial coverage. After early language decoder layers process this representation, a learned selector prunes visual tokens that later layers no longer need, reducing repeated access to already integrated information. Across three LLaVA backbones and 13 benchmarks, Varest outperforms 10 training-free and 5 trained baselines in mean performance retention at every evaluated budget, preserving 86.10-92.33% of uncompressed performance using only 5.56% of tokens. This SOTA performance further generalizes to modern VLMs like Qwen3.8-27B.

title: CryoTracer: Synthetic-to-Real Filament Instance Tracing in Cryo-EM
summary: Filament picking in cryo-electron microscopy requires tracing continuous centerlines while preserving filament identity through crossings and low-contrast regions. Established pickers such as Topaz and crYOLO construct traces by linking local predictions, which can fragment filaments or connect them incorrectly. Preserving filament identity helps keep segments associated for the analysis of polymorphic specimens. However, expert centerline annotations for training are scarce and costly to obtain. We introduce CryoTracer, a synthetic-to-real framework that predicts individual filaments as ordered centerline polylines. Its transformer decoder jointly refines filament predictions using image features sampled around each curve. A discrete Fréchet objective guides instance matching and curve regression while treating both tracing directions as equivalent. Procedural micrographs vary filament geometry, crossings, and image appearance, providing exact centerline labels for pretraining. We then fine-tune the model on annotated real micrographs. We compare CryoTracer with five reference methods on EMPIAR-10022 and a private, in-house $α$-synuclein collection. The standard regime uses the full training partition, while the practical regime limits training to 50 annotated micrographs. A separate $α$-synuclein split tests transfer to held-out sessions. CryoTracer achieves the highest complete-filament mF1, continuous coverage, and crossing accuracy among the evaluated methods in both regimes. We release new filament centerline annotations for EMPIAR-10022. Code and data are available at https://github.com/cryotracer/cryotracer

title: Scaled Companion Linearizations for Coefficientwise Backward Stability
summary:
A backward stable eigensolver applied to a linearization of a matrix polynomial does not necessarily produce eigenpairs with small coefficientwise relative backward errors. Scaling the polynomial can help, but a single scaling may not provide coefficientwise backward stability across the entire spectrum, particularly when the eigenvalues have widely varying magnitudes.
  To address this difficulty, we use different scalings in different regions of the spectrum. We partition the nonzero complex plane into radial regions and, for each region, construct a scaled companion linearization with an eigenvector recovery rule. On each assigned region, we bound the polynomial backward error by the pencil backward error multiplied by an explicit degree-dependent constant and the ratio between the pencil-vector norm and the recovered-vector norm. We prove degree-dependent bounds for these ratios at exact pencil eigenvectors. When computed eigenvectors satisfy the same ratio bounds, the resulting backward-error amplification is \(O(d^{5/2})\), independently of coefficient norm disparities.

title: The Ephemeral Cost of Switching Optimizers Across LLM Training Stages
comments: Camera Ready for Transitioning from Pre-Training to Post-Training Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Recent work suggests that switching optimizers between pretraining and subsequent training stages incurs a performance cost, but systematic investigation of this phenomenon is lacking. We study the mismatch between AdamW and Muon optimizers by pretraining 1.2B Llama-3 models from scratch while varying the proportion of updates taken with each optimizer, and similarly interpolating between the two optimizers during continued pretraining and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Surprisingly, we find little evidence of a meaningful optimizer mismatch penalty: final performance is largely explained by the independent effects of the pretraining and post-training optimizers, with downstream performance generally improving as the proportion of Muon updates during SFT increases. Although matching the pretraining optimizer can reduce forgetting during SFT, this does not translate into improved final benchmark performance. We further evaluate AdamW and Muon for task-general SFT of open-weight models, across the Llama and Qwen families up to 14B parameters, where Muon remains competitive with AdamW, despite these models having been pretrained with AdamW. Finally, we investigate whether our findings extend to RL via experiments on our 1.2B models as well as Qwen3-1.7B and 4B, and find that AdamW and Muon achieve comparable final performance in math RLVR. Together, our results suggest that the choice of optimizer for post-training can be made largely independently of the optimizer used during pretraining.

title: Optimized linear multistep methods for stiff problems
summary: We design and test optimized linear multistep methods for stiff problems. Each method is A-stable, implicit, and second-order accurate. We focus on achieving the smallest possible error constant while also ensuring that stiff modes are damped. We recover some known optimal L-stable three- and four-step methods and prove their global optimality, and provide a new five-step method with essentially optimal error constant. We also study methods that are not L-stable but provide a prescribed rate of damping in the infinitely stiff limit; in particular, we prove that a known two-step family is optimal. Variable-step-size formulae are also provided for the L-stable methods. Numerical tests demonstrate that the improved error constants lead to improved accuracy.

title: UniField++: A Unified Agentic Framework with Loop Reasoning for MRI Field-Strength Enhancement
comments: 10 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. Updated author list, abstract, and manuscript formatting
summary: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) field-strength enhancement seeks to combine the accessibility of low-field scanners with the image quality of high-field scanners. Yet, existing methods remain prone to anatomical hallucinations: scarce paired data limit knowledge of field-strength-dependent tissue contrast and anatomical visibility, while uniform processing leaves difficult brain regions with insufficient reasoning and refinement. To address these challenges by better coupling field-aware learning with region-adaptive reasoning and refinement, we propose UniField++, a two-agent framework for unified multi-field enhancement, including 64mT-to-3T and 3T-to-7T. Unified learning exposes both the vision-language model (VLM)-based planner and the flow-matching-based enhancer to field-dependent image characteristics across tasks. Trained with radiologists' annotations of field-dependent hallucination-prone brain regions and corresponding tissue- and anatomy-specific correction plans, the planner predicts regional risk and formulates targeted restoration strategies. Guided by these plans, the enhancer performs loop reasoning along the flow-matching trajectory, repeatedly processing high-risk brain regions for additional reasoning and refinement. Together, multi-field unification and risk-guided reasoning support anatomically faithful enhancement across field strengths. Across the evaluated tasks, UniField++ improves PSNR by an average of 2.74 dB and SSIM by 14.05 percentage points over comparison methods, with corresponding gains of 3.97 dB and 13.92 percentage points over the ablation baseline. It also maintains enhancement quality on an external cohort with an unseen field strength and improves downstream whole-brain segmentation Macro Dice by 0.1457 on average over original low-field inputs. Code: https://github.com/CUHK-AIM-Group/UniField_plusplus.
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. Updated author list, abstract, and manuscript formatting

title: FlashReFocus: Interactive Image Refocusing in Seconds
summary: Single-image refocusing changes the focal plane and depth of field of a photograph after capture. Users compare focal choices on one photograph, so content stability across edits matters alongside quality and speed. Recent generative methods rerun large diffusion models for every edit, even when they first restore an all-in-focus image, so content can change inconsistently between edits. Yet only this restoration is highly ill-posed and benefits from a generative prior, whereas rendering blur is largely determined by depth and the focal plane. We therefore propose FlashReFocus, which runs diffusion once per photograph and renders each edit with a lightweight network. A one-step diffusion deblurrer with a decoder refiner recovers fine detail efficiently while balancing fidelity and perceptual quality. The renderer uses an explicit defocus map for control and defocus-bias attention to promote information exchange between tokens with similar blur magnitudes. Because every edit reuses the same reconstruction, in-focus content stays consistent across edits, and editing the map enables tilt-shift and two-plane effects. We further collect 3CReal, a benchmark of 89 pairs from three camera-lens systems, to evaluate generalization to unseen optics. For zero-shot bokeh rendering on EBB! Val176 and 3CReal, FlashReFocus leads the evaluated methods in fidelity and perceptual quality. At 1536x1536, a complete refocus takes 2.45 s and each subsequent edit 0.46 s on one RTX PRO 6000.

title: ShadowCast: On-the-Fly Context-Aware Shadow Augmentation for Remote Sensing Image Segmentation
comments: Accepted to IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Letters (GRSL)
summary: Shadows cast by elevated objects alter the spectral appearance and obscure the boundaries of objects in remote sensing images, thereby degrading semantic segmentation performance. Most existing approaches handle shadows as degradations to be detected and removed, requiring additional costs from dedicated networks and shadow-specific annotations. We propose ShadowCast, which takes the opposite approach: it synthesizes shadows and injects them during training for remote sensing segmentation. It extracts masks of elevated objects, such as buildings and trees, directly from the segmentation labels and estimates an image-specific cast-shadow direction cue by probing the brightness around them. It then projects synthetic shadows along the inferred cast-shadow direction, requiring no learned network and no acquisition metadata. Experiments on three widely used remote sensing benchmarks, Vaihingen, Potsdam, and LoveDA, show that ShadowCast consistently outperforms the baseline across diverse state-of-the-art segmentation architectures. Moreover, it brings additional performance gains when combined with standard augmentation and regularization techniques, indicating that stochastic shadow injection serves as a simple and complementary augmentation strategy for remote sensing segmentation.
comment: Accepted to IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Letters (GRSL)

title: Learning to Generate in the Right Order
summary: We introduce PONDER, a method that learns in which order an image generator should fill in content and which of its earlier predictions to revise. Masked generative models construct a sample by repeatedly filling in subsets of missing variables. The order of these partial predictions determines the context available in subsequent steps and therefore affects the quality of the final sample. Common strategies are to choose the order randomly or based on local confidence estimates. Conditioned on the partially generated sample and the generator's features, our policy chooses which positions to fill next and/or which previously filled positions to mask for later regeneration, a mechanism we call rethinking. In this way, the generation process is able to adapt to the evolving context and also to revise earlier predictions. We optimize the policy using group-relative policy gradients, with rewards that measure constraint satisfaction, human preference, or distribution quality. For the latter, we introduce FIDgrad, an image-level reward derived from the (first-order) change in Fréchet Inception Distance caused by adding a generated sample to the current feature distribution. With the generators frozen, learned ordering reduces MAR-B ImageNet FID from 4.09 to 2.78, improves MaskGen-KL-XL HPSv2 from 24.50 to 26.50, and raises the accuracy on hard visual Sudokus from 4.5% to 56.6%, surpassing uncertainty-based greedy ordering (41.0%). Rethinking further improves these results to 2.70 FID, 27.80 HPSv2 and 96.7% accuracy.

title: A Paired RGB-Sonar Dataset for Fish Monitoring with Consumer Sonar
summary: Imaging sonar enables underwater observation in conditions where optical imaging is ineffective due to darkness and turbid water. However, imaging-sonar systems previously used for ecological monitoring have typically been expensive, limiting their accessibility. Consumer forward-looking sonar has the potential to make fish monitoring more accessible, but its noisy imagery makes annotation and the development of automated methods challenging. We introduce the Huntington and Caltech Koi RGB and Sonar dataset (HaCKRS), which pairs Garmin LiveScope imaging-sonar recordings with top-down RGB video of koi carp. The dataset contains more than 105,000 temporally matched frame pairs, spanning approximately 3.3 hours of recordings across four range and orientation configurations. We provide frame-wise metadata, sonar geometry and coordinate information, synchronization data for all four configurations, and planar registration for the three horizontal configurations. The release focuses on paired observations and calibration rather than task-specific fish annotations. We intend HaCKRS to support annotation and the development of fish detection, tracking, and counting methods, and investigations into the potential of consumer sonar for ecological monitoring. The dataset, code, and OpenScope, the open-source tool we used to record the sonar, are publicly available.

title: Announced Breaks Separate Conformal Reliability from Frequency Calibration
comments: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). 44 pages, 8 figures
summary: A prediction interval should contain the outcome at a stated rate. Conformal prediction sets its width from past forecast errors. When the process behind a time series changes on an announced date, intervals set from errors before that break can stop covering. After Australia moved to five minute electricity settlement, a 90% interval fixed beforehand covered 51.5% of the next 400 days. One forecaster needs the next interval to cover, another a finished period's share of misses at 10%. We show that each need calls for its own restart at the date. We recompute the next interval from the $n$ errors since the break. If these errors are independent, its coverage comes within $O(n^{-1/2})$ of the stated rate, the best order attainable. For a finished period, we restart adaptive conformal inference (ACI). On bounded errors, if a floor under its width adds a bounded total, it brings the share of misses within $O(n^{-1})$ of target but promises nothing about the next interval. After a simulated mean shift of 5.0 noise standard deviations, recomputed intervals cover within 3.5 percentage points of 90% on average at the 50th forecast, a third closer than the 5.2 of the best of five baselines. Of nine announced breaks in power markets and at a central bank, restarting ACI gives a detectable gain only at the one large break.
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). 44 pages, 8 figures

title: Red-Teaming Multi-Agent Attacks for Loss-of-Control Risks
summary: AI agents are growing more capable and persistent, and are being deployed in ever larger numbers. As more start collaborating, AI control measures must remain effective when they covertly collude on a harmful objective. We introduce MiniLab, a synthetic series of live services and codebases (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives), adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure. We demonstrate distributed attacks, in which different agents carry out separate attack fragments, and how their covertness evades frontier monitors when reading their trajectories individually. We show how distributed attacks spread across diverse contexts and harmful objectives through 16 human-optimized attacks (weight exfiltration, unmonitored rogue deployment, permission elevation, and more). A frontier monitor, GPT-5.6 Sol, reading each agent separately flags only 3.4% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 82.4% when a single agent carries out the same side task. Individual attacks can also be composed into longer attack sequences toward a greater loss-of-control outcome, without any individual agent being flagged. Finally, we tested whether models can plan these covert attacks: even with execution and monitor feedback, the best model-planned attacks succeed covertly under both their feedback monitor and GPT-5.6 Sol in at most 32% of executions, compared with 82% for human-crafted plans, though this may scale with model capabilities. By turning worst-case coordinated attacks into reproducible red-team cases, our work provides a foundation for preventing locally benign agent actions from accumulating into system-level loss of control.

title: HiPPO Functional Memory: Coordinate-Queryable Attention for Irregular Time Series
comments: This submission was inadvertently posted as a duplicate record of the same work. The updated and authoritative version is available at arXiv:2611.28465. Please refer to arXiv:2611.28465 for the current version. This older duplicate submission is withdrawn to avoid confusion
summary: Irregular time series require models to answer temporal queries at arbitrary coordinates, yet existing approaches typically retain observation-dependent representations that must be repeatedly resolved for each query. We introduce HiPPO Functional Memory (HiPPO-FM), a functional-memory attention operator that compiles an irregular history into a reusable coordinate-addressable state. Instead of storing observation-indexed tokens or latent trajectories, HiPPO-FM writes observations into a fixed-rank functional space and performs direct coordinate evaluation through matched functional geometry. Kernel-smoothed HiPPO coordinates and Gram-based readout define a shared write/read mechanism, while observed-support self-attention enables content-dependent representations before compression. We characterize the induced finite-dimensional query space and derive an error decomposition separating functional geometry approximation from learned-memory mismatch. Across continuous-coordinate reconstruction, irregular representation learning, real-world extrapolation, and event-sequence prediction, HiPPO-FM consistently improves strong irregular time-series baselines, achieving strong reconstruction accuracy on Spiral, competitive performance across 20 UEA datasets, improved real-world extrapolation, and superior results on several irregular event benchmarks. After encoding, the compact functional state can be reused across different query sets without reprocessing the observation history.
