title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
summary: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2% and 42.9% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation. See https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-amp/ for code and videos.

title: From Reflection to Co-Evolution: Self-Evolving Agents with Locally Verified Memory
summary: LLM agents have made impressive progress in coding and mathematical reasoning, motivating growing interest in learning from long-horizon interaction. Memory supports this process, but plausible lessons can be redundant or reinforce inappropriate actions. Can a memory's source decision provide a practical test for whether to retain it? We localize consequential trajectory steps, extract candidate memories, and replay each source decision with and without its candidate under the same context. This reveals two properties: most candidates barely shift the probed distribution, and both successful and failed source actions can be reinforced or suppressed. These observations motivate Anchor, which tests shift magnitude and source-role alignment before retention. Admitted memories guide later trajectories, enabling experience-driven improvement under a frozen policy. On held-out ALFWorld and WebShop tasks, Anchor improves success rate and mean score by up to 19.9% and 17.2%, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline for each backbone. With Qwen3.5-27B, it retains 41% fewer ALFWorld cards than unfiltered retention and outperforms all four WebShop cost-comparison baselines while using fewer tokens.

title: QUASI: Post-Quantum Quorum Attestation of Pre-Validated Statements
summary:
We present QUASI, a newly conceived class of hash-based, post-quantum-secure protocols that enable a group of parties to produce a publicly verifiable attestation about a pre-validated statement. QUASI produces attestations that reduce the size and verification cost to a fraction of a full hash-based signatures collection, without relying on SNARKs or a trusted setup.
  QUASI rests on a surprising discovery: each party need not sign the entire statement. Authenticating only a small subset of symbols suffices for a quorum to attest to the whole. We turn this insight into a randomized construction that achieves reductions of more than 10x in per-party contribution size and hash computations for generation and verification, compared with full hash-based signatures.
  QUASI is a generic primitive supporting diverse applications. Operationally, QUASI requires no additional interactive setup or preprocessing beyond independent key generation by parties for the underlying hash-based authentication scheme. Two principal use cases are external attestation for signature-free consensus, enabling clients to verify statements about committed state; and preprocessing for SNARK-based aggregation, compounding QUASI's savings with succinct-proof compression.

title: RoadState: A Domain-Prior-Enhanced Vision-Language System for Industrial-Grade Lane-Level Map Updating
comments: 12 pages, 5 figures, including appendices. Accepted to AAAI-IAAI 2027
summary: Lane-level maps provide foundational structured road information for navigation, intelligent driving, and intelligent transportation systems. Understanding road-scene semantics from structural and contextual cues is essential for reliable lane-level map updating, yet remains challenging in production due to occlusions, ambiguous lane markings, temporary obstacles, and viewpoint changes, while downstream workflows require temporally consistent, physically valid, and auditable outputs rather than free-form descriptions. We present RoadState, a production-deployed vision-language system that transforms sequential road-scene observations into structured lane-level semantics for Baidu Maps' map-updating pipeline. Its core model, RoadState-VLM, formulates road-scene understanding as autoregressive state estimation, predicting the current structured road state from the previous observation, previous symbolic state, and current observation. To improve semantic consistency and reasoning fidelity across interdependent road-state dimensions, we introduce Geometric Chain-of-Thought (Geo-CoT), which encodes a directed acyclic graph of semantic dependencies as a domain prior. On a real-world dataset, RoadState-VLM achieves 94.33% mean accuracy across six road-state dimensions, outperforming the strongest fine-tuned VLM baseline, with ablations confirming the complementary gains of Geo-CoT and temporal transition context. In production, a cascaded routing pipeline directs routine cases to lightweight models and reserves complex cases for RoadState-VLM. Deployed since March 2025, RoadState supports lane-level map updating across 360+ cities, reduces overall production costs by 30%, and maintains robust performance under stress testing with human-in-the-loop auditing.
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, including appendices. Accepted to AAAI-IAAI 2027

title: Off-Policy RL with Online Inference Tuning: 1st Place Solution to the CoRL 2026 RoboEval Challenge
comments: 1st place solution of the RoboEval Challenge at CoRL 2026. Code: https://github.com/IliaLarchenko/RoboEvalSolution ; checkpoint: https://huggingface.co/IliaLarchenko/RoboEvalSolution ; project page: https://ilialarchenko.com/projects/roboeval2026/
summary: The CoRL 2026 RoboEval challenge has eight bimanual tasks, and it ranks a policy not only on whether it succeeds but on how: every stage of the task, done safely, efficiently and with both arms in coordination, scored against human demonstrations. My solution has two parts. The generic part, carried over from my LeHome challenge solution, is off-policy RL on a $π_{0.5}$-based policy that is also its own value function. It is trained with AWR and RECAP on advantages of the exact official score, in a loop where every rollout is at the same time a Thompson-sampling trial of about 20 inference parameters. Out of the box, it took the policy to 0.85 RDS on held-out seeds in two days (and it was still very far from convergence). The competition-specific part adds data that local exploration cannot find: generated demonstrations that reach the full reward, and recovery episodes that start from the policy's own failures. The submitted policy reaches 0.990 RDS on my held-out seeds and 0.987 on the official seeds, and it won first place in the challenge, with 0.988 in the organisers' final evaluation on 1,000 unpublished seeds per task.

title: Rethinking Geometric Depth in Monocular 3D Object Detection: A Projection-Consistent Reformulation
summary: Monocular 3D detection (Mono3D) hinges on recovering depth from a single image, for which the geometric formulation $z \approx f \cdot H / h_{2D}$ is widely adopted due to its simplicity and direct grounding in projective geometry. We show that this formulation harbors a systematic, projection-induced bias: substituting the 2D bounding-box height $h_{2D}$ recovers the depth of an object's visible front surface rather than its center, causing size-dependent underestimation that persists even under ground-truth inputs. We address this front-surface bias with MonoPCA, a unified framework built on a projection-consistent reformulation. At its core, PCDepth retains the measurable $h_{2D}$ and closes the gap to center depth through an orientation- and size-aware correction derived from perspective geometry, eliminating the bias without introducing ill-posed regression targets. Because PCDepth couples depth to predicted object size and orientation, attribute perception becomes essential. We therefore introduce GeoAlign, a teacher-student framework that transfers geometric representations from Vision Foundation Models into a lightweight student, strengthening attribute perception at no inference cost. Across four challenging benchmarks, MonoPCA achieves SoTA performance, including a +1.44% AP$_{3D}$ gain on the KITTI leaderboard and +2.80% on Omni3D$_{OUT}$. Code is available at https://github.com/alanzhangcs/MonoPCA.

title: Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization
comments: NeurIPS 2026. 26 pages, 8 figures, 12 tables. Project page: https://ssd-distill.github.io/ Code: https://github.com/ShayanTalaei/SpeculativeSelfDistillation
summary: Many real-world applications require language models to internalize knowledge that was absent from pretraining, to incorporate continually updated facts, or to learn new domain skills. Self-distillation has emerged as a natural approach for this task. A model conditioned on the source material acts as the teacher, and an unconditioned student is trained to reproduce the teacher's behavior closed-book. We propose Speculative Self-Distillation (SSD), an efficient per-token mixed-policy method for self-distillation. The student generates each rollout by default, while the teacher intervenes only at positions where its next-token distribution substantially diverges from the student's. Unlike off-policy distillation with teacher-generated prefixes, this design keeps training rollouts close to the student's test-time behavior, while avoiding the low-signal states that fully on-policy rollouts drift into. In effect, SSD lets the teacher steer the rollout exactly where the privileged context changes the prediction. On three closed-book QA benchmarks measuring fact recall, knowledge updates, and skill acquisition, SSD nearly matches on-policy distillation while using 38-69% fewer supervised tokens and consistently outperforms off-policy distillation on the held-out test set. On a forgetting stress test, SSD retains the most general capability while also achieving the best in-domain accuracy and using less supervision than the on-policy baseline. Overall, SSD establishes a new accuracy-efficiency-forgetting Pareto frontier for self-distillation.

title: GigaEdge Enhance: An SDK for Practical Streaming Speech Enhancement
summary: We present GigaEdge Enhance, an open source SDK for streaming speech enhancement on CPU servers, mobile devices, and in browsers. Applications can build enhancement channels from neural denoising, normalization and dynamics blocks, sample rate conversion, and acoustic echo cancellation where supported. These stages can be combined, while normalization can also run with out a neural model. The release includes an 8 kHz INT8 denoiser and discriminative and hybrid 48 kHz FP32 models. A shared C++ core supports ONNX Runtime and TensorFlow Lite through native interfaces, Android and iOS SDKs, and WebAssembly integration. Independent stream contexts share model resources, and consecutive frames from one stream can be processed in a single inference call. We evaluate the released models on EARS-WHAM v2 and compare their quality and processing costs with RNNoise and DPDFNet2. All tested native and Web configurations process files faster than real time, although larger chunks require more time to collect input. We also measure how many streams a shared model can process on a CPU. Our contribution is a configurable deployment system and an experimental study of how model choice, chunk size, and execution environment affect its use. All reported SDK timing uses ONNX Runtime. Keywords: speech enhancement, streaming inference, cross-platform deployment, temporal frame grouping, computational efficiency

title: From Attack Surface to Defense Architecture: Compositional Security for Agentic Coding Harnesses
summary:
AI coding harnesses couple language models to shells, filesystems, and network sockets so that agents can resolve issues and run tests. That coupling turns the harness into an automated Living-off-the-Land (LotL) platform: once an adversary can inject instructions into retrieved content, dual-use binaries such as bash, curl, and find become the payload rather than a vulnerability to be separately exploited. We argue that security in agentic systems is not an emergent behavioral property of individual language models, but a structural property of the cognitive architecture and of the composition of permissions across interacting agents and humans. Static regex blacklists miss flag permutations and structural attacks, whereas LLM-as-a-Judge guardrails ask a second model to guess physical invariants at tens to hundreds of milliseconds per call while over-blocking benign work.
  We present ActiveSecHarness, a neurosymbolic reference-monitor architecture organized around Separation of Intelligence and Authority across four pillars: (1) Macaroon-inspired HMAC capability tokens across four Trust and Authority Rings; (2) a product taint lattice L_trust x L_sens and a compositional Separation-of-Duties ledger over shared workspace provenance; (3) deterministic OS/subprocess guards; and (4) extended bytecode certificates, split-horizon dual-key audit logs, a self-healing verification loop (CodeVerifier, DualModelReviewer, SecurityTestSynthesizer), and a progressive pedagogical UserWikiManager. On N=252 fixtures and a 12+12 multi-step trajectory suite, Ring 0 achieves FPR=0.000 (0.939 unfitted out-of-sample / 0.962 OS-inert; 1.000 post-audit conformance ABR) in 31.5 us median latency (4,517x faster than a live local LLM-judge) and blocks 12/12 multi-step kill chains at 0.000 benign trajectory FPR (266.7 us/step; ~24 us/step O(1) ledger state folding).

title: Visual Similarity in Adult Word Extension and Artificial Word Learning
comments: v2: multi-encoder study (eight trained encoders plus random-network and pixel controls); 34 pages. Code: https://github.com/patriciomvera/lexical-consensus . Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/MrPatoVera/lexical-consensus-data and https://huggingface.co/datasets/MrPatoVera/lexical-consensus-data-cifar10h
summary: When two objects share a name, how much does their visual similarity explain, and what do the teaching examples add? We studied word extension across ten visual representations: eight trained encoders, a randomly initialized network, and raw pixels. Reanalyzing trial-level data from a large adult word-extension study (Lewis & Frank, 2018; 520 people), we computed each test image's distance to the teaching examples. Within the taught domain, greater distance was associated with less extension for all eight trained encoders and for the untrained network, so the association cannot be attributed only to what the encoders learned; raw pixels showed no negative association. In post hoc models that let the distance slope vary across images, seven of the eight trained encoders retained a negative estimate and five had 95% intervals entirely below zero; the interval of the reference encoder included zero. Whether trial order changes the distance slope, the frozen primary question, remained inconclusive. Example composition changed extension at comparable distances: after three examples, adults extended a word to 1.1% of superordinate items when the examples were subordinate and to 77.5% when they were superordinate. In artificial learners, words joining more distant categories were learned less accurately for six of the eight trained encoders. Every trained encoder correlated with human similarity measures from three datasets, and so did the untrained network, although far more weakly than the trained encoders other than MAE on two of them. In an exploratory comparison on the same images, no common threshold on any trained encoder reproduced the adults' narrow-to-broad gain (at most 66.67 vs. 76.43 percentage points). Cosine distance to the centroid of the teaching examples predicts part of word extension, but does not capture the effect of example composition.

title: RS-JEPA: Remote Sensing Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with Scan-Path Views for Cross-Sensor Image Retrieval
summary: Cross-sensor remote sensing image retrieval aims to find scenes with the same content across heterogeneous sensors, such as SAR and optical or panchromatic (PAN) and multispectral (MS) imagery, without manual labels. Existing self-supervised methods either reconstruct sensor-specific pixel detail, align each image only with its co-registered twin, or rely on large transformers with 118-173M parameters (and up to 398M). We introduce RS-JEPA, a compact joint-embedding predictive framework built on a Vision Mamba encoder shared by both sensors. Since a state-space encoder reads an image as an ordered sequence of patches, we propose scan-path views, which treat two reading orders of the same image as two views with identical pixels and predict the hidden patches in one order from the visible patches in the other.To keep this prediction challenging, we propose Adversarial View Coupling (AVC), which learns the hardest split of the visible patches, and a neighbourhood consensus loss that aligns the scene similarities of both sensors. Extensive experiments on SAR-optical (BEN-14K, CBRSIR-VS) and PAN-MS (DSRSID) benchmarks demonstrate that RS-JEPA achieves the highest F1@5 among twelve re-implemented methods (72.92, 80.35 and 94.43) with a retrieval network of only 3.88M parameters (14.57M in training, 8-16times fewer than prior JEPA retrievers). Like prior methods, RS-JEPA trains on co-registered pairs. Our results highlight reading order as a source of self-supervised views. code: https://github.com/Tanishq251/RSJEPA.

title: eDMD: Endpoint Distribution Matching for Few-Step Diffusion Distillation
summary: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) has emerged as a leading paradigm for distilling diffusion models into few-step students, where an auxiliary fake score model tracks the student's distribution and the discrepancy between the teacher and fake predictions drives the student toward the teacher. In multi-step distillation, although only the student's final output is delivered, existing methods train the fake model on intermediate states or across all denoising steps. Consequently, the student's update signal becomes entangled with intermediate distributions, which can distort the matching direction and remain nonzero even after the student's final outputs already match the teacher distribution. To resolve this mismatch, we propose Endpoint Distribution Matching Distillation (eDMD), which trains a single shared fake model exclusively on the student's final outputs and uses it to correct every denoising step. Our theoretical analysis proves that this endpoint reference guarantees that the distribution matching term vanishes if and only if the student's final output distribution matches the teacher's, regardless of intermediate distributions. Beyond the fake reference, we further strengthen teacher supervision through a precise teacher (PT) that replaces single-step guided predictions with short multi-step trajectories on the final noise interval, paired with a calibrated query density for intermediate steps. Experiments on SD3-Medium, FLUX.2-klein (4B and 9B), and Qwen-Image-2.1 demonstrate that eDMD consistently outperforms existing distribution matching methods for 4-step generation.

title: Quantum Algorithm with Quadratic Speedup for 2D Pattern Matching
summary:
We consider the problem of 2 dimensional pattern matching under Quantum Query model. Here, we are given a rectangular text $T[0..n_1-1][0..n_2-1]$ and a pattern $P[0..m_1 -1][0..m_2-1]$. We take $N = n_1n_2$ and $M = m_1m_2$ as the sizes of text and the pattern respectively (we assume $M < N$). Based upon the Quantum Advantage given by Grover's search (and subsequent Dürr-Høyer search), we create a solution which takes $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{N})$ query complexity to answer if the pattern $P$ exists in $T$.
  Our solution uses deterministic sampling as a primary component. As noted by earlier work in the literature, deterministic sampling is inadequate and witness tables are essential components for 2D matching. In our settings, we assume that the witness table of the pattern is precomputed classically and is available as an oracle to the quantum algorithm. Our main novel component is how to compute and employ a geometric structure called ``skyline" without losing the quantum advantage.

title: Antidistillation is Cheap: Lightweight Distillation-Resistance via Stylistic Corruption
summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a highly effective paradigm for transferring capabilities from large language models (LLMs) to smaller, more specialized student models. In commercial deployments where frontier models are restricted behind black-box APIs, sequence-level distillation remains a potent vector for competitors to clone proprietary capabilities at a fraction of the development cost. Existing defenses mostly rely on surrogate models to manipulate next-token sampling, which increases computational overhead and real-time inference latency. In this work, we propose a lightweight defense that injects style-steering vectors into the teacher model's activations upon malicious queries. The framework allows hosts to customize the target defensive styles and switch among them per request, thereby making it harder for adversaries to identify a stable, learnable signature. Because this inference-time intervention largely preserves answer correctness and avoids the degenerate artifacts of prior defenses, adversaries are misled into believing they are extracting valid teacher outputs. Meanwhile, standard consumers continue to receive original, unmodified responses. Our experiments demonstrate that the framework consistently degrades student learning across model families, with minimal inference overhead. Our approach serves as a low-cost deterrent that raises the attacker's extraction and post-hoc sanitization costs. Code is available at https://github.com/anhtu96/distill-resist.

title: Certificate-Based Verification of Pulsed Field Ablation Models
summary: Computational models of cardiac pulsed field ablation predict the lesion as the tissue where the electric field exceeds a lethal threshold. Their numerical error is rarely bounded, and automated pipelines increasingly run them without an expert checking each result. To verify each run, we separate the question "was the stated model solved correctly?" from the solver that answers it. An untrusted solver returns its answer with a certificate, which consists of a potential with the correct electrode and ground values and an exactly charge-conserving current. A small independent checker verifies the certificate against a written specification of the physics. Using the Prager-Synge hypercircle theorem evaluated in ball arithmetic, it turns the certificate into guaranteed two-sided bounds on the impedance and on the root-mean-square field of every tile of a lesion map, also over a range of blood/tissue conductivity ratios. The bounds cover numerical error only; whether the model describes tissue is a question of validation. A vectorized version of the checker takes about a tenth of our solver's time. For a focal electrode in contact, the tile-resolved depth at 1000 V and 700 V/cm is proven to lie in 3.50-3.75 mm for every ratio from 1.7 to 3.75. For a bipolar catheter, certified depths overlap published in-vivo depths. Where they differ from a published reference model, the certificates prove that the difference is not our numerical error. We compare the certificate with a grid convergence study on the same solver. On graded grids, the study is sharper for local fields but remains an estimate. On uniform grids, it fails to converge at the electrode edge, where the certificate still gives a valid bracket. Solvers that deliberately solve equations other than the specified ones pass the grid convergence study, but the certificates refute the impedances they report or leave them unsupported.

title: Grid-Forming AI Data Centers: Coordinated Grid Support Control from IT Loads and Energy Storage
summary: To exploit the grid-support capability of AI data centers (AIDCs), this paper proposes a grid-forming (GFM) control scheme which coordinates the IT loads and energy storage (ES) in the AIDC. First, the framework of a grid-connected AIDC is presented, with the multi-stage power conversion from the grid to the IT loads presented. A dual GFM scheme is then proposed for the back-to-back converters to provide grid support through coordinated power adjustments from IT loads and ES. In addition, an aggregated power response model is established to characterize the IT-load flexibility considering multiple IT servers executing diverse tasks. Time-domain simulations of a 100 MW grid-connected AIDC demonstrate that the proposed control scheme can effectively support the grid.

title: Editable Video Context: Mid-Context KV-Cache Reuse for Context-Managing Video LLMs
summary: Context Language Models let a model edit its own context, while Suffix Cache Reuse makes edits to text efficient by adjusting the positions of cached keys for surviving tokens. We extend these ideas to video language models with multimodal rotary position embeddings (M-RoPE). We represent a long video as timestamped segments. After viewing a sparsely sampled version, the model selects segments for decoding at 4x the frame rate, and the remaining segments are removed from its context. Our rebuild method reuses the KV cache of surviving segments by rotating their keys with a single offset shared by the temporal, height, and width components of Qwen2.5-VL's M-RoPE. A content-hashed cache also avoids repeating vision-encoder computation for those segments. In preliminary experiments with Qwen2.5-VL-7B on synthetic needle-in-a-video-haystack questions over public-domain films, the method reduces prefill tokens and end-to-end rebuild latency relative to full recomputation while usually producing the same answer. Densifying the segment containing the answer improves accuracy when that segment is known. When the model selects segments itself, accuracy does not improve: it rarely identifies a needle that was absent from the sparse sample. We release the code, raw logs, and scripts used to reproduce the paper's results.

title: Robot Demonstration Videos Should Include Transparency Disclosures
summary: This paper argues that the robotics and AI community should adopt disclosure standards for demonstration videos. As physical and financial constraints limit direct public access to embodied AI, public dissemination of progress in robotics is mainly through curated demonstration videos rather than direct experience with the technology. In a large-scale (N=9,341), pre-registered experiment across six countries, we find that the general public struggles to discern both the visual authenticity (e.g., distinguishing real footage from CGI) and behavioral authenticity (e.g., distinguishing autonomy from teleoperation) of robot demonstration videos. The omission of these details distorts public perception, leading people to overestimate the ability of robots to perform tasks and navigate real world environments. Using evidence from behavioral science, we design a disclosure intervention and demonstrate that the inclusion of clear disclosures in robot demonstration videos significantly improves discernment of visual and behavioral authenticity, as well as understanding robots' capabilities. We propose the adoption of disclosure standards for robot demonstration videos to accurately calibrate public expectations and promote transparency in robotics research.

title: On-policy distillation as a Backdoor Propagation Channel
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is emerging as an important paradigm for the post training of large language models, improving student models by leveraging supervision generated online by teacher models. However, whether this process also transfers latent security risks from teacher models to student models remains insufficiently studied. In this work, we reveal a new security risk in which an attacker first implants a conditional backdoor into the teacher model through supervised fine tuning (SFT), after which OPD can transfer the backdoor to the student model with only an extremely small proportion of trigger prompt exposure. More concerningly, we find that such backdoor transfer is substantially stronger under OPD than under conventional distillation methods, suggesting that OPD may provide an efficient channel for propagating backdoors across models. Our mechanistic analysis shows that the backdoor signal is primarily transmitted through anomalous differences in the conditional probabilities produced by the teacher model for triggered and clean inputs, and is gradually internalized into the internal representations of the student model during training. Furthermore, we investigate how to suppress such anomalous conditional probability signals at the source of distillation supervision and, based on this analysis, propose an OPD training method tailored to this conditional backdoor propagation setting to mitigate the risk of backdoor transfer induced by untrusted teacher supervision.

title: SplatFlow3D: Learning Scene Flow via 3D Motion Feature Splatting
summary: Considering the motion continuity and stability of 3D objects over short inter-frame intervals, introducing multi-frame settings in scene flow estimation can potentially address occlusion. In this paper, we propose a two-frame backbone, SimpleFlow3D, which integrates dense information from the image plane and sparse information from the depth dimension in a decoupling-followed-by-coupling manner by hierarchically constructing the 3D motion feature. SimpleFlow3D achieves SOTA results with minimal parameters. We also propose a weight-sharing multi-frame framework to splat the previous 3D motion feature to the current estimation process. The framework unifies the first and non-first frame inference by constructing pseudo inputs. After combining the proposed framework and backbone, the newly born multi-frame method SplatFlow3D further advances the state of the art. It achieves lower errors than the two-frame backbone, with fewer parameters than current methods. On both KITTI and Spring, SplatFlow3D ranked 1st over all published and submitted methods. Experiments show that SplatFlow3D improves occlusion handling, non-rigid motion estimation, and generalization to real-world scenes. Code is available at https://github.com/wwsource/SplatFlow3D.

title: Offline-First Quantized AI: Design and Evaluation of an On-Device Maternal-Health Assistant for Low-Connectivity Environments
summary: Offline language models could extend access to maternal-health information where internet connectivity is unreliable, but deployment requires both clinically appropriate responses and feasible local execution. This study evaluated an Android assistant using ready-made quantized models, a clinically validated local knowledge package, conversation history, and optional local retrieval. Gemma 4 E2B and Qwen3.5 0.8B were compared on 45 conversations and 312 turns per configuration. Gemma retained context more consistently, whereas Qwen generated faster and used less memory. Clinician assessment of 150 Gemma responses across nine clinical domains yielded a mean quality score of 3.80/4, with 147 responses meeting the acceptance criterion. In 74 matched RAG-on/off questions, 11 RAG-on answers improved, 52 were comparable, four were degraded by returned content, and seven were lower-rated without clear evidence that retrieval caused the difference. Full-cohort mean differences were small and uncertain. In a sensitivity analysis excluding flagged cases, RAG-on had descriptively higher mean usefulness, safety, correctness, and actionability in the conditional 70-pair subset excluding the four flagged pairs from both conditions. Physical- device testing demonstrated offline responses on a 6 GB Android handset, with a 14.3 s median latency, alongside successful reconnection synchronization in the integrated application. Together, the findings characterize the integrated offline maternal-health assistant within the designed and tested benchmark, retrieval pipeline, and handset conditions.

title: Quadrature-Induced Local Minima in Structure-Preserving Lotka-Volterra Control
summary:
We study how the choice of harvest quadrature affects optimal control in a positivity-preserving Lotka--Volterra scheme. With harvesting alone, counting the prey removed at each step gives a strictly convex cost. Using the prey density at the start of the step overestimates the catch and can create a strict local minimum with cost above the global minimum. We certify the global minimizers in a two-step example by rational root isolation. A second example shows that, with both species present and positive diffusion, a strict local minimizer for the old-state rule admits a descent direction under the flux rule.
  For nonnegative $H^1$ initial data and positive diffusivities in one space dimension, the two rules give costs, weighted gradients and Hessians that differ by $O(τ)$ at the same control, uniformly in the spatial mesh. Here $τ$ is the time step. If the old-state Hessian is uniformly coercive near a stationary control, the flux objective has a local minimizer within $O(τ)$ of it. With uniformly bounded tracking targets, a large enough effort penalty makes both objectives strongly convex for all sufficiently small time steps. We also derive exact discrete adjoints and Hessian actions, prove a common variational limit with an IMEX discretization, and compare stationary controls across grids. The same harvest accounting applies to weighted production--destruction systems.

title: When Should Decision Models Compare Candidates?
summary: Language-model agents frequently select among candidate actions, such as tools and web elements. Should decision models score candidates independently or allow their scores to depend on other candidates? We investigate this question by comparing three approaches: Pointwise scoring, Setwise scoring, and Candidate Attention. Across five agent-decision benchmarks, Pointwise scoring remains competitive, while Setwise scoring performs better on some tool-selection and binary-decision tasks. Candidate Attention does not consistently improve upon Pointwise scoring, despite allowing cross-candidate interaction. Using two controlled synthetic tasks, we further examine whether models learn to use candidate-set information. With targeted relational training, Setwise models learn candidate dependencies and generalize to shifted inputs, while Candidate Attention shows weaker transfer. Our results show that access to other candidates does not guarantee effective comparison, and that its benefits depend on both task requirements and training.

title: A staggered discontinuous Galerkin neural network method with a computable error decomposition
summary: We develop a staggered discontinuous Galerkin neural network (SDGNN) method for scalar elliptic problems with a computable error decomposition. The staggered discontinuous Galerkin (SDG) method requires only local continuity of its trial functions and gives a square, inf-sup stable system without stabilization parameters; we carry this structure over to neural networks. Networks on the patches of a staggered mesh satisfy the SDG continuity conditions for all parameter values, and the loss, the squared dual norm of the SDG weak residual, is computed without the SDG finite element approximation or any solution data, so that the training is unsupervised. By the inf-sup stability, the loss is equivalent, with computable constants, to the square of the training error, the distance between the SDG projection of the network and the SDG finite element approximation, so that the full error is bounded by the discretization error, a multiple of the square root of the loss, and the network projection error. For a fixed network on uniform square meshes, this error decays exponentially in the polynomial degree. The weak residual requires no derivatives of the networks and no penalty or stabilization weights, and the scalar trial functions may jump across the midlines of the primal cells. Numerical experiments show that the square root of the loss tracks the error during training, that prescribed jumps across a square and a circular interface are captured consistently over the initializations, and that the method is more accurate than physics-informed neural networks at the same parameter counts.

title: ThinkWAM: Rethinking Latent Futures for Action Refinement
comments: 21 pages, 12 figures, 15 tables, including references and appendix. Project page: https://thinkwam-project.github.io/
summary: World-action models (WAMs) couple action generation with predictions of future states. However, an initial action chunk may deviate from the correct plan implied by the predicted future, and the predicted future often fails to reflect how it relates to the specific action output, leaving the prediction-action coupling underexploited and making the action hard to correct before execution. We introduce ThinkWAM, a latent WAM that establishes bidirectional feedback before execution through a proposal-rethink-refine loop: the policy first proposes a complete action chunk, the proposal corrects multi-horizon future latents through a learned residual, and the corrected latents are injected into a second pass of the same action head, which generates the executable chunk. An affordance-guided observation-action memory and a near-fine, far-coarse multi-horizon prediction scheme, both motivated by predictive coding, support this loop, and all prediction stays in latent space. ThinkWAM achieves 98.70% success on LIBERO, 84.76% on LIBERO-Plus without OOD fine-tuning, 85.75%/65.85% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean/Random, and 65.17% on RoboCasa24. ThinkWAM achieves 64.4% mean success across three real-world OOD conditions. The mean two-pass inference latency per action chunk is 153.48 ms on LIBERO, 164.61 ms on RoboTwin, and 101.2 ms on the Galaxea A1Z. Ablations show complementary gains from rethinking and affordance guidance. Diagnostics indicate that proposal-conditioned corrections change both predicted futures and action trajectories, consistent with the gains from rethinking in these ablations.

title: RegimeCouncil: Paired-Evidence Routing For Memory Conflict Governance In LLM Agents
summary: Alongside memory storage and retrieval, a fundamental challenge in long-term LLM agent systems is how the agent should act when stored memories conflict with an evolving world. Facts often go stale without explicit deletion, so the conflict surfaces before the store is refreshed: delayed feedback shows that acting on one outdated record hurt, but not whether suppression should stay on that fact (a local policy) or extend to other stored facts (a global policy). Existing systems hard-code one of these scopes at design time. We formulate this online choice, under hidden validity and delayed feedback, as memory conflict governance, and propose RegimeCouncil, a lightweight router that keeps both scopes as advisors and arbitrates between them without retraining the LLM. Each memory-assisted response is scored against a no-memory anchor, by off-path paired comparison or by inverse-propensity estimation from the executed action alone. A Local Advisor tracks only the queried fact, a Global Advisor pools recent outcomes across the store, and an asymmetric Meta Governor follows Local by default, switching to Global only when pooling yields a strictly positive recent utility margin. We prove that using delayed outcomes escapes the prompt-only regret floor, that neither fixed scope suffices alone, and that this margin gate switches within bounded time. On LongMemEval streams, historical drift in TempLAMA and TAQA, delays $τ\in [1, 96]$, and sparse or bandit feedback, with Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed scope in all 30 held-out settings, by 5.2-7.3 points on disagreement episodes and +27.9 points over standalone cold-start fallback under clustered shifts, while cutting harmful stale-memory use at microsecond overhead.

title: Connections Between Instrumental Variable, Pseudo-Linear Regression, and Prediction Error Methods in Terms of Their Minimized Criteria
summary: This paper explores the connections between the criteria directly or indirectly minimized by Prediction Error (PE), Instrumental Variable (IV), and Pseudo-Linear Regression (PLR) algorithms for the identification of output-error models. By definition, PE methods aim to minimize the variance of the prediction error. In contrast, the correlation functions appearing in the stationarity conditions of IV and PLR algorithms are not the gradients of any underlying loss function involving a signal variance. Nevertheless, if the true system lies in the model set, we show that one IV algorithm minimizes asymptotically the variance of an unmeasurable signal called the equivalent prediction error. This signal was introduced previously to analyze the bias distribution of PLR schemes. It turns out that, regardless of whether the true system lies in the model set, some iterative IV and PLR algorithms aim to minimize the prediction error variance and can therefore be interpreted as indirect PE algorithms.

title: Data-driven model reduction: An identification perspective using Generalized Bases of Orthonormal Functions
summary: This paper proposes a data-driven model order reduction approach based on system identification concepts. A revised equation error formulation is introduced, in which the model is parameterized using Generalized Bases of Orthonormal Transfer Functions (GBOFs). The generalized reduction problem is formulated in the Hambo frequency domain associated with the GBOF transform. The frequency-domain fit of the reduced-order model is adjusted through the selection of the basis poles. A fit indicator depending on these poles is introduced, providing valuable heuristic guidance for their selection.

title: As Student Rollouts Continue, Visual Backdoors Keep Growing
summary:
Conventional knowledge distillation can facilitate the propagation of backdoors from teacher models to student models. However, how this risk manifests in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remains insufficiently studied. OPD has recently emerged as an important post-training paradigm for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Unlike traditional offline distillation, OPD does not require teacher-generated responses. Instead, it uses the teacher's probability distributions to supervise response trajectories generated online by the student. Since the initial student model typically generates benign responses and receives no explicit supervision from malicious target responses, OPD appears to offer some inherent resistance to backdoor propagation.
  In this paper, we challenge this intuition and reveal a more subtle risk of visual backdoor propagation in OPD. Through experiments across multiple model families and datasets, together with theoretical analysis, we identify three main findings. First, unlike the relatively gradual propagation observed in traditional offline distillation, backdoors rarely emerge in OPD at low poisoning ratios. However, the attack success rate rapidly approaches 100% once a critical threshold is exceeded. Second, backdoor propagation does not depend on explicit malicious responses. Instead, it is driven by the continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass assigned by the teacher. Finally, based on these findings, we propose a novel trigger design that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection. These findings further reveal an overlooked mechanism of backdoor propagation in OPD and highlight its potential security risks.

title: Unified Residual Translation for Paired Image Restoration
summary: Paired image restoration spans changes in imaging contrast, sensor modality, and spatial resolution. These settings differ in their input channels and target grids, raising the question of how much of the prediction pipeline must be specialized to each task. We present the Unified Residual Translator (URT), which separates fixed channel and scale mapping from learned residual prediction. A deterministic reference uses channel averaging, replication, or bicubic interpolation to match the target dimensions, while a NAFNet encoder-decoder predicts an additive correction from the complete input. Separately trained instances share the prediction rule, $\ell_1$ objective, and optimizer across MRI contrast synthesis, visible-to-infrared translation, SAR-to-optical translation, and real-camera super-resolution. Across six task and scale settings, URT achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM among the evaluated baselines on IXI, SEN1-2, and RealSR $\times3$ and $\times4$. It reaches 30.774dB on IXI and 13.478dB on SEN1-2, with luminance PSNR of 33.596, 28.742, and 27.342dB at the three RealSR scales. On LLVIP, it ranks second in PSNR and SSIM. A study of four spectral alternatives identifies complementary benefits of fitted references and bandwise residual gains. Together, these results support explicit dimensional alignment and learned residual correction as a common formulation for heterogeneous paired imaging tasks.

title: LoopZip: Visual Token Compression for Efficient Looped Vision-Language Models
summary: Looped vision-language models (VLMs) deepen computation by reusing shared layers, approaching larger models' capabilities with fewer parameters and easing the storage and deployment burden of stacking independent layers. However, repeatedly processing long visual sequences still incurs substantial compute and GPU memory costs. Visual token compression reduces these costs by shortening sequences. Existing methods mainly select original tokens directly or combine selection with aggregation. In looped models, the former may overlook changing token importance across calls and discard information needed later; the latter lack joint consideration of output changes across calls, limiting information preservation. We propose LoopZip, a training-free visual token compression algorithm addressing both issues. Visual aggregation builds a compact candidate pool before the looped backbone, and cross-invocation selection averages instruction attention from the first two existing calls of the same shared attention layer to retain tokens needed by both states. Weight-tied value correction then jointly fits shared visual-value adjustments to both pre-selection layer outputs, reducing output deviations across states. To validate LoopZip's effectiveness, we conduct extensive experiments covering two open-source looped VLMs, eleven benchmarks, and three pruning ratios. On LoopVL-1B, LoopZip retains 97.16% of the original model's performance at 50% pruning ratio and exceeds the strongest baseline by 5.36% at 87.5% pruning ratio. Across Hugging Face Transformers, vLLM, and SGLang, LoopVL-1B with LoopZip reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 58.36%-58.98% and achieves 2.01-2.47x end-to-end speedups over the original model.

title: LoopPrune: Recurrent Pruning for Looped Diffusion Transformers
summary: Looped diffusion Transformers reuse shared blocks to deepen computation and match larger models with fewer parameters, reducing storage and deployment burdens. Yet repeated attention and MLP computations remain costly. Pruning reduces storage and computation by removing redundant parameters or units. Training-free methods struggle to resolve recurrent contributions, while training-based methods lack explicit constraints on position-specific errors affecting later inputs and final outputs. We propose LoopPrune, a pruning and recovery framework addressing these requirements. Recurrent importance estimation combines shared-removal effects and position variation to select a shared structure; shared reconstruction pools recurrent input statistics to compensate weights. Loop-position recovery compares complete denoising predictions at identical student states and matches text guidance, updating all student parameters against a fixed dense teacher. Extensive experiments across four open-source models, six benchmarks, and three pruning paradigms demonstrate effectiveness. At 30% structured parameter pruning, Looped-DiT B/16 retains 93.14% of dense six-benchmark average accuracy, exceeding the best baseline by 9.49%. Across PyTorch, vLLM-Omni, and SGLang Diffusion, pruned SDXSv3 reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 34.36-44.64% and accelerates denoising 1.46-1.74x over dense models.

title: Dissecting the GPU Load/Store Unit and Exposing Its Security Risks
summary: GPUs are the main platform for large-scale machine learning and power the largest supercomputers. Their load/store units (LSUs) often determine kernel performance and have been exploited in prior attacks. Yet what is known about the LSU is only a few isolated mechanisms and parameters, and even a single one has been enough for an attack. In particular, it is still unknown what a load costs, where loads contend, and even whether a warp can starve due to contention. Until each is measured, neither its security risk nor a defense is known. We reverse-engineer how the LSU serves load instructions on recent NVIDIA GPUs with microbenchmarks and analyze the security implications. We give a cycle-accurate latency formula for a global L1 hit or shared memory access from the addresses it touches, whose address-dependent terms are bank conflicts and the L1 tag lookup; we show that loads contend at both, and that when the LSU pipeline is full a warp can starve a warp of a later-launched block. We then show that the LSU's attack surface is far broader than prior attacks revealed: through channels never exploited before, it can leak information, communicate covertly, and degrade colocated workloads. Through either global bank conflicts or tag lookups alone, we recover a full AES-128 key under the threat model of prior GPU AES timing attacks. Under NVIDIA's Multi-Process Service (MPS), the bank access and the tag lookup each open a covert channel across processes, whose rate rises with each GPU generation. Also under MPS, this starvation lets one warp slow a colocated cuBLAS matrix multiplication by up to 750x on the A100 and 563x on the H100.

title: Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving
comments: Equal contribution: John Gideon and Anshul Gupta. 24 pages, 8 figures. Supplementary video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IvG7YobBwdY Project page: https://toyotaresearchinstitute.github.io/DIVERT/
summary: Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. We plan to publicly release the code and data.

title: Asymmetric Optical Image Watermarking
comments: 29 pages, 14 figures, 20 tables. v2 adds an appendix and two reference hardware designs
summary: Watermark detectors held by a provider cannot be checked by third parties, and a party that can detect a mark can usually also forge it. We study a two-layer image watermark in which the Fourier transform at the core of the pipeline is performed by a coherent optical 4F unit. Layer 1 carries an Ed25519 signature bound to the image content in Fourier magnitudes, so anyone with the public key verifies offline. Layer 2 is a key-defined carrier written by a secret phase hologram and read by a matched-filter correlator. The optics is a scalar-diffraction simulation with finite modulator bits, pixel aperture, pupil, defocus, misalignment, and sensor noise. No hardware is built. All criteria were fixed in a hashed specification before any optical result. The simulated optical signer reproduces the digital pipeline (field error 1.7e-15, bit agreement 99.997%), verifies at least 99.5% of 877 images under each of 8 post-sensor settings, one unattacked, and accepts none of 40,670 unmarked images. The optical carrier is key-selective: the matched key detects it on 99.8% of the unattacked images, and detection falls to 0% under a scale error of 1% and to 0% under a mask shift of 1 bin. Security rests on the signature and the content binding, for which we separate what is provable from what is measured.

title: NIRJALA: Draining the Sea out of Gaussian Splatting with Three-Path Optics and Reversible Physics
comments: Withdrawn by the authors due to unresolved data provenance and authorization issues affecting the experimental results, tables, and figures in Sections 4--5 (Tables 1--6 and Figures 4--9). The manuscript was submitted prematurely without complete verification
summary: Water does not just tint an underwater photograph; it rewrites it. Each pixel mixes attenuated scene radiance, backscattered light, and scene light scattered forward on its way to the camera, and many combinations of scene and water explain the same pixels. Most Gaussian-splatting methods for underwater scenes model only the first two effects and remove the water by dividing by a transmission that decays exponentially with range, so their inversion gain grows without bound. We present NIRJALA (Sanskrit for "without water"), a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that recovers water-free appearance and geometry together. TRIVENI, a three-path image formation model, adds a range-saturating forward-scattering term to direct transmission and backscatter; we prove that this keeps the inversion gain bounded at every range and bound how errors in the estimated backscatter and attenuation propagate into the recovered colours. PRATIBIMBA, a reversible physics anchor, ties a flexible neural water model to a ten-parameter physical model in both directions, so scene content cannot hide inside the water. SAMARASA collects the physics-informed objectives, including a range-binned colour prior. To score water removal against ground truth, we built SAJALA ("with water"), a 30-scene suite path-traced in Blender Cycles with water-free images, depth, and normals under controlled water colour and turbidity. On SAJALA, NIRJALA raises PSNR from 24.34 to 24.76 dB and lowers depth AbsRel from 0.109 to 0.091 against the strongest baseline; on real SeaThru-NeRF scenes it lowers LPIPS from 0.194 to 0.175 while rendering at 44 FPS. We also discuss where appearance metrics and geometry disagree underwater, and the limits of our evaluation.

title: Safe to Omit, Worth Omitting? Keeping the Answer and Cutting Latency When an LLM Agent Skips Another's Message
comments: 61 pages, 11 figures, 45 tables. v2: revised presentation (Algorithm 1; the two prospective tests and batched serving in the main results); appendix reordered by question and audit records moved to the code repository. Code: https://github.com/Piedpiperrr/safe-to-omit; data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/AgentsSci/ICLR2027-SafeToOmit
summary: In multi-agent systems, a receiver agent often waits for a helper agent's message (text or its latent KV cache), which can improve performance but adds latency. We study when a receiver agent can skip the message safely (the final answer rarely changes) and beneficially (the time saved exceeds the cost of deciding). Our mechanism reads the receiver agent's confidence without the message and uses a finite-sample test to certify a threshold at which, with high probability, at most 5% of skipped answers change; if none passes, the system keeps communicating. We test it on OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU-Pro with three Qwen model pairs, on cross-family agents, and on SQuAD and GSM8K. Four insights emerge. First, oracle headroom is weak evidence that messages help: control inputs without answer-specific content, matched to change answers as often as real messages, reproduce a median 76% of the oracle's gain. Second, whether a message can be skipped depends on how often and how predictably it alters the answer, not on its accuracy; every certified KV-cache path is less accurate than the receiver agent alone. Third, where text messages help, skipping keeps most of their gain: on unseen questions in the four such settings, the policies skip 59 to 80% and keep an estimated 76 to 95% of the gain. In two prospective tests with all rules fixed in advance, our mechanism skips a three-agent system's verifier on 39.9% of sealed questions, keeping 12.55 of its 12.80-point gain, and a 32B helper on 68.4% of held-out questions, keeping its whole gain. Fourth, safety does not determine efficiency: at batch size one, skipping text saves hundreds of milliseconds per query and skipping KV cache far less. Certification extends to SQuAD but not to GSM8K. In eleven tests on unseen questions, every certified policy we could test kept its change rate's 95% upper bound below 5% under our answer parsers.

title: DOCK: Dual-Stream-Inspired Self-Supervised Object-Centric Representations Grounded in Robot Kinematics
summary: Latent-space planners select actions by comparing the embedding of a predicted future image with that of a goal image. This assumes that distance in the embedding reflects how far the scene is from the goal. We profile this assumption with simulator-executed futures, which removes prediction error. For six frozen DINO and V-JEPA encoders, feature distance barely tracks the object's distance to its goal: the rank correlation is at most 0.11, against 0.87 for object-mask centroids. It is dominated by background and robot patches, and frozen-feature readouts capture the arm far better than the object. Inspired by the ventral (what) and dorsal (where/how) visual streams, we propose DOCK, which learns an object representation whose changes agree with measured physical motion. A grasped object moves with the gripper, so forward kinematics on the joint angles gives a proxy for the object's displacement without annotation. From 9,951 held-object transport trajectories in 21 simulated kitchen scenes, we mine 404K displacement pairs and train three components: an object token pooled from patch features (what), a spatial ruler that makes differences of readout coordinates equal to measured displacements (where), and a dynamics predictor over object tokens (how). Used as a planning cost, the learned representation places the object in 15 of 21 tasks, as many as an oracle that reads the true object position, while mask geometry reaches 10 and frozen feature distance 9. It still solves the most tasks when the unseen robot arm is visible, and its ranking transfers to held-out layouts with unseen object instances and categories without any adaptation.

title: Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge
summary: Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.

title: ReCoCo: From Patches to Compositions for Visual Representation Learning
summary: Self-supervised learning has produced powerful visual representations, yet learning strong dense features remains challenging. While consistency between augmented views provides strong image-level supervision, extending this principle to local visual content is less straightforward. Existing approaches often match individual patches across views or identify coherent regions, introducing uncertainties in correspondence estimation and assumptions about how visual content should be grouped. We introduce ReCoCo (Regional Composition Consistency), a principled approach that extends cross-view consistency to the regional level without requiring such correspondences or semantic grouping. ReCoCo represents the content shared between augmented views through compositions of their patch-level predictions over learned visual prototypes. By aligning these compositions, the model learns from regions containing multiple visual concepts without requiring them to be separated beforehand. ReCoCo integrates naturally with teacher-student self-distillation and introduces no additional learned parameters. Extensive experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in frozen-feature segmentation, clustering, and regional retrieval while maintaining competitive image-level recognition, alleviating the trade-off between dense and global representation quality.

title: Hardness of "Infinite Energy" Puzzles
comments: Appears in the Proceedings of the 52nd International Conference on Current Trends in Theory and Practice of Computer Science (Sofsem 2027)
summary:
Infinite Energy (by Light Potato, 2025) is a single-player puzzle in which one wires a network of sockets so that, after every power source is unplugged, energy keeps circulating and leaves every board energized. We study several variants of the game and the complexity of deciding whether an instance can be won. The variants can be played at https://infinite-energy-peer-review.netlify.app, which also has worked examples of the reduction techniques.
  The colorless game, with connectability given by an arbitrary matrix, is NP-hard (by reduction from Hamiltonian Path) and lies in PSPACE. We give a seven-socket instance winnable only by charging a temporary battery loop and then breaking it, so the natural "charge and keep" strategy fails. We reduce NP-membership to one conjecture: that every winnable instance has a winning play in which no socket is charged twice.
  Two variants bound the complexity more tightly. The unconstrained variant, in which connectability is unrestricted, is $\mathsf{TC}^0$-complete under $\mathsf{AC}^0$ Turing reductions (hence in L). The geometric variant, in which connectability is set by proximity of points in $\mathbb{R}^k$, stays NP-hard for every fixed $k \ge 2$ via reduction from Hamiltonian Path over grid graphs. The one-dimensional case is open. The colored variant is NP-hard, though a matching upper bound remains open.

title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report
summary: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.

title: LLM-based Personalized Travel Planner
summary: Effective travel planning requires handling multiple information sources, managing constraints, and tailoring recommendations to user preferences. While LLMs have introduced dynamic, context-aware decision-making, single-agent models often struggle with complex multi-step reasoning, constraint adherence, and modular execution. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hierarchical multi-agent framework where a supervising chatbot agent coordinates specialized agents for schedule validation, user query formulation, real-time data retrieval, and constraint-aware itinerary generation. By integrating LLM reasoning, external APIs, and iterative refinement mechanisms based on a deterministic, multi-dimensional scoring framework, our approach ensures adaptability, efficiency, and personalization. Evaluations on the well-known TravelPlanner benchmark demonstrate improvements in Budget Constraint planning by 10\%, wider constraints set-based planning by 25\%, and personalized planning results by 45\%. compared to the ReAct baseline. Our code is available at https://github.com/nimashaklaa/TravelPlanner_Research

title: Bradley-Terry Training Can Distort Outcome Probabilities of Initially Accurate Language World Models
summary: Comparative feedback, in which a judge says which of two candidate outcomes is closer to what happened, is a practical way to train language world models that assign probabilities to an action's outcomes. We show that, fitted with a Bradley-Terry objective, it need not teach the true outcome probabilities and can distort accurate ones. On a simulated robot push with enumerated outcome distributions, this objective takes a model that is accurate on unseen layouts (hazard error 2.4 percentage points, pp) and moves 33 to 43 pp of its probability onto outcomes that none of a condition's enumerated branches produces. The cause is the objective, not the comparisons: its optimum, computed before training, predicts where the model ends up, and a likelihood that knows the judge's rule learns from the same comparisons without the shift. The shift is robust: it recurs on unseen conditions, under five candidate laws and a three-fold denser enumeration, and about 29 pp remain without the physically impossible events. Its cost is conditional: with those events it inflates hazard probabilities, and a threshold inherited from the pre-feedback model costs about 3 pp of utility per decision on trained and 1 to 2 pp on unseen conditions, through false rejects; without them the utility loss averages below 1 pp over six seeds, though a small regret in action choice remains. Audits of readout, response and decision trace the effect from probabilities to actions.

title: LoopedWAM: Looped World Action Models for Elastic Inference
summary: World action models (WAMs) couple generative video modeling with robotic action prediction but typically require large video and action transformers, limiting deployment efficiency. We present LoopedWAM, a compact WAM that recurrently applies a shared six-block core in each expert, executing 30 transformer layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert. To account for their asymmetric inference costs, the video and action experts can operate at different depths: visual features are computed once per query, whereas action computation repeats at every sampling step. We further propose elastic self-distillation, which trains a single elastic checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, across action-depth and sampling-step budgets. With only 0.58B policy parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM achieves 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, while using $7.4\times$ less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched inference measurements. On LIBERO, LoopedWAM-E achieves 96.0% success in 27.6 ms or 95.2% in 24.7 ms on an H100, providing multiple accuracy-latency operating points from a single checkpoint; with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of LoopedWAM on all three benchmarks. Ablations demonstrate that weight-shared depth preserves competitive performance, while aggressive action-depth reduction requires explicit budget-aware training. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, LoopedWAM succeeds in 71.3% of 80 trials across four tasks.

title: CACO: Coverage-Aware Coordinated Optimization for Continuous Generative Retrieval
summary: Continuous generative retrievers powered by flow matching and diffusion sample multiple queries in item embedding space for approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search under fixed budgets. However, existing generative retrievers can suffer from retrieval overlap under uncoordinated sampling, whereas explicit diversity guidance to broaden the candidate set may induce relevance drift as it lacks direct feedback on the value of additional items. We introduce CACO (Coverage-Aware Coordinated Optimization), a self-supervised post-training framework coordinating queries from frozen flow-matching and diffusion retrievers toward complementary item coverage with negligible latency overhead. Using empirical retrieval frequencies across sampled reference queries as a relevance proxy, CACO formulates a label-free coverage objective that improves recall across all 30 backbone-dataset settings in offline experiments. To avoid the overhead of sampling reference queries at inference, CACO employs a coordinated query adjustment network combining inter-query bidirectional attention with gated relative directions, updating queries via bounded tangent-space projection and spherical retraction. During training, CACO applies tangential antithetic perturbations and counterfactual single-query replacement to measure each query's marginal gain, yielding an unbiased gradient estimator of smoothed set coverage across non-differentiable ANN search. On eight public benchmarks and an in-house 24-partition streaming industrial dataset, CACO improves Recall@100 and Recall@400 by up to 23.7% and 23.9% over the strongest baseline, cuts inter-query overlap by 53.3%-64.9%, and adds only 0.5%-3.0% inference latency.

title: When Safety Rationales Hallucinate: Diagnosing and Grounding Multimodal Safety Guards
summary: Multimodal safety guards increasingly generate rationales alongside safety predictions, yet whether these rationales are reliable remains largely unexplored. We systematically study *rationale hallucination* from two perspectives: visual rationale hallucination, where rationales contain unsupported visual facts, and safety attribution hallucination, where grounded content is assigned an incorrect safety interpretation. Across rationale-generation methods, multiple vision-language backbones, and safety datasets, we find that rationale hallucination is widespread and does not consistently diminish with higher classification accuracy or increased model scale. Further analysis of the Think-with-Image paradigm shows that hallucination is concentrated in fine-grained attributes and relations, while visual tools are often invoked infrequently or without sufficient spatial focus. Based on these findings, we propose *Tool-Contrastive Grounding Reinforcement Learning* (TCG-RL), which rewards tool use only when it improves rationale grounding over a tool-free reference. TCG-RL substantially reduces rationale hallucination while maintaining competitive safety prediction performance. By revealing the gap between prediction correctness and rationale reliability, our study motivates a shift in multimodal safety guarding from outcome-only evaluation toward safety decisions that are both accurate and verifiably grounded.

title: Agentic Scaling of Embodied Tasks in Simulation for Synthetic Data Collection and Policy Evaluation
comments: Version 1 was posted on arXiv before all listed authors had agreed to make this version public. After discussing the matter, all authors agreed to withdraw the paper and authorized the submitting author, Xiaolei Zhou, to request withdrawal on their behalf
summary: Scaling embodied interaction data requires a broad collection of usable tasks, yet specifying and validating each task instance remains costly. We present AgenticTask, an agent-based framework that expands existing task collections under human intent. Its central representation links interaction requirements to object and part bindings, scene and robot configurations, initial conditions, and completion criteria. A task-generation agent reuses interaction structure to construct supported variations and revises incompatible configurations using validation feedback. A task-execution agent uses the same bindings and geometric records to select robot-supported skills and check completion against the original task criteria. On RoboCasa, the framework builds the AgenticTask collection, saving 16,450 task instances from 20,323 construction attempts at a throughput of 166.97 saved instances per elapsed hour, with 62.26% of construction attempts passing the configured physical checks. The execution agent completes approximately 38% of evaluated tasks, with successful cases spanning object placement, articulated manipulation, and sequential arrangement. Diagnostic analysis identifies improvement priorities in construction reliability, action selection, task-robot compatibility, and runtime integration. Together, these results demonstrate task-collection expansion with measured construction productivity and concrete execution evidence, providing a foundation for subsequent interaction-data collection for embodied AI.
