title: Perfect Clustering in Extremely Sparse Multilayer Networks with Groupwise Subspace Structure
summary: The paper studies a multilayer network on the same collection of nodes, where each layer follows the Generalized Random Dot Product Graph Model. Furthermore, all layers can be partitioned into groups, each group with its own unique latent subspace structure, but otherwise the matrices of connection probabilities can all be different. This setting is extremely general and includes most multilayer network models as special cases. In addition, we are interested in the situation where the layer networks may be extremely sparse and, therefore, the layer-by-layer analysis is unreliable. This problem can also be seen as a generalization of the classic setting in which one recovers a shared structure across an entire collection of matrices, extending it to the case where such structures are shared only within specific groups of matrices. The key task in this setting is to recover the groups of layers with unique subspace structures, since, after that, the information in those groups of layers can be pooled together by well-studied methods. Until now, clustering of layers in such networks was based on layer-by-layer analysis, which required the multilayer network to be sufficiently dense. Our paper is the first to provide a tensor-based approach to the problem that combines information from all layers in an unconventional manner. Our theoretical results, established under intuitive and non-restrictive assumptions, assert that the new technique achieves perfect clustering under sparsity conditions that, up to logarithmic factors, coincide with the computational lower bound derived for a much simpler model. The paper also delivers a nuanced message about the applicability of the new technique.

title: Fractional domatic number and minimum degree
summary:
The domatic number of a graph $G$ is the maximum number of pairwise disjoint dominating sets of $G$. We are interested in the LP-relaxation of this parameter, which is called the fractional domatic number of $G$. We study its extremal value in the class of graphs of minimum degree $d$. The fractional domatic number of a graph of minimum degree $d$ is always at most $d+1$, and at least $(1-o(1))\, d/\ln d$ as $d\to \infty$. This is asymptotically tight even within the class of split graphs.
  Our main result concerns the case $d=2$; we show that, excluding $8$ exceptional graphs, the fractional domatic number of every connected graph of minimum degree (at least) $2$ is at least $5/2$. We also show that this bound cannot be improved if only finitely many graphs are excluded, even for bipartite graphs of arbitrarily large girth. This proves in a stronger sense a conjecture by Gadouleau, Harms, Mertzios, and Zamaraev (2024). This also extends and generalises results from McCuaig and Shepherd (1989), from Fujita, Kameda, and Yamashita (2000), and from Abbas, Egerstedt, Liu, Thomas, and Whalen (2016).
  Finally, we show that graphs of sub-exponential expansion and sufficiently large girth $g$ have fractional domatic number $3 - o_g(1)$.

title: Adaptive Microwave Reception with Diamond Spin Sensors
summary: In a diamond-spin microwave receiver, pilot measurements can identify the spin-control phase that best separates binary phase-shift keyed symbols. Applying that phase takes time, during which carrier drift can erase the gain in alignment. We derive an exact feedback-delay threshold for a single payload spin from the phase information in the pilot record. On a finite menu of control phases, the pilot record enters the minimum-error update decision only through the direction of its first circular moment when that moment is nonzero. This result motivates a controller that estimates the direction from orthogonal pilot measurements and retains the existing phase whenever the predicted gain is lost to diffusion. For finite spin ensembles, we bound the distinguishability of the photon-count distributions in terms of optical readout and carrier-phase uncertainty, including fluctuations shared across spins. Packet simulations at matched spin budgets show that gated feedback can improve reliability with a single readout channel. With independently readable quadratures and sufficient spin preparations, decision-directed software tracking achieves lower packet error without a hardware phase update.

title: Conditional Deep Levy Models for Exotic Derivatives: History-Aware Path Generation and P-Q Payoff Diagnostics
comments: 43 pages, 4 figures, 18 tables. Extended version of the paper accepted at ICAIF '26 (7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance)
summary:
We develop a history-aware equity-index path generator based on Denoising Levy Probabilistic Models (DLPMs) and evaluate its predictive distributions through path-dependent derivative payoffs. A conditional U-Net combines contract state, index identity, 60- and 252-day return histories, and financial regularization with coordinate-wise stable mixing. A matched experiment holds initialization, training data, batch order, objective, computational budget and evaluation checkpoint fixed while comparing $α=1.9$ with the Gaussian limit $α=2$. On 6,824 chronological windows from eight Chinese and U.S. indices, terminal CRPS falls from 0.050585 to 0.048031, a 5.05% reduction, and path energy improves by 4.03%. The paired 60-calendar-day CRPS interval is [-0.004022, -0.001298]. Coverage rises from 56.68% to 71.00% while the proper 90% interval score improves by 20.30%. Empirical references remain competitive: the full-pool terminal control attains CRPS 0.047566.
  A common P-Q protocol translates the forecasts into vanilla, Asian and floating-strike lookback outcomes against an independent martingale-corrected Student-t GARCH benchmark. With quote-error filtering and a fixed-state initial Delta hedge, the matched Lookback difference is 0.285% of initial spot, with a 60-day interval [0.061%, 0.489%]. The evaluation also applies the same recorded ensembles to accumulator and snowball scenarios. These contracts expose different responses of early termination and downside cashflows to the noise specification. The study connects conditional historical path generation, a controlled stability-parameter comparison, empirical forecasting references, and payoff-sensitive derivative evaluation.
comment: 43 pages, 4 figures, 18 tables. Extended version of the paper accepted at ICAIF '26 (7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance)

title: Binding Constraints in a Strategic Technology: An Industrial Vulnerability Index for the Foundation Model Industry
summary: Industrial policy directed at artificial intelligence has become substantial. Public investment concentrates on compute, where private capacity expansion is already underway, and is largely absent from grid interconnection and generation. Whether that allocation accurately reflects the most binding constraint in production has not yet been systematically measured. This paper introduces the Artificial Intelligence Industrial Vulnerability Index (AIIVI) as a framework for assessing potential production constraints in frontier AI. We construct a composite index of input vulnerability for the foundation model industry from fourteen concentration and sustainability parameters, aggregated by an O-Ring functional form in which capability is strongly influenced by the most constrained input. AIIVI should not be interpreted as a direct measurement of production constraints. Rather, it provides an index-based approximation derived from observable indicators and weighting assumptions designed to capture relative exposure to input vulnerabilities. Using this transparent and reproducible framework for estimating the relative vulnerability of frontier AI production to disruptions across key input dimensions, we also evaluate the index at 31 August 2026 for the nine developers at the capability frontier. We find values of 0.75 under AI-elicited weights and 0.62 under equal weights. The analysis identifies compute and energy as the principal drivers of input vulnerability. Marginal changes in these dimensions produce substantially larger variations in AIIVI than comparable changes in capital, talent, or data. We highlight three exposures that receive limited attention in existing assessment frameworks: the increasing reliance on external debt for data-centre financing, local opposition as a constraint on data-centre siting, and export controls targeting deployed AI models rather than hardware.

title: Generalized Guarantees for Variational Inference in the Presence of Even and Elliptical Symmetry
summary: Variational inference (VI) approximates a target density $p$ by the best match $q$ in a family $\mathcal Q$ of tractable distributions. The variational approximation is found by minimizing a divergence, most commonly the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence $\text{KL}(q||p)$, although other divergences can be considered. In practice, $p \notin \mathcal Q$ and so the optimal variational approximation is misspecified. Despite this misspecification, it was recently shown that the minimizer of $\text{KL}(q||p)$ is guaranteed to recover the mean in the presence of even symmetry and likewise the correlation matrix in the presence of elliptical symmetry for a log-concave target $p$. We extend this result in several directions. First, we relax the assumption of log-concavity and instead merely require $p$ to be unimodal, allowing for heavy-tailed targets. Second, we obtain guarantees for cases where $p$ exhibits symmetry along some but not all of its coordinates. These partial symmetries arise naturally in Bayesian hierarchical models, where the prior induces a challenging geometry but still possesses axes of symmetry. Third, we extend these guarantees to $f$-divergences, a broad class which includes the forward and reverse-KL divergences and the $α$-divergences.

title: Fast Queries of Fibered Barcodes
comments: 45 pages, 10 figures; see also earlier preprint arXiv:1512.00180; to appear in Foundations of Computational Mathematics
summary: The fibered barcode $\mathcal{F}(M)$ of a bipersistence module $M$ is the map sending each non-negatively sloped affine line $\ell \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ to the barcode of the restriction of $M$ along $\ell$. The simplicity, computability, and stability of $\mathcal{F}(M)$ make it a natural choice of invariant for data analysis applications. In an earlier preprint [arXiv:1512.00180], we introduced a framework for real-time interactive visualization of $\mathcal{F}(M)$, which allows the user to select a single line $\ell$ via a GUI and then plots the associated barcode. This visualization is a key feature of our software RIVET for the visualization and analysis of bipersistent homology. Such interactive visualization requires a framework for efficient queries of $\mathcal{F}(M)$, i.e., for quickly obtaining the barcode along a given line $\ell$. To enable such queries, we introduced a novel data structure based on planar line arrangements, called an augmented arrangement. The aim of the present paper is to give an updated and improved exposition of the parts of our preprint [arXiv:1512.00180] concerning the mathematics of the augmented arrangement and its computation. Notably, by taking the input to be a minimal presentation rather than a chain complex, we are able to substantially simplify our main algorithm and its complexity analysis.
comment: 45 pages, 10 figures; see also earlier preprint arXiv:1512.00180; to appear in Foundations of Computational Mathematics

title: Statistical Inference for Fuzzy Clustering
summary:
Clustering is a central tool in biomedical research for discovering heterogeneous patient subpopulations, where group boundaries are often diffuse rather than sharply separated. While soft clustering methods such as fuzzy $c$-means (FCM) allow mixed memberships, principled statistical inference for fuzzy clustering remains limited.
  We propose a weighted fuzzy $c$-means (WFCM) framework for settings with cluster-size imbalance. Cluster-specific weights $\mathbf{w}$ re-balance the classic FCM criterion to adjust the relative influence of clusters of unequal size, and we construct a normalized working density from the weighted objective with scale parameter $σ$ and fuzziness parameter $m$. Estimation is performed via FCM-style alternating initialization followed by numerical likelihood refinement; the intractable normalizing constant is approximated by importance sampling using a data-adaptive Gaussian-mixture as the proposal distribution. We further develop bootstrap-based confidence intervals.
  We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator, validate the method in simulations, and illustrate it on single-cell RNA-seq, Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), and TCGA-BRCA data. These applications illustrate uncertainty quantification and interpretable soft memberships, ranging from imbalanced cell populations to graded compatibility with AD-like and non-AD-like prototypes.

title: On Approximate Computation of Critical Points
summary: We show that computing even coarse approximations of critical points is intractable for simple classes of nonconvex functions. We first present a family of $n$-variate cubic polynomials with coefficients in $\{-1,0,1\}$ that have exact critical points but for which no polynomial-time algorithm can write down a $\sqrt{n}/4$-approximate critical point in its standard representation. We then show that computational hardness persists when an exact critical point has a short representation. More specifically, we prove that for every fixed $η>0$, unless P $=$ NP, no polynomial-time (or even pseudo-polynomial-time) algorithm can take an $n$-variate cubic polynomial with rational coefficients ${c_α}$ and return a point with gradient norm at most $(\max_α|c_α|)n^{1/2-η}$ whenever the polynomial has a critical point in $\{-1,0,1\}^n$. The algorithm may return an arbitrary point on all other inputs. Both results are essentially tight in their dependence on the dimension $n$. We also prove hardness results for lower-bounded functions and for an alternative notion of approximation, in which approximation is measured by distance to an exact critical point. Overall, our results stand in contrast to the commonly held belief that, in nonconvex optimization, approximate computation of critical points is a tractable task.

title: Instance-optimal high-precision shadow tomography with few-copy measurements: A metrological approach
comments: 69 pages; several technical errors from the earlier version fixed including the wrong order of optimization over measurements and references states; key messages remain unchanged
summary:
We study the sample complexity of shadow tomography in the high-precision regime under realistic measurement constraints. Given an unknown $d$-dimensional quantum state $ρ$ and a known set of observables $\{O_i\}_{i=1}^m$, the goal is to estimate expectation values $\{\mathrm{tr}(O_iρ)\}_{i=1}^m$ to accuracy $ε$ in $L_p$-norm, using possibly adaptive measurements that act on $O(\mathrm{polylog}(d))$ number of copies of $ρ$ at a time. We focus on the regime where $ε$ is below an instance-dependent threshold.
  Our main contribution is an instance-optimal characterization of the sample complexity as $\tildeΘ(Γ_p/ε^2)$, where $Γ_p$ is a function of $\{O_i\}_{i=1}^m$ defined via an optimization formula involving the inverse Fisher information matrix. Previously, tight bounds were known only in special cases, e.g. Pauli shadow tomography with $L_\infty$-norm error. Concretely, we first analyze a simpler oblivious variant where the goal is to estimate an observable of the form $\sum_{i=1}^m α_i O_i$ with $\|α\|_q = 1$ (where $q$ is dual to $p$) revealed after the measurement. For single-copy measurements, we obtain a sample complexity of $Θ(Γ^{\mathrm{ob}}_p/ε^2)$. We then show $\tildeΘ(Γ_p/ε^2)$ is necessary and sufficient for the original problem, with the lower bound applying to unbiased, kurtosis-bounded estimators when $p \geq 1$. Our upper bounds rely on a two-step algorithm combining coarse tomography with local estimation. Notably, $Γ^{\mathrm{ob}}_\infty = Γ_\infty$. In both cases, allowing $c$-copy measurements improves the sample complexity by at most $Ω(1/c)$.
  Our results establish a quantitative correspondence between quantum learning and metrology, unifying asymptotic metrological limits with finite-sample learning guarantees.
comment: 69 pages; several technical errors from the earlier version fixed including the wrong order of optimization over measurements and references states; key messages remain unchanged

title: ProFed: Projection-Guided Personalized Federated Learning for Low-Dose CT Denoising
summary: Low-dose computed tomography (CT) reduces radiation exposure but introduces noise and artifacts whose appearance depends on acquisition conditions. Federated learning enables collaborative restoration without centrally pooling images, yet variation in anatomy and scanning protocols complicates learning a shared denoiser. We present ProFed, a personalized federated framework that combines image-domain feature modulation with projection-domain supervision. Anatomy and protocol descriptors condition a shared encoder--decoder, while differentiable forward-projection, backprojection, and cycle-consistency losses encourage agreement with client-local measurements. An uncertainty-weighted aggregation rule combines shared parameters and retains anatomy-specific heads locally. Following the SCAN-PhysFed benchmark, we train on eight Mayo Clinic patients and evaluate two held-out patients under eight known acquisition protocols. ProFed achieves protocol-averaged PSNR of 42.56~dB with RED-CNN and 44.83~dB with Uformer, exceeding SCAN-PhysFed by 1.42~dB and 1.18~dB, respectively. Per-protocol measurements and qualitative comparisons show both improvements and remaining failure cases. The results support projection-guided supervision as a promising component of federated image restoration within this controlled setting; independent deployment validation and larger multi-institutional studies remain necessary.

title: Differential Privacy for Network Connectedness Indices
comments: Code to replicate all of our analyses is available at: https://github.com/TomRutter42/Privacy-for-Connectedness-Indices
summary: Researchers increasingly use data on social and economic networks to study a range of social science questions, but releasing statistics derived from networks can raise significant privacy concerns. We show how to release network connectedness indices that quantify assortative mixing across node attributes under edge-adjacent differential privacy. Directly adding noise to connectedness indices based on global sensitivity can result in poor accuracy both because connectedness indices have high global sensitivity and because a single node's attribute can potentially be an input to connectedness in thousands of cells, leading to poor composition. Our method, which is straightforward to apply, first randomizes node attributes, then analytically debiases downstream statistics, and finally adds noise to protect the presence or absence of individual edges. We prove consistency and asymptotic normality of our estimators for both discrete and continuous labels and show our method works well in simulations and on real networks with as few as 200 nodes collected by social scientists.
comment: Code to replicate all of our analyses is available at: https://github.com/TomRutter42/Privacy-for-Connectedness-Indices

title: Subword enumeration up to stack-sorting equivalence
comments: 17 pages; minor corrections; formatted for DMTCS
summary: Defant and Kravitz introduced generalizations of West's stack-sorting map $s$ from permutations to finite words. This raises questions as to how such generalizations could be applied in the field of combinatorics on words. The Defant-Kravitz generalizations of $s$ depend on how repeated occurrences of the same character within a word may be repositioned, according to their $\textsf{tortoise}$ and $\textsf{hare}$ operations. As demonstrated in this paper, these operations provide a natural way of extending abelian complexity functions for infinite sequences, in a way that gives light to structural properties associated with infinite words. We apply these new ideas to two famous infinite words: the paperfolding word and the Thue-Morse word. In the case of the Thue-Morse word, we discover an interesting connection to the previous work of several authors, such as de Luca and Varricchio, on the ``special'' factors of the Thue-Morse word. This may be seen as providing a basis for a new and interdisciplinary area linking the combinatorics about the stack-sorting of permutations with the field of combinatorics on words.
comment: 17 pages; minor corrections; formatted for DMTCS

title: Jacobian-Velocity Bounds for Deployment Risk Under Covariate Drift
summary: We study long-horizon deployment of a frozen predictor under dynamic covariate shift. A time-domain Poincaré inequality first reduces temporal risk volatility to derivative energy, and a Jacobian-velocity theorem supplies the corresponding pathwise control. A remainder extension separates the model-mediated, controllable term from conditional-risk variation not transmitted through the score Jacobian. Under low-rank drift, the bound decomposes the controllable term into tangent energy parallel and orthogonal to the drift subspace. This motivates drift-aligned tangent regularization (DTR), its anisotropic extension with a weaker orthogonal guardrail, and a matched monitoring proxy. Controlled experiments verify the temporal inequality, the efficiency of directional smoothing, and the necessity of the remainder term. The main field study uses a 128-dimensional gas-sensor array over ten chronological batches. A rank-4 basis estimated entirely before deployment beats ten matched random subspaces, and validation-selected anisotropic DTR improves deployment cross-entropy and volatility over pure DTR in all ten matched seeds while retaining substantially more accuracy than isotropic smoothing. Air Quality and power-consumption studies provide complementary regression evidence. Together, the results support a precise design rule: concentrate smoothness along expected motion, and use limited orthogonal smoothing when the estimated drift subspace may be incomplete.

title: Robust stochastic first order methods in heavy-tailed noise via medoid mini-batch gradient sampling
summary: We consider a first order stochastic optimization framework where, at each iteration, $K$ independent identically distributed (i.i.d.) data point samples are drawn, based on which stochastic gradients can be queried. We allow gradient noise to be heavy-tailed, with possibly infinite variances. For the considered heavy-tailed setting, many algorithmic variants have recently been proposed based on gradient clipping or other nonlinear operators (e.g., normalization) applied over noisy gradients. In this paper, we take an alternative approach and propose a novel gradient estimator. The core idea of proposed estimator is to split the $K$-sized data batch into $M$ distinct data chunks, form for each chunk the stochastic gradient, and select the stochastic gradient of the chunk that is medoid of gradients of all data-chunks. For a broad class of symmetric heavy-tailed gradient noise distributions, we show that the proposed estimator has a finite second moment even when the underlying gradient noise has an infinite second moment. For nonconvex objectives, this yields convergence to a neighborhood of zero in expected squared gradient norm at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1})$. We explicitly characterize the size of this neighborhood in terms of the noise and algorithm parameters. When the time horizon $T$ is known in advance, we establish an $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$ convergence rate. A diminishing step size achieves the same rate up to a logarithmic factor. Incorporating clipping or a more general nonlinear transformation yields high-probability convergence guarantees with the same rate up to logarithmic factors. Experimental results indicate that R-SGD-Mini and its clipped or nonlinear variant consistently perform favorably compared to SGD, clipped SGD, Nonlinear SGD and Median-of-Means based methods.

title: Minimum-Length Permutation-Invariant Qudit Codes from Edge-Colorings of Complete Graphs
comments: 17 pages, 1 figure. Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Information Theory. Added a self-contained proof of the minimum block length, expanded the discussion of physical motivation and prior work, and improved the exposition
summary: We study permutation-invariant quantum codes in the symmetric subspace $\mathrm{Sym}^n(\mathbb{C}^q)$ of $n$ qudits of local dimension $q$. For every integer $q\ge 2$, we construct a permutation-invariant code with parameters $((4,q,2))_q$. Thus four physical qudits suffice to encode one logical qudit with distance two in the symmetric sector for every local dimension. We also show, using a self-contained decoupling and rank argument, that no permutation-invariant code of dimension $q$ and distance at least $2$ exists in $\mathrm{Sym}^n(\mathbb{C}^q)$ for $n\le 3$. Hence four qudits are necessary and sufficient. The construction has simple representation-theoretic and combinatorial descriptions. On $\mathrm{Sym}^4(\mathbb{C}^q)$, the distance-two Knill--Laflamme conditions split into root and Cartan parts. By restricting supports to the even-entry occupation layer, all root-error conditions vanish automatically. The remaining Cartan conditions reduce to linear balancing constraints on packets of occupation vectors. These packets admit a natural graph-theoretic interpretation in terms of the vertices and edges of the complete graph $K_q$: for odd $q$, they are organized by the midpoint rule, while for even $q$, they are organized by a decomposition of $K_q$ into perfect matchings. In this way, the existence of minimum-length $((4,q,2))_q$ permutation-invariant codes is reduced to a parity-dependent edge-coloring problem on $K_q$.
comment: 17 pages, 1 figure. Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Information Theory. Added a self-contained proof of the minimum block length, expanded the discussion of physical motivation and prior work, and improved the exposition

title: qshap: Fast Shapley Decomposition of $R^2$ for Gradient-Boosted Trees
summary: Numerous methods have been developed to quantify feature attributions in individual predictions for tree ensembles. However, many applications require global measures of feature contributions to overall model performance. Although local attribution scores can be aggregated to characterize feature importance, such summaries do not directly decompose measures of predictive performance, such as $R^2$. This article introduces qshap, available in both R and Python, which provides Shapley decomposition of $R^2$ values for gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) to quantify feature-specific contributions to model performance. By decomposing the quadratic loss of individual observations, qshap provides flexible tools to explore the importance of individual features and observations. qshap currently supports widely used GBDT implementations, including xgboost, lightgbm, and catboost, through a unified tree representation and efficient C++ backends. Its modular design can accommodate other GBDT implementations built from binary decision trees. In addition, we introduce a specialized backend for oblivious trees that exploits their symmetric structure to substantially accelerate computation.

title: On the exact discretization of the $L_2$-norm in spaces generated by Rademacher functions and their $p$-adic analogues
summary: Sufficient conditions for the exact discretization of the $L_2$-norm in the space spanned by generalized Rademacher functions are proved. It is shown that the sufficient number of nodes for discretization with the minimal number of nodes is equal to $N$ or $N+1$ and depends on the dimension $N$. The conjecture of F.~Dai, A.~Prymak, V.~N.~Temlyakov, and S.~Yu.~Tikhonov on the positivity of weights in the exact discretization of the $L_2$-norm with a minimal number of points considered. It was investigated in which cases it holds and in which it fails for the spaces spanned by the $N$ generalized Rademacher functions with base $p$, and how the validity of the conjecture in this case depends on the parameters $p$ and $N$. The connection with generalized Hadamard matrices, the Hadamard's conjecture and Seberry's conjecture is demonstrated.

title: AutoXRD: Autonomous Large Language Model Agents and Comprehensive Evaluation for Powder X-Ray Diffraction Analysis
summary: Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) is a foundational technique for structural and phase characterization in materials science, yet automating its analysis and evaluating it end-to-end remains challenging. Doing so requires an agent to interpret diffraction patterns, run refinement software, manage strongly coupled parameters in a physically meaningful order, and assess both numerical fit quality and physical validity. We propose AutoXRD, an LLM agent framework that organizes powder XRD analysis into refinement stages, uses diffraction diagnostics to select actions, and checks the resulting fits against crystallographic and physical criteria. We further introduce XRDBench with two complementary tracks. XRDBench-QA contains 100 tasks assessing scientific reasoning and decision-making, whereas XRDBench-E2E contains 34 end-to-end workflows requiring data interpretation, crystallographic software execution, iterative refinement, evidence preservation, and reporting. Across 1,340 runs of ten recent LLMs, models average only 57.8 out of 100, falling from 61.9 on XRDBench-QA to 53.7 on XRDBench-E2E. At the task level, they perform best on refinement-history assessment and result acceptance, but remain substantially weaker on refinement-action selection, phase quantification, indexing, and Rietveld refinement. Among individual models, GPT-5.6 Sol achieves the highest overall score of 81.1, GPT-5.6 Terra scores highest on XRDBench-E2E (81.0), and GPT-5.6 Luna provides the best score-cost trade-off. Moreover, ablations confirm that all six AutoXRD components consistently improve performance. Finally, execution-trace analysis reveals recurring failures in coupled-parameter control, quantitative reasoning, evidence preservation, and workflow termination, motivating stronger scientific constraints, uncertainty quantification, and more efficient planning.

title: Beyond Point Forecasts: A Survey on Probabilistic Forecasting for Time Series and Spatiotemporal Data
comments: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (11/2026). OpenReview version available at https://openreview.net/forum?id=F140ECa1HO
summary: Probabilistic forecasting is central to decision-making under uncertainty, yet its methodological landscape has become increasingly fragmented across temporal and spatiotemporal forecasting, statistical modeling, machine learning, and deep generative modeling. This survey develops a unified perspective by organizing probabilistic forecasting methods according to where and how uncertainty is introduced into the forecasting pipeline. Our taxonomy connects model-agnostic approaches including ensembles and distribution-free calibration, with model-intrinsic approaches spanning Bayesian modeling, parametric predictive distributions, distributional regression, and modern generative models, and further examines the emerging role of time series foundation models. Beyond methodological synthesis, we identify the assumptions, computational demands, and forms of uncertainty represented by different paradigms, and translate these distinctions into data-driven and domain-specific guidance for method selection. We complement the survey with a cross-paradigm empirical study on univariate, multivariate, and spatiotemporal forecasting tasks. The results reveal that no single uncertainty-quantification paradigm dominates across settings. Calibration, sharpness, predictive accuracy, and computational efficiency can lead to substantially different model preferences, while expressive generative models and zero-shot foundation models exhibit markedly different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. Lastly, we identify unresolved challenges surrounding uncertainty in evolving dependency structures, physics-informed predictive distributions, forecasting extreme events, handling count-valued, directional, and continuous-time series, and the development of unified software resources. Our survey provides both a conceptual framework and a practical roadmap for probabilistic forecasting research.
comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (11/2026). OpenReview version available at https://openreview.net/forum?id=F140ECa1HO

title: Log-concavity and Approximate Counting for Totally Unimodular Polytopes
summary: We present a new lower bound on the number of lattice points of all totally unimodular polytopes, generalizing previous lower bounds on contingency tables, integer flows, and beyond. Our bound is based on the Gurvits capacity convex optimization problem, and thus our result implies an efficient deterministic algorithm for approximate counting of the lattice points up to an explicit exponential factor. We achieve our bounds by showing that the associated generating polynomials fit into a new general class of log-concave polynomials called VLC ("variable-wise log-concavity''). This also implies a conjecture of Ferroni and Higashitani on the evaluations of the Ehrhart polynomials of unimodular polytopes. The essential ingredient for these results is the resolution of Barvinok's log-concavity conjecture for contingency tables on lines, which was proven using ChatGPT 6 Astra. We conjecture a generalization of Barvinok's conjecture, which we believe will lead to stronger and more general bounds.

title: Learning joint predictive distributions from observations with coordinate-aware covariance bounds
comments: 80 pages (main text 37 pages, supplementary information 43 pages)
summary: Quantifying uncertainty in derived quantities requires forecasts that capture cross-variable dependence. From station observations alone, CLARA predicts the mean and full covariance of a Gaussian joint distribution in one forward pass per lead, trains on a CPU and recalibrates the covariance without altering correlations. On two nationwide Korean weather networks, ten regions on six continents and a nationwide air-quality network, CLARA outperforms learned comparators in lead-mean energy score, by 5.2-5.5% against comparably sized iTransformers with the same temporal-phase inputs on the Korean networks, with gains that persist in two held-out seasons. We prove that the same lower bound on the Cholesky diagonal admits different covariances in different output coordinates. Changing only these coordinates lowers the pressure-difference continuous ranked probability score by 40-67%, lets the learned correlations outperform a fixed correlation matrix in joint likelihood at every lead and, on an electricity grid, improves the joint likelihood with two other backbones.
comment: 80 pages (main text 37 pages, supplementary information 43 pages)

title: $\mathsf{EFI}\Leftrightarrow\mathsf{1PRS}$
summary: A series of recent works has established EFI pairs as the "minimal" assumption for quantum cryptography. Recently, Cavalar et al. [CCC+26] showed that EFI pairs are equivalent to non-uniform expanding single-copy pseudorandom state generators (1PRS), and obtained a non-uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs. We remove the non-uniformity in their construction and prove that EFI pairs are equivalent to expanding 1PRS. As a corollary, we obtain the first uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs. Together with the equivalence of statistically verifiable one-way state generators and commitments proved by Batra and Jain [BJ24], this gives a quantum analogue of the classical equivalence between one-way functions, commitments, and pseudorandom generators.

title: Superlinear Convergence of Cyclic Gradient Methods with Historical Ritz Step Sizes
summary: The long-step Barzilai-Borwein (BB1) method, cyclic BB1, and limited memory steepest descent (LMSD) are special cases of limited memory steepest descent with retards (LMSDR), a family of methods using historical Ritz step sizes. We analyze a cyclic Ritz-step rule within LMSDR and a sampled LMSDR variant on strictly convex quadratics, seeking R-superlinear convergence guarantees in higher spectral dimensions. Let $n$ be the problem dimension and $m$ the history length. In exact arithmetic, we begin at $n=m+1$, the first dimension beyond the finite-termination case, and obtain an exact doubly exponential rate per gradient update for rolling reuse outside an explicit, possibly empty exceptional set. We extend this rate to nonempty open sets for $m+1<n\le2m$ when each Ritz step is reused $\ell\ge4$ times. To go beyond this range, we rebuild the history with $m$ sampling updates at each cycle. With positive sampling steps $τ$ chosen in advance and factors $1-τλ_i$ uniformly bounded in modulus and away from zero, this gives almost-everywhere doubly exponential convergence when $(2\ell-1)^m>\binom{n-1}{m}$. For any $n>m$, increasing $\ell$ eventually satisfies this condition. Geometrically spaced choices among finitely many sampling lists preserve the guarantee.

title: Atom as an Agent: Emergent Order by Collective Predictive Coding
comments: 33 pages, 10 figures; v2: references and descriptions added, 34 pages
summary: What is the intrinsic reason of emergence of macroscopic order parameter out of microscopic systems? In this article, we apply to physics the collective predictive coding (CPC), the theory of language/symbol emergence. As our language emerges out of our human communications, physical macroscopic order parameter emerges out of communications among atoms --- each atom is regarded as an agent who predicts each other's behavior through inference. We present three examples of classical spin systems: two-dimensional ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, a two-dimensional spin model with competing stripe orders, and the fully connected Sherrington--Kirkpatrick spin-glass model. In all of these examples, proper macroscopic order parameters including the replica overlap emerge automatically through communication informatics of CPC, only from observed spin configurations. We call the learned macroscopic coordinate the collective predictive order. Furthermore, for the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, the equilibrium distribution of the collective predictive order yields an emergent potential with the symmetry and thermal evolution characteristic of a Landau potential. Notably, the emergence of the collective predictive order does not refer to any structure of microscopic Hamiltonians/Lagrangians. Thus our ``Atom-as-an-Agent" (AaaA) principle offers a completely data-driven method for the emergence of macroscopic order, that is, machine learning physics.
comment: 33 pages, 10 figures; v2: references and descriptions added, 34 pages

title: Confidence-Aware Speed-over-Ground Estimation from Doppler Spectra via Reconstruction-Based Representation Learning
summary: Reliable speed-over-ground estimation from ground-facing Doppler spectra is essential for mobile platforms such as railway systems. Classical signal-processing approaches can provide accurate estimates under favorable conditions, but often degrade in challenging conditions. We propose confidence-aware speed-over-ground estimation trained on rail-domain data that estimates speed over ground and frame-level confidence from Doppler spectra with several novel contributions: First, we transfer the idea of exploiting a reconstruction task by an autoencoder for performance estimation from previous work to Doppler RaDAR. Second, we append a speed-over-ground estimation head operating on the autoencoder's latent space features. Third, we omit the reconstruction decoder during inference but add a low-cost dedicated confidence head for frame-wise error-bound estimation. Fourth, we reveal how noise augmentation training can provide high robustness to the method. Experiments show that our approach improves speed estimation accuracy over classical baselines while providing informative confidence estimates that indicate the reliability of individual predictions, even under adverse signal conditions.

title: How many sorted projections determine any n points in k dimensions?
comments: 33 pages, 9 figures. v2: added word "any" to title, improved a bound following comment from ZM26, added three small special cases, removed unicode from an anc file, and added a statement about deep sets. v3: no new results, but many small text edits for clarity, and also added appendix with four new figures to aid in indexation of results. v4 text edits for clarity
summary: Let $d_1,\dots,d_m$ be directions in $\mathbb{R}^k$, where $k\ge 2$. A multiset $X$ of $n$ points of $\mathbb{R}^k$ projects to the $m$ multisets of numbers $\{\{x\cdot d_j : x\in X\}\}$, or equivalently to the $m$ sorted lists of these numbers. How many directions are needed for these projections to determine every multiset of $n$ points? Two simple bounds are known in every dimension: more than $(k-1)\log_2 n$ directions are always needed, and $(k-1)n+1$ directions in general position always suffice. In the plane much more is known: Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron showed that almost every choice of $O(\log n \log\log n)$ directions suffices. Whether anything similar holds in higher dimensions was left open by Dym, Wellershoff, Tsoukanis, Levy and Balan. We observe that two lemmas of Hair and Sahai, proved for list recovery of random linear codes, answer that question, and by tightening their argument we show that in every dimension almost every choice of $(4k-2)\ln(2n)\ln(k\log_2 2n)+k+1$ directions suffices. For $k\le 10$ this beats the linear bound once $n$ is larger than about 100: for example, 144 directions suffice for multisets of 1000 points in the plane, and an exact computation lowers this to 133. Letting some of the random blocks in their argument fail removes a factor $\log k$: almost every choice of $O(k\log n\log\log n)$ directions suffices, uniformly in $k$ and $n$. We also show that $2k-1$ directions never determine three points, so that the logarithmic lower bound is not tight; that every $m$ directions in the plane fail on some pair of multisets of size $O(1.65^m)$, improving the bound $O(1.80^m)$ of Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron; and that for each $k$, $m$ and $n$, either almost every choice of $m$ directions works or almost none does.

title: No free lattice contains an infinite ascending chain of copies of FL(3)
comments: 60 pages, 13 figures. The main theorem is checked in Agda; the formal development is https://github.com/ualib/agda-deans-problem at its tag v0.1.0, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24375155. v2: footnotes and a reference added; the formal development cited at its tag
summary:
No free lattice contains an infinite strictly ascending chain of sublattices isomorphic to FL(3), the free lattice on three generators; this answers a question that R. A. Dean asked and the second author's 1997 notes on the problem left open. Every such chain would yield, inside FL(3), a coherent chain of proper self-embeddings $Θ_0, Θ_1, Θ_2, \dots$ with $Θ_k \circ Θ_j = Θ_j$ for $j < k$, so that each later embedding fixes the image of each earlier one pointwise. Every proper self-embedding of FL(3) whose fixed sublattice contains a free generating triple fixes one of the three generators, say $z$, because a power of it or of its dual lies above the identity, and a self-embedding that moves every generator and lies above the identity fixes at most eleven elements. Up to duality, a proper self-embedding fixing the image of such a $Θ_1$ pointwise fixes only elements above $z \wedge (x \vee y)$, where no free generating triple containing $z$ can lie. We also verify the one-step example of the 1997 notes, prove that no step toward such a chain is self-similar, and show that the configuration the argument rules out at length three does occur at length two.
  Without freeness the answer reverses: FL(3) contains an infinite strictly ascending chain of 3-generated sublattices, so the lattice analogue of Takahasi's chain condition for free groups fails. The theorem itself is checked by the Agda proof assistant under its safe flags, for free lattices over generators with decidable equality, and its formal proof uses no classical principle: finite searches and an induction on a finite set replace the infinite pigeonhole principle by which a chain yields a coherent chain.

title: Observable Spectral Framework for Noisy Amplitude Amplification: Stopping Stability and Correction
comments: 64 pages (28 main text including references, 36 supplementary), 5 figures, 4 tables, 10 supplementary figures
summary: Stopping rules for noisy amplitude amplification often rely on channel-specific success-probability formulas, limiting their transfer across noise mechanisms. We develop an observable spectral framework for stationary noisy standard amplitude amplification with a known ideal success fraction, under explicit leading-mode, spectral-separation, and residual-control conditions. Within this class, the first amplification lobe has a damped-oscillatory leading component and a bounded non-leading contribution. We derive how frequency shift, damping, and observable phase offset displace the leading peak, and establish sampled-gap criteria for retaining the ideal integer stopping depth, certifying recalibration, or selecting a robust candidate window. In single-target Grover search, frequency and damping errors have stopping-coordinate sensitivities proportional to the search-space size, whereas phase offsets scale with its square root; residual modes can independently reverse the ordering of neighbouring depths. Analytical constructions, circuit simulations, finite-shot inference, and calibration-derived device-like trajectories examine these predictions and their operational limits. For a 64-element search, an a posteriori sampled-set check selects depth five over six, with success probability increasing from 0.595 to 0.626. The resulting theory links observable spectral dynamics to conditional integer stopping guarantees without requiring a separate microscopic channel solution.

title: Polynomial bounds for quasiplanar graphs
comments: This paper arose by merging arXiv:2611.01509, arXiv:2611.07314 and arXiv:2611.21416 and adding a new lower bound construction
summary:
A graph $G$ is $k$-quasiplanar if it can be drawn in the plane without $k$ pairwise crossing edges. It was a longstanding conjecture that $n$-vertex $k$-quasiplanar graphs have $O_k(n)$ edges. Recently, using AI tools, we discovered that a theorem in topology proven by Beeker and Lazarovich essentially resolves this conjecture, with the implicit constant depending superexponentially on $k$.
  In this paper, we greatly improve this bound, showing that every $k$-quasiplanar $n$-vertex graph has at most $O(k^2n)$ edges. Our proof is purely combinatorial, based on a geometric charging scheme and Erdős-Szekeres type arguments. We also construct $k$-quasiplanar graphs on $n$ vertices with $Ω(k^{8/7}n)$, disproving the widely held belief that the right order of magnitude is $Θ(kn)$.

title: MADJEPA: Enhanced Multi-Stage Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Medical Anomaly Detection
summary: Anomaly detection in medical images is a complex task, requiring the development of a robust model using only healthy patient data. Without access to labeled data, modern approaches typically employ self-supervised learning to obtain a model of normality. Since world models promise to build strong internal representations of their environment, we consider them as suitable candidates for the medical anomaly detection environment, namely medical investigations of healthy patients. To this end, we propose MADJEPA, a medical anomaly detector based on an enhanced multi-stage joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). We design a multi-stage training pipeline to produce a robust detector: (1) image-based JEPA (I-JEPA) training aims to learn a strong representation of normal training data; (2) target encoder distillation aims to modulate over-generalization of I-JEPA representations to abnormal data; (3) pseudo-anomaly classification aims to calibrate anomaly predictions by learning a tight boundary around the normal data manifold. To demonstrate our design, we carry out comprehensive experiments on six datasets covering various medical image domains (e.g. MRI, OCT, X-ray, histopathology), comparing our MADJEPA with numerous state-of-the-art methods. The results show that our carefully designed world model, MADJEPA, attains competitive results, ranking first on three datasets. Our ablation studies further confirm the utility of each training stage, indicating that I-JEPA alone is not sufficient to obtain competitive results in medical anomaly detection. We publicly release our code at https://github.com/Sabina085/madjepa.

title: Sparse Hodge Preference Optimization: Fine-Tuning Language Models toward Alignment beyond Transitive Preferences
summary: The growing adoption of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which leverages pairwise preference data, reflects its great success in fine-tuning large language models to align with human expectations. It directly optimizes the policy from human preferences without explicit reward modeling or the complexities of reinforcement learning-based approaches. However, the classic DPO relies on the Bradley--Terry sampling model and cannot effectively capture intransitivity or cyclic structures in aggregated human preference data. In this article, we propose Sparse Hodge Preference Optimization (SHPO), a preference optimization algorithm that augments DPO with a sparse antisymmetric curl residual motivated by the combinatorial Hodge decomposition. We prove that SHPO strictly enlarges DPO's hypothesis class on comparison graphs containing at least one triangle, under some mild regularity conditions on the response representations. We further establish a theoretical guarantee for $\ell_1$-regularized estimation of the curl coefficients under fixed policy and representations. Qualitative studies on three preference datasets under the same QLoRA budget, SHPO-aligned LLM achieves satisfactory performances in preference accuracy, cyclic structure recovery, and GPT-4o-judged generation quality.

title: Lorentz symmetry in self-supervised representation learning
summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) and explicit physical inductive biases have driven major advances in jet tagging, yet they are typically pursued along separate tracks. In this work, we unify both paradigms by integrating the Lorentz-equivariant Geometric Algebra Transformer slim (L-GATr-slim) architecture with the LeJEPA framework for representation learning. Pre-training on 100 million jets from the JetClass dataset, we optimize towards a latent space, which is invariant across physics-motivated jet augmentations. We demonstrate that enforcing Lorentz symmetry in the latent space is critical for representation quality and that this can be achieved either architecturally or learned via kinematic augmentations. With a standard non-invariant Transformer backbone, LeJEPA outperforms established autoregressive, masked particle modelling, and self-distillation baselines in linear- and MLP-probe accuracy, with L-GATr-slim providing further complementary gains. Across downstream benchmarks, our pre-trained models consistently outperform baselines trained from scratch or through different pre-training objectives.

title: GeoCANO: A Geometry-Conditioned Adaptive Neural Operator for Physical-Field Prediction on Varying Domains
summary: Industrial design requires repeated evaluation of candidate configurations. Integral performance measures alone do not resolve critical local phenomena, while high-fidelity simulation remains costly. Existing physical-field surrogates often couple geometry representation and coordinate evaluation through prescribed mesh topologies, limiting reuse across resolutions. We propose the Geometry-Conditioned Adaptive Neural Operator (GeoCANO), which maps a sampled complete three-dimensional geometry to a coordinate-dependent field function. An attention-based encoder extracts a geometry state from unordered surface coordinates. A multiresolution axis-factorized hash encoding and query-wise sparse mixture-of-experts decoder enhance multiscale expressiveness. GeoCANO constructs the field representation before introducing output coordinates, allowing one geometry encoding to be reused across regions without rebuilding the graph for each output topology. We evaluated GeoCANO on transonic aerodynamic-field prediction over complete aircraft configurations using a Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes dataset of 10,484 wing-body-nacelle geometries. For unseen configurations within the sampled design family, GeoCANO outperformed baselines in complete-surface prediction, high-gradient pressure reconstruction, and pressure-drag recovery. It reduced pressure-coefficient mean absolute error by 77.9% relative to the strongest baseline and retained an advantage over a finite range of wall-normal distances. Ablation studies showed that geometry-modulated coordinate encoding achieved comparable accuracy with substantially fewer parameters than conventional three-dimensional hash encoding. Routing analysis indicated spatially structured, query-dependent expert specialization. These results demonstrate a reusable continuous-coordinate representation for rapid physical-field evaluation over varying geometries.

title: InterGS+: Inter-Frame Gaussian Splatting Compression with Geometry-Aware Transformer Prediction and Adaptive Residual Coding
comments: Accepted for poster presentation at the 2027 Data Compression Conference (DCC 2027)
summary: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides real-time photorealistic rendering, but representing each frame as irregular Gaussian primitives with high-dimensional attributes creates substantial storage and transmission cost. Exploiting temporal redundancy is challenging because Gaussian primitives do not preserve fixed identities across frames. We propose InterGS+, a lightweight post-hoc inter-frame codec that jointly improves temporal prediction and residual representation. Current-frame geometry is coded with G-PCC and reconstructed before prediction, enabling consistent temporal neighborhoods at encoder and decoder. Attributes are predicted using lightweight KNN and bilateral predictors together with a geometry-aware transformer for spherical-harmonic (SH) appearance, with per-Gaussian mode selection. Residual coding is adapted to each attribute: SH innovations are coded in a shared PCA domain using vector quantization with refinement, opacity and scale in activated gamma-companded domains, and rotation as canonicalized quaternion innovations using vector quantization and refinement. On MPEG dynamic sequences, InterGS+ achieves average BD-rate reductions of 45.48% over G-PCC Amd. 1 and 7.78% over InterGS-Lite, with corresponding BD-PSNR gains of 9.98 dB and 1.10 dB. Average decoding complexity is 0.049 ms/Gaussian, demonstrating efficient streamable dynamic 3DGS compression.
